summary: No established statistical data exists for additive-manufactured metals to meet MMPDS requirements, forcing expensive destructive testing (100 samples from 10 heats at $2M+ per material system) before aerospace qualification.
verbatim: You have to have a hundred samples from 10 different lots and statistically average these. You have to have that data before you can ever put it in an aircraft. So just because you can make a part, do you really want to make a hundred of them at twenty thousand dollars a piece, to tear up and measure and throw away, before you can actually put one in an aircraft?

summary: Real-time or faster chemical composition measurement during BOP refining could unlock millions in productivity gains.
verbatim: If you got a faster way to do the chemical analysis, or if you could do it in situ... This facility is turning out steel at a value of $4 million an hour. A few minutes is worth a lot of money.

summary: No systematic understanding exists of how manufacturing tolerance stack-up and housing flexibility interact to produce closed conformity in large slender bearings.
verbatim: The thing that gives the shape to the bearing is the swashplate aluminum housing... There was no way to go back and prove what happened to this aluminum housing.

summary: Develop automated or improved detection method for flaws in the final 18 inches of seamless pipe that currently relies on manual magnetic particle inspection.
verbatim: Since they can't measure the last 18 inches where they grab it, they have a bunch of lowly paid employees — most of them can't speak English as a first language — doing magnetic particle testing by hand... it's not automated, and sometimes people will miss something.

summary: Measure and characterize the potato-chip (saddle-shaped) distortion of aluminum swash plate housings and how it couples to bearing performance under high-speed helicopter rotor loads.
verbatim: If I'm getting different shaped barrels in each quadrant, that means my aluminum housing is potato-chipped. A potato chip is a saddle shape. It's not circular.

summary: Develop or validate a non-destructive inspection method that can reliably detect flaws between one-sixteenth and one-eighth inch, the size range where detection probability currently drops below acceptable thresholds.
verbatim: The Air Force did a big study, and you can't find flaws with more than 50% accuracy at a sixteenth of an inch. You have like a 95% probability of finding a flaw at an eighth of an inch.

summary: Empirical measurement of actual lightning strike impedance behavior on flexible gas tubing installations under realistic residential conditions.
verbatim: It's only in the last three months they've added the word 'impedance' to their vocabulary. That's because I've been telling them what impedance is for three years, so they finally learned.

summary: The quantitative relationship between defect type, size, and location in carbon nanotubes and their resulting strength degradation has not been systematically measured or modeled.
verbatim: I can take a sheet of paper — you'll see me doing this on the History Channel when I talk about the Titanic — and pull on that piece of paper with pounds of force. But if I put a flaw in, that takes ounces.

summary: Ultra-fine-grain alloys stabilized by solubility and diffusivity constraints (like Schuh's nickel-tungsten) should have excellent forming characteristics, but the mechanical window before grain growth is poorly defined and requires characterization.
verbatim: Some of those alloys should have excellent forming characteristics in certain temperature ranges. But you have to do your mechanical shearing before the grains get so big that they lose their elongation capability.

summary: Fresh plasma-cutting fume composition differs from aged fume, but standard measurement protocols collect and age fume before analysis, masking the actual hexavalent chromium exposure a welder breathes.
verbatim: Most people don't measure fresh fume, which is what a welder or operator will breathe. They collect the fume, wait a month to ship it to the lab, and analyze it when it's been exposed all that time — so they get bad results.

summary: Direct measurement of electrode-tip temperature profiles in GTAW shows unexpected surface cooling, but the underlying physics of this electron-cooling phenomenon needs systematic investigation.
verbatim: People put pyrometers on the electrode in gas tungsten arc welding, and if they measure — temperature versus distance — they find it's very hot, and then it actually cools off at the surface where the electrons are coming out. The electrons cool the tip of the electrode, and they heat the surface of the anode as a result.

summary: Characterize the precise depth-dependent thermal and stress profiles for laser versus electron beam surface hardening to explain the critical difference in residual stress sign at the surface.
verbatim: Both high-intensity processes, but because one has high-energy particles and the other doesn't, you get slightly different heating patterns. Only about four-thousandths of an inch, a tenth of a millimeter difference, but it makes a world of difference.

summary: Develop a non-destructive testing technique better than the current 2% thickness sensitivity limit, which misses defects smaller than 3/16 inch in 8-inch sections.
verbatim: most of your non-destructive test techniques can see something about 2% of the thickness. So if you have 2% sensitivity on something that's 8 inches thick, the smallest defect you're going to find is about 3/16 of an inch.

summary: Thin titanium sheets used in modern aircraft exhibit significantly higher fracture toughness than the plane-strain values used in submarine design specifications, suggesting a mismatch between design assumptions and actual material behavior.
verbatim: Titanium sheets, if you go back, have a much higher toughness. The thin titanium sheets we put on fancy aircraft now have a much higher toughness than the plane strain fracture toughness.

summary: Measure the rate and extent of surface flaw initiation on glass fibers as a function of humidity exposure time to quantify the corrosion kinetics.
verbatim: If I want to make something out of good fiberglass, I've got to make my glass fibers and coat them with that plastic within an hour or two, or I'm going to lose most of the strength of those fibers... But once the humidity attacks them, then I have little surface flaws, and fracture mechanics tells me I'm going to have lousy strength.

summary: Long-term moisture resistance of adhesives in engineered composites is poorly documented beyond 3–4 years despite aerospace and marine applications requiring 10–20 year durability.
verbatim: You can get plenty of things that are good for three or four years, but not everybody likes their whole thing to delaminate, just like the Qantas airline reinforced composites.

summary: Develop a non-destructive or economical method to distinguish conflict diamonds from non-conflict diamonds, since current destructive testing is uneconomical.
verbatim: It's pretty hard to tell the difference between a conflict diamond and a non-conflict diamond. There are actually some ways, but you have to do some destructive testing on the diamond, and that's not very economical.

summary: Need systematic characterization of how corrugated stainless steel tubing responds to lightning perforation and internal ignition in residential gas lines.
verbatim: if you have lightning come through — if you live in Florida, which is lightning alley... you get hit by lightning, and you can perforate this, and now you have a flamethrower in your wall, in the interior of your house.

summary: Rapid chemical composition analysis of molten steel remains a bottleneck; five-minute analysis to 0.01% precision on all alloying elements would unlock significant profit.
verbatim: Can you get a detailed analysis of steel in five minutes, from molten steel, to a hundredth of a percent of all your alloying elements? Because you're talking about a hundred thousand dollars an hour of profit in this vessel. Minutes count.

summary: Develop detection methods for subsurface hydrogen-induced microcracks smaller than eighth-inch that evade standard non-destructive testing in high-strength welds.
verbatim: The inspectors look for flaws an eighth of an inch in size or larger, and they found none in the welds... they came in and did more thorough non-destructive testing — and all the welds, 18 percent of the hull had been completed, all the welds were full of little microscopic cracks they had never seen before.

summary: The critical flaw size in corroded glass fibers is on the order of angstroms to tens of angstroms, but direct measurement and mapping of these hydroxide etch pits as a function of exposure time and humidity is absent.
verbatim: if you go through the fracture toughness of this glass... calculate the minimum flaw size — it's like 10⁻⁴ millimeters. We're talking angstroms of critical flaw size, or tens of angstroms. You don't have to have very much corrosion.

summary: Quantify how quickly oxide layers form on freshly fractured aluminum surfaces under various atmospheric conditions to inform 3D printing and welding process design.
verbatim: Does anyone know how long it takes for the oxide to form on a piece of aluminum? Out of sight: about 10 nanoseconds, 10 to the minus 8 seconds... If you're going to do 3D printing, you can reduce the pressure to a high-vacuum atmosphere, but then you have to do all your 3D printing in one second to avoid oxide formation.

summary: Nobody has successfully measured the tensile strength of individual carbon nanotubes under controlled conditions.
verbatim: There's the Bob Spray quote that material scientists know it's defects that control properties. A perfect carbon nanotube would have a strength of 3 million psi, but does anyone know of anyone who's ever measured that? How do you grip a little carbon nanotube to measure tensile strength?

summary: Develop or improve non-destructive inspection techniques capable of reliably detecting flaws smaller than 2 mm in deep, narrow holes (10 inches deep, 0.25 inch diameter) in spinning centrifuge discs.
verbatim: You had to inspect this thing — it was about 10 inches deep. It's only a quarter-inch hole, but it was about 10 inches deep. How do you get in there to inspect it?

summary: Quantify the relationship between atomic-scale surface roughness and bonding strength in ultra-clean metal pairs under pressure.
verbatim: But on an atomic scale, you actually have some surface roughness.

summary: The mechanism by which explosive bonding creates a jet and breaks surface contamination at the impact point remains unmodeled experimentally.
verbatim: People have modeled this — I don't know if they've ever taken high-speed movies — but you're breaking up that surface right at the impact angle point, and you're creating new surface and slamming it together so fast that it can't recontaminate.

summary: Quantify the depth and rate of erosion from modern inhibitor-containing braze alloys versus the historical 82-gold/18-nickel standard in turbine shroud seals.
verbatim: The gold-nickel does not erode the base material. These other alloys could erode two thousandths, 50 microns deep. Your four-thousandths sheet metal gets eroded from both sides and you've got nothing left.

summary: Spot weld quality control in automotive assembly lacks reliable inspection methods, with roughly one-third of welds failing despite being structurally necessary.
verbatim: they put three thousand spot welds in the average automobile because you need two thousand good ones. I'm trying to make a point about the quality of spot welds and the inability to inspect them.

summary: A real-time or rapid measurement method for nitride layer thickness is needed to enforce hydrogen bake-out timing correctly, rather than waiting days for metallographic results.
verbatim: They also wanted to make sure they had the right thickness of the nitride coating... they would take one destructive sample from the lot, cut off an end, send it off to the met lab, and two or three days later they would get back the reading of how thick the nitride layer was.

summary: Hydrogen loss from welds occurs so rapidly (half lost in 2 minutes) that direct measurement is currently impossible, forcing reliance on back-calculation.
verbatim: You can lose half your hydrogen in the first two minutes, and it's very difficult to actually measure it. So no one's really measured it — you can back-calculate how much hydrogen was there originally, but you can't really measure it because it comes out so quickly.

summary: Quantify the mechanical stress conditions that define low, medium, and high restraint categories in welding.
verbatim: This is not quantified — we don't know how much stress you've got. But this basically says it's thicker steels or repair welds where the members can't move.

summary: Large forging heat treatments create property gradients between prolongation test specimens and the main component due to different cooling rates, but no standard method exists to verify if small test pieces truly represent bulk properties.
verbatim: Well the little piece is not going to cool at the same rate as the big piece, duh. They measured the properties and it just barely made spec in terms of impact toughness and strength. They said well, we'll assume that this is the same as that — which is not.

summary: No systematic comparison of tensile or fatigue behavior in aluminum 355 castings welded with 4043 (undermatching) versus 4009 (matching composition) in actual service conditions.
verbatim: You have experience with 4043, and it's hard to suggest changing from a proven performer. If it's not broke, don't fix it. 4009 is matched composition, and 4010 and 4011 are very close. They probably give intermediate strength.

summary: Heavy-section titanium welding (1–4 inches) lacks documented process parameters and mechanical property data compared to aerospace industry experience with thinner sections.
verbatim: The top aerospace companies — Boeing, McDonnell Douglas, Northrop — were coming in and talking about welding heavy section titanium. The heaviest section we heard about that first day was three-eighths of an inch. One person had done one weld in three-eighths of an inch. Most of the rest, heavy to them was a quarter inch, in the aerospace industry.

summary: Current inspection technologies cannot reliably detect flaws smaller than 0.015–0.020 inches, yet aircraft specifications demand detection down to 0.010 inches, creating an unbridgeable gap between capability and requirement.
verbatim: We don't really have inspection technologies that can do it, and Boeing has specs of 0.010". No one can find it, but it's in the spec.

summary: Develop a practical method to detect when low-hydrogen electrodes have absorbed sufficient moisture to compromise their low-hydrogen specification.
verbatim: However, improperly maintained low-hydrogen electrodes can introduce approximately as much hydrogen as a cellulosic electrode.

summary: No systematic quantitative relationship exists between hydrogen tolerance and yield strength across the full range of high-strength steels.
verbatim: I'll put up this little table, which you will not find in a book — this is a Tom Eagar table, but it's approximately correct... At 120 ksi, you could probably tolerate ten parts per million.

summary: Measure or map hydrogen concentration profiles in thick steel plates during multi-pass welding to validate diffusion-equation predictions and optimize preheat hold times.
verbatim: It takes time for hydrogen to diffuse a millimeter... at four inches thick, the distance squares again, and it's going to take a whole day for hydrogen to get out of a four-inch-thick plate.

summary: The welded turbine blade repair microstructure from 25 weld passes has not been systematically characterized for property retention and long-term service reliability.
verbatim: They built it up by welding — 25 passes, that's one millimeter. So they built up less than a centimeter, seven-tenths of a millimeter or so, and they machined it. They're refurbishing this blade, and the different microstructures show lots of little bitty weld passes to build that back up.

summary: Measure how mechanical machining and hole-drilling operations reintroduce residual tensile stresses into pre-stress-relieved T7351 aluminum, negating the original heat treatment benefit.
verbatim: What Sikorsky had done is they bought a bar of material, they sliced it up into little pancakes, and they did all their anodizing and drilling holes and machining. When they were all done, they had bought the material as T7351, so they figured they had good stress relief. But after they did all this machining, they hadn't stress-relieved.

summary: Real-time monitoring method to verify nitriding case depth without destructive sampling, eliminating the dangerous three-day delay in hydrogen bakeout.
verbatim: They would go through the whole process, they'd cut a piece off one of them — destroy one part — cut it, send it to the met lab, and three days later they would get the analysis back to tell them if they had enough nitriding. And if they had, they would *then* do their hydrogen evolution heat treatment.

summary: Determine the maximum buildable feature size before residual stress–induced cracking becomes prohibitive in laser or electron-beam surface processing.
verbatim: most of these processes build up residual stresses. You can see what happens with the residual stresses if you're trying to electron beam or laser glaze or melt the surface — you're going to end up cracking. Later Alex goes through and has a nice little plot... and it shows the maximum size when you get to blogs 9 or 10.

summary: Columnar grain formation in high-energy additive manufacturing produces anisotropic microstructures, but the mechanisms and mitigation strategies remain poorly understood despite industry awareness.
verbatim: A lot of really high-energy processes will produce what are called columnar grains, where a lot of heat penetrating into the part creates anisotropic crystal structures, which most industries do not want to see. Someone like Boeing wants a part that's isotropic — equal strength, equal properties in all directions — because it's easier to design for, easier to validate. So this is one of those dirty secrets about 3D printing that a lot of people don't talk about, but it's something that people who use the technology are very aware of and need to be pretty experienced with.

summary: Aerospace-grade high-strength aluminum cannot be reliably 3D printed with current powder bed processes due to cracking, while only casting grades are processable.
verbatim: When you look at aluminum, one of the most widely used materials, powder bed processes have really only been able to process casting grades of aluminum, which are difficult or low strength. They haven't been able to process typical aerospace-grade high-strength aluminum because of issues with cracking.

summary: Optimal toolpath strategy for minimizing defects during layer turns in wire-arc additive manufacturing is still being explored.
verbatim: There's a lot of science and thought to what the best tool path strategy is... the point in our tool path that is potentially the lowest quality is when we have to do a turn — that's the most complex part.

summary: Why does bolt reuse cause torque-to-preload relationship to degrade by ~50%, and what is the quantitative mechanism of friction coefficient change during reuse?
verbatim: When you reuse bolts, the torque to acquire the preload goes down and down as the bolt works its way in and smooths out all the rough spots and the friction coefficient drops. It takes less torque to get the same clamp-up. So if you reuse bolts, who knows where you are on this curve? It's a factor of two, it's more than 30% — it's 50%.

summary: The mechanism driving premature cracking in bulk metallic glass golf clubs after ~100 impacts is not explained.
verbatim: The only problem is people have learned you get about 100 shots from the golf club and then it starts to crack.

summary: The practical consolidation pathway from rapidly solidified foils or powders into bulk solids without losing the glassy structure remains unsolved.
verbatim: All you had to do was figure out how to consolidate those foils or powders into a solid material. How do we do that? We heat things up. You heat them up and all of a sudden the atoms rearrange into a crystalline form.

summary: Bismuth contamination from lead-free solder replacements will render steel scrap unusable; the scale and timing of this transition is unquantified.
verbatim: However, they're going to replace lead in solders, and a lot of them are using bismuth. Well, you know what that's going to do to a lot of the world's steel? It's going to make all the scrap useless. We're going to have to landfill it. We don't have enough of those bismuth alloys replacing lead alloys yet, but in the next 10 or 20 years they're going to have to segregate the scrap more carefully than they do today.

summary: In-situ chemical analysis during basic oxygen steelmaking remains unsolved despite decades of effort.
verbatim: A guy over here in Building 12 was working for years trying to take the chemical analysis machine and put it right down that lance into the 3,000-degree furnace. Never worked, but he was trying to figure out how to do it.

summary: Whether thick steel shafts (40+ inches) can be reliably welded together to replace large forgings, and what welding technique would work best at that scale.
verbatim: So they wanted to know if they could make smaller ones and weld them together and make big forgings. I had to figure out how — could we weld forty-inch-thick steel shafts together? We never did it. No one wanted to spend the money to actually do the trial.

summary: Develop predictive models or experiments for grain selection mechanisms during directional solidification through helical or spiral geometries in single-crystal blade casting.
verbatim: When you slowly solidify, you start with a seed crystal that has a particular crystallographic orientation... If you get nucleation of multiple grains, as they curl around that pigtail three or four times you select out a single grain.

summary: Ceramic core shift during investment casting of thin-walled turbine blades causes wall thickness variation and scrap rates exceeding 30%—the root causes and prevention methods are not well understood.
verbatim: The problem with going thinner — you've got a ceramic core in the middle while you're growing it — and if you get a little core shift of 5 or 10 thousandths, you've got no wall left. So they inspect these by putting them in a CAT scan machine… They do 100% CAT scan, measure wall thickness, and hopefully scrap less than 30% of the production.

summary: Continuous casting of steel strip has eluded solution for 50 years despite enormous economic incentive; the fundamental thermal and mechanical barriers at 2600°F remain inadequately understood.
verbatim: People have been trying to make continuously cast steel strip for 50 years and no one's really been able to do it. They still make it as a 10-inch continuously cast plate and roll it down. There's a lot of steel sheet used in the world, and if you could start with quarter-inch-thick strip, it'd be worth billions of dollars.

summary: No reliable consolidation method exists for converting thin amorphous metal sheets into solid bulk material despite decades of effort.
verbatim: All the way through the 1980s and 1990s no one figured out how to consolidate these thin sheets into a solid bulk material. They tried explosive bonding, where you just slam them together with an explosive charge, they tried everything and nothing worked.

summary: Friction stir welding with steel remains unsolved due to lack of suitable electrode material that maintains mechanical strength at temperature without excessive wear.
verbatim: For the last twenty years people have been trying to do steel. The problem with steel is there's no electrode material that really works well — you've got to have something with good mechanical strength at welding temperatures that doesn't wear out.

summary: Water pooling on curved aluminum plate ends during rolling causes localized cooling and strength variation that produces out-of-spec thickness; the root cause mechanism and quantitative cooling dynamics deserve deeper study.
verbatim: 700° aluminum, boiling water right there. Thin film of boiling water cools this down, right on the end where it collects. Now this is cooler than the main body of the plate, and so when it rolls, it doesn't roll as much, and you get something that's a little thicker on one end or the other, depending on whether you pulled your water.

summary: The mechanism by which cadmium oxide suppresses arcing in electrical contacts remains unexplained, despite its critical importance to switch safety.
verbatim: If you don't put the cadmium oxide in there it can only carry seven amps. That's a fifteen amp switch. The reason it can tolerate fifteen amps rather than seven is because the cadmium oxide suppresses the arc when you shut the thing off.

summary: Fatigue strength of welded high-strength steel does not improve proportionally with base metal strength, unlike static strength.
verbatim: You can weld 100 ksi strength steel, but the fatigue strength is terrible. I cover this somewhere in one of the joining courses — you don't get a significant increase in fatigue strength even though you're using higher strength steel. You tend to get the same fatigue strength as if it was lower strength steel.

summary: It is unclear why gas pipelines require 80 foot-pound toughness to arrest running cracks when such toughness would theoretically prevent brittle fracture initiation altogether.
verbatim: They were looking for 80 foot-pounds in the plate to stop a running crack. Except if you're at 80 foot-pounds, you never get a brittle fracture anyway, so it never made sense to me why they needed that.

summary: Why corrugated stainless steel gas tubing fails from lightning strikes at rates (hundreds per year) inconsistent with electrical codes written for thicker pipe.
verbatim: The lightning protection code says anything 3/16 of an inch thick is considered self-protecting. Officially this corrugated stainless tubing isn't that thick, but no one had ever seen one perforated by lightning before — well, we get two or three hundred a year that are perforated by lightning.

summary: Identify copper alloys capable of withstanding extreme thermal gradients (liquid hydrogen at 20 K on one side, 2000 K Mach wind on the other) without failure.
verbatim: They were going to have liquid hydrogen in the wings, and a copper alloy skin — some copper alloy they hadn't figured out. So you've got liquid hydrogen at 20° Kelvin on one side, and a half-inch or inch away you've got Mach wind blowing by at about 3,000 Fahrenheit — say 2,000 Kelvin. That's the temperature gradient between hot air and liquid hydrogen, with a material in between that, if it failed, kaboom.

summary: Blowout preventers fail repeatedly in the oil industry, but failures are only investigated when they cause major disasters; the underlying failure mechanisms and design vulnerabilities remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: But there have been plenty of BOPs — blowout preventers — that have failed. They fail all the time. I had three fail in Louisiana about a year and a half before the one in the Gulf, something I looked at. I looked into the design by the manufacturer, and it all came up empirically.

summary: Characterize the critical flaw size range (40–87.5% wall loss) where hydrostatic and ultrasonic inspection give conflicting pass/fail verdicts.
verbatim: Now we have a bit of conflict within the same spec, because the hydro test is only done at about 40% of yield, but the non-destructive test is looking for something that's 12 and a half percent loss. This is never-never land between 87.5% and 40%, where you could fail one but pass the other.

summary: No principled engineering method exists to distinguish between cosmetic flaws detectable by x-ray magnification and flaws that actually compromise mechanical performance in titanium welds.
verbatim: Where did they get that spec? If you take an x-ray and use a five-times magnifying glass... at high enough magnification, someone found that was the smallest flaw they could find... There was no acceptance criterion that made engineering sense. It was just what could be found.

summary: Carbon nanotubes fail at 1/10 theoretical strength due to atomic vacancies, but the actual mechanism and quantitative relationship between defect types and strength loss remains unclear.
verbatim: A carbon nanotube should have two or three million PSI strength. That's only true if you don't have a vacancy. If you have an atomic vacancy, then it's just like having a defect. If you really made a real carbon nanotube, it would fail at 1/10 the theoretical strength.

summary: Unclear whether vacancy formation in carbon nanotubes at operating temperatures fundamentally limits their use as structural materials, as it does in bulk metals.
verbatim: I know that if you have a vacancy — and if you're a materials scientist you know that at any temperature above absolute zero you will have vacancies in the material. You can prove that, second law of thermodynamics. You will have a mixture of atoms and vacancies at any temperature above absolute zero.

summary: The fundamental physical limit controlling manufacturing tolerances at the 10^-4 level remains unknown.
verbatim: No one knows what the fundamental limitation is. [regarding why tolerances cannot exceed one part in 10^5, or why polishing/lapping/honing maxes out at ~two parts in ten thousand]

summary: Characterize the mechanisms driving dead zone formation and shear banding in extrusion of different alloys, and how material properties (work-hardening behavior) determine the deformation pattern.
verbatim: Look at the dead zones. Copper has a little dead zone — you can see the grain refinement. This is a reduction ratio of about 85% on both. But look at the shear bands in the brass. The different work hardening between copper and brass gives you a very different pattern and these dead zones.

summary: Predict or control the folding and inversion behavior of fluid elements in static mixer geometries, which chemical engineers typically misinterpret through boundary-layer thinking rather than as a deformation instability.
verbatim: He's a chemical engineer. In his mind — and if you read some of the stuff, he explains this in terms of a boundary layer, because a chemical engineer or a mechanical engineer understands boundary layers and they think of the world in terms of boundary layers.

summary: Current flow behavior through copper-steel couples changes fundamentally when steel passes the Curie temperature and loses ferromagnetism, but the coupled electromagnetic-diffusion problem remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: I had a problem once which was a problem in current flow through copper and steel when we were doing welding. The steel would go past the Curie temperature and become non-ferromagnetic, and that's going to really affect the way the current flows through the thing.

summary: The physics of why light deformation passes (under 9% reduction) can create worse downstream stresses than aggressive passes (35-40% reduction) in drawing operations.
verbatim: Some of the dies at 40% might be cracking, giving high failure rates. The other ones at 9% could have been setting up stresses that actually could have been bad later on. Remember, I told you, you want to get a fair amount of deformation in. You don't want to do these little light passes. They can do more harm than good.

summary: Develop transparent electronic conductors beyond indium tin oxide to overcome its poor wear resistance in touchscreen applications.
verbatim: It's the only material in the world that I know of that both conducts electrons and is transparent. Ordinarily if you have free electrons it will absorb light and therefore it's not transparent. I'm sure people are trying to develop other materials.

summary: The mechanism by which c-over-a ratio in hexagonal crystals controls twinning tendency under different stress states (compression vs. tension) is empirically observed but lacks a complete theoretical explanation.
verbatim: Most of the common metals that are BCC or hcp have a c-over-a ratio different from the ideal, and that means they will promote twinning. If c-over-a is greater than the ideal, in compression it will want to twin, because it can accommodate the strain by twinning. If c-over-a is less than the ideal, in tension it will accommodate the strain by twinning.

summary: The large discrepancy between uniaxial (95 ksi) and biaxial (145 ksi) yield strengths in alpha titanium sheet deserves systematic investigation to understand the role of stress state and crystallographic texture.
verbatim: If he actually did biaxial stretching in the laboratory, he could get strengths up to 145 ksi. So it really makes a difference. This is not a small change. This is real material.

summary: The practical contradiction in sheet metal design: achieving high R-value anisotropy for cup drawing while simultaneously avoiding planar anisotropy that causes earring defects remains unresolved.
verbatim: You want anisotropy to give you a good R, but you don't want planar anisotropy, which gives you ears, which wastes material.

summary: The effect of vacancies on nanotube strength at non-zero temperatures remains unquantified; current theoretical predictions assume perfect crystals.
verbatim: Except the problem is, the physicists assume a perfect crystal with no dislocations. At what temperature is that true? Absolute zero. At any temperature above absolute zero, you're going to have some vacancies in those nanotubes. And guess what's going to happen to the strength of that nanotube when you have a vacancy?

summary: Resistance spot welding of aluminum presents unresolved challenges compared to steel, affecting the economics of aluminum vehicle bodies.
verbatim: The problem that she didn't recognize in her thesis: she assumed that you could resistance spot weld aluminum just like you do steel.

summary: Steel with ASTM 16 grain size (1–5 microns) has never been observed, yet theory suggests it would exhibit superplastic behavior; achieving and characterizing such material is an open goal.
verbatim: But if you really want superplasticity in steels, you've got to be down at ASTM 16, where you're getting down to one to five microns grain size — one or two microns. I've never seen a steel with ASTM 16. About the finest I've ever seen is ASTM 13.

summary: Eagar discovered hydrogen cracking in drawn stainless steel cookware but the mechanism by which hydrogen enters during Teflon coating and then causes delayed cracking remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: I don't know where you're getting your hydrogen. How are you getting hydrogen into your steel to cause this cracking? They said, well, would it have anything to do with the fact that to put the Teflon coating on, we spray stainless steel powders on the inside surface to make a porous surface to impregnate the Teflon, and we do that in an argon 5% hydrogen atmosphere?

summary: The mechanism by which heat affected zone grows during cooling (versus heating) in high-intensity laser and electron beam welds needs clarification and experimental validation.
verbatim: But in a laser or electron beam weld, you actually melt the material so quickly that the heat affected zone grows on cooling — it's the time it takes the heat to diffuse into the material.

summary: No reliable method exists to remove or cut frozen aluminum from buried potlines in foundries and smelters, unlike the proven oxyacetylene method for steel.
verbatim: In a steel mill, you have a breakout and you can cut up a big blob with oxyacetylene...But aluminum you can't. So how do you do it?

summary: The mechanism by which the first deep dive mechanically stress-relieves nuclear submarine welds is not explicitly characterized.
verbatim: Nuclear submarine hulls are not stress-relieved in the conventional sense. You create all kinds of residual stresses, but they are stress-relieved — the first deep dive stress-relieves the welds mechanically.

summary: Unknown optimal parameters for mechanical peening stress-relief cycles in thick armor-plate welds.
verbatim: They decided not to repair that gun turret on the Iowa. Back in the 80s I used to go down to David Taylor [Naval Ship Research and Development Center] in Annapolis during the summer, and they were trying to figure out how to repair it, because no one knew in 1985 how to make the welds they were making in 1945. What they used to do is weld a certain number of layers, then come in and mechanically peen the surface. Then more layers, peen again — that was their stress relief. They would mechanically stress-relieve every half inch or so. But no one really knew how many layers to put on before peening, or how to do the peening, or how long.

summary: The creep-fatigue interaction in titanium under cyclic loading at depth remains unsolved and causes fatigue crack formation.
verbatim: The Naval Research Laboratory had identified certain problems: when you go down a deep dive, you've got a lot of compressive stress, and something they called the creep-fatigue interaction. They had never really solved that problem. Titanium under continuous compression — if you put some cyclic load on it, it doesn't like it, and it will start forming fatigue cracks.

summary: The mechanism by which hafnium oxide protects electrodes in air-plasma cutting torches is not well characterized, limiting predictive models for electrode life.
verbatim: They form a little skin of hafnium oxide on the surface of the electrode, and the hafnium oxide is fairly stable. You can get about a half an hour's worth of cutting out of these things.

summary: Determine whether water cooling of resistance spot-weld copper electrodes is effective during the weld pulse or only between cycles.
verbatim: You might pass 10,000 amps through the copper electrodes for a third of a second. Copper has thermal diffusivity of one. You've got a third of a second. During the time of the weld, is the water cooling here effective in cooling the tip, or not?

summary: Understand why laser surface hardening of camshaft lobes produces severe surface cracking while electron beam does not, despite both being high-intensity heating processes.
verbatim: The problem is, they always got cracking. Why? Since it's all surface heating, the hottest part is right on the surface... they heated the surface of this lobe, ended up with very severe tensile residual stresses, and started getting surface cracks and spalling.

summary: Thermocouple-induced beam deflection in dissimilar heavy-section steel welds remains unsolved and prevented practical electron beam joining.
verbatim: When the Japanese were doing very heavy section, 6 to 8 inch thick electron beam welds for coal gasification pressure vessels, they found that when they were welding dissimilar steels you would actually set up a thermocouple effect between the two different metals... That current has a magnetic field, and it would cause a straight beam to curve, and you would end up missing part of your joint if you were more than 4 inches thick... No one ever found a solution to that.

summary: Cracking from residual stress accumulation in multi-layer electron beam deposition limits build-up thickness to roughly half an inch.
verbatim: As you build up bigger and bigger things, you have these small little weld zones and you put one on top of another, and the residual stresses get worse and worse. Typically you get to about more than a half an inch and you find that you end up cracking.

summary: Eagar notes that laser welding selectively vaporizes oxide and sulfide inclusions in HY-80 steel, producing mechanically superior weld metal, but the mechanism and practical scalability remain unclear.
verbatim: The laser was selectively vaporizing the oxide inclusions in the steel — oxides and sulfides — and just blasting them away as vapor, leaving behind a more refined weld metal. So there are certain advantages you can get in changing the chemistry of the weld bead.

summary: Electron beam welding of thick sections produces intermittent defects every 10–15 minutes due to beam instability, with no established repair technique for deep-seated flaws.
verbatim: What they found was long-term beam stability. If you're going to weld one of these 30-foot diameter pressure vessels 6 or 8 inches thick, it takes about an hour to go around, and typically you'll have some hiccup in the beam every 10 or 15 minutes, which means you're going to produce a defect every 10 or 15 minutes. When you produce a defect as you're welding continuously, you now have to worry about how you repair those defects in this narrow little weld.

summary: Characterize why the process window for thick steel (80 mm) narrows to ~5% tolerance on power, versus 30–40% for thinner sections.
verbatim: As you get thicker and thicker, the range of process variables gets less and less... if you go to 80 mm thick — four times as thick, a little over 3 inches — you have like a 5% process range, not a 40% process range on your power.

summary: Joining aluminum to steel without galvanic corrosion remains a critical unsolved challenge for cost-effective all-aluminum vehicles.
verbatim: The real problem for aluminum is the joining technology... how do you do that without having a serious corrosion problem because of the galvanic action and the salt on the roads?

summary: Welding turbine blades to disks (BLISKs) for weight reduction in large commercial aircraft remains unresolved despite massive Air Force investment.
verbatim: People are trying welding. The Air Force has spent tens, if not hundreds, of millions of dollars trying to figure out how to weld blades to disk, because there's tremendous value.

summary: Long-term durability of HDPE plastic pipes in underground service is unknown; no accelerated aging data exist for materials only 10–15 years in the field.
verbatim: Have there been any studies to see how this will be a hundred years from now? Generally this stuff is not — you can do an accelerated test, but you have to make some assumptions, and these haven't been in service. They've probably only been using these maybe 10, 15 years.

summary: CSST wall thickness and sheath insulation design inadequacy under lightning strike energy is not well characterized; designers lack clear design rules for arc puncture resistance.
verbatim: When you substitute materials, you don't know whether a designer took everything into account. If I'm switching from this to this, the wall thickness is going to be critical, because you can't have a material in your house where there's a chance it could go up in flames if it gets a lightning strike.

summary: Mechanism not fully characterized: micro-cracking ahead of crack tips in granite allows obelisks to withstand their own weight, contrary to predictions based on known toughness values.
verbatim: What he found was that you get micro-cracking ahead of the crack tip... the current knowledge was that if you tried to raise it up like this it should fracture under its own weight with just the natural flaw sizes there.

summary: Continuous caster breakouts (steel skin rupture during high-speed casting) cause massive downtime and losses but lack systematic prevention or prediction methods.
verbatim: The only problem is if you have a breakout, where you try to run too fast and you break through the solid skin, and all of a sudden you dump 20 or 30 tons of steel on the floor — not a good day. About two weeks shut down to clean it up and get started again, and a million or two million dollars a day, you run into real losses.

summary: Fusion welding of aluminum–silicon carbide composites causes cracking via aluminum carbide formation and humidity reaction, blocking a potential application.
verbatim: When you melt silicon carbide in the presence of aluminum in a fusion weld, you're going to form aluminum carbide, and aluminum carbide reacts with the humidity in the air and causes cracking.

summary: Scandium extraction from oxide remains economically unviable despite aerospace alloy potential.
verbatim: So there's a challenge: can we get the scandium from the oxide. These rare earths are not really that rare, but it turns out 97% of the rare earths over the last twenty-five years have come to be manufactured in China.

summary: The mechanism by which gallium-treated aluminum ball bearings generate hydrogen through rapid corrosion in water needs investigation.
verbatim: He takes little aluminum spheres, ball bearings, and treats them with a gallium alloy at about two or three tenths of a percent. He treats them a certain way and drops them in water, and within ten or twenty seconds they all convert to hydrogen and oxygen, just by very rapid corrosion.

summary: Scandium addition to aluminum alloys dramatically improves strength through grain refinement, but the mechanism and optimal processing conditions remain unclear for automotive applications.
verbatim: The Soviets tried this. They weren't worried about economics thirty years ago, and they showed that scandium can really improve the properties of aluminum alloys. So people are looking to see if they can drop the price of scandium, because it's not a rare element — there's a lot of it out there in the world.

summary: Fracture mechanics of clustered porosity in welds remains incompletely understood despite recent advances in stress-field overlap calculation.
verbatim: Only in the last five to ten years has fracture mechanics been able to actually calculate the fracture behavior of clustered porosity — it's very complex, getting those stress fields to overlap.

summary: Brittleness of niobium silicide intermetallics remains unsolved despite their high melting points, blocking their use in next-generation turbines.
verbatim: They're not 1250 centigrade as a melting point — it might be 2,000 degrees centigrade — but they're brittle as can be. No one's solved that brittleness problem.

summary: Refactory lifespan in molten iron furnaces remains a major cost driver, with industry ceramists worldwide working to extend refractory life from 1.5–2 years to 3 years, but the fundamental chemistry of how sodium and chlorine degrade refractories is not fully resolved.
verbatim: There are ceramists all over the world trying to improve the refractory so they could last three years rather than a year and a half. It's worth hundreds of millions of dollars to the steel company to get the longer life out of those refractories.

summary: The mechanism by which sodium and chlorine lower the melting point and degrade refractory materials in molten iron deserves deeper investigation beyond the empirical observation that they cause rapid failure.
verbatim: Sodium and chlorine lower the melting point of the refractory, and it actually melts — it will last for months rather than years.

summary: Titanium mandrel wear during friction welding is severe and limits the process, but the underlying wear mechanisms are not systematically studied.
verbatim: Friction welding is a problem for anything above aluminum because you've got to have a mandrel that doesn't get consumed by the heat. You can do it with titanium, but titanium is pretty reactive and you get a lot of wear and tear on your mandrel, whereas aluminum works great.

summary: Understand the mechanism and prediction of breakouts in continuous steel casters, a catastrophic failure mode that halts production for weeks.
verbatim: If you have a breakout — breakouts are really exciting in a continuous caster, that means the skin broke and you dump about fifty tons of steel on the ground. [...] It will kill you. And it typically shuts the caster down for several weeks.

summary: The instability mechanism causing waves in steel rebar at high rolling speeds (above ~60 mph) remains unexplained and constrains production.
verbatim: Typically a steel hot mill runs at sixty miles an hour. So they tried to speed up — seventy miles an hour. It turns out there are instabilities. The stuff starts getting waves in it when you go too fast. They couldn't run it faster.

summary: Why high-temperature superconductors fail to achieve usable critical current density despite high critical temperature and field.
verbatim: Those of us who had worked on superconductivity, in 1989, knew that a huge critical temperature increase was going to translate to real problems in trying to get any decent critical current. You can't make a magnet without putting current through it. You would have great critical temperatures and critical magnetic fields, but you had to have pinning centers that were smaller than an electron.

summary: Why do aluminum–silicon carbide composites lose corrosion resistance when combined, despite aluminum's good baseline corrosion performance?
verbatim: Yeah, you can get the strength you need as you add the hard silicon carbide particles to the aluminum, but your toughness is lousy, your formability is lousy, your joinability is lousy, your corrosion resistance turns out is lousy, and your affordability bites the dust.

summary: Distinguish hydrogen embrittlement from stress corrosion cracking in high-strength submarine steels using polarity-reversal testing.
verbatim: Most of the time metallurgists don't even make a distinction. But there can be a distinction, and in that case it was a big distinction, and all of a sudden we had the right mechanism and everybody was happy.

summary: Understand why stress corrosion cracking occurs in 304 stainless steel at unexpectedly low chloride and oxygen levels in nuclear reactor coolant.
verbatim: No one in the world thought you could get stress corrosion cracking in 304 stainless steel at those extremely low levels of oxygen and chlorine. Except in a nuclear reactor environment, where you have high residual stresses, you don't — but they did.

summary: Beverage can recycling is complicated by three different incompatible aluminum alloys mixed together; separating them efficiently from the 40%+ recycling stream remains unsolved.
verbatim: Recycling these gets to be a bit of a problem, because you've got aluminum-manganese alloys, aluminum-magnesium alloys, and another 5000 series. If you mix them all together and melt them all at once, you've got a problem, because you don't want manganese in your 5000 series.

summary: Why residual stresses from aluminum heat treatment specifically trigger stress-corrosion cracking in 6061-T6 but not T73 remains mechanistically unclear.
verbatim: The residual stresses from heat treatment can lead to stress corrosion cracking, which is exactly what happened to the washer... T73 is over-aged... the stress corrosion cracking resistance increases by about a factor of two on stress, which is like a factor of ten on life in terms of corrosion fatigue.

summary: The mechanism by which yttrium improves high-temperature oxidation resistance in turbine blade coatings remains unexplained.
verbatim: If you want to have the absolute best high-temperature oxidation resistance, you put a little yttrium in with the cobalt-chrome-aluminum that you may have in your nickel-based superalloy. Or if you don't have any cobalt because it's expensive, you have iron in there, and you will grow an oxide on the surface that has about 200 degrees higher temperature capability of oxidation resistance.

summary: The mechanism behind cobalt's exceptional wear resistance (10× better than other metals) remains unexplained despite empirical success in applications.
verbatim: Cobalt is hexagonal close-packed, and it has an interesting property — ten times lower wear than any other metal. They say it's because of hexagonal close-packed. But empirically, if you have a wear problem, do a cobalt overlay weld, and you may get around the problem.

summary: Hydrogen embrittlement in titanium during acetic acid production causes occasional catastrophic failure, but the mechanism and conditions triggering hydrogen uptake are not well characterized.
verbatim: Make it out of titanium, the only problem is, every now and then you get hydrogen into your titanium and the plant explodes. But aside from that, titanium is very good in acetic acid, except it sometimes will pick up hydrogen.

summary: The technical feasibility and cost-benefit of direct welding turbine blades to discs to eliminate heavy attachment flanges.
verbatim: They attach the blades — which are this fancy material that can't be welded generally — with what they call a Christmas tree structure. This flange and all this weight, this is actually probably half the weight or more of the blade. If I could weld the blade directly to the disc, I could get rid of this big heavy flange on the end of the disc.

summary: The design methodology for aluminum welded structures differs fundamentally from steel, and shipbuilders lack systematic knowledge of how to manage fatigue cracking in aluminum at scale.
verbatim: The problem with the larger boats made of aluminum is cracking, fabrication, fatigue cracking. They don't have the experience. It's not really a problem that they didn't have when they first started building steel ships, but there's a learning curve of how to do the design. The way you design for aluminum is not the same way you design for steel in terms of welded construction and fatigue cracking.

summary: Composite structures lose stiffness (modulus) in ways that degrade seakeeping ability under realistic ocean conditions—a property gap between calm-water performance and North Sea operational demands.
verbatim: the modulus of all those plastics — the stiffness — was such that the sea-keeping ability, when you go out there in those rough North Sea conditions, the Visby just would flex. So the Visby had a lifetime of about three years before it had so many cracks.

summary: The specific electrochemical materials and voltage generation constraints for Don Sadoway's molten-metal battery design remain poorly optimized.
verbatim: That's one of the problems with Don Sadoway's company — Ambri now. There are probably only one or two elements on the periodic table that will work for his cell. Most of them give you two or three tenths of a volt, and your losses in the resistivity of the copper wires bringing the current in — you can lose half a volt.

summary: Delrin's stress corrosion cracking mechanism under low chlorine concentrations (5 ppm) remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: it turns out if you have five parts per million chlorine — which is sort of what you get if you condense the air in Cambridge, Massachusetts — it stress corrosion cracks.

summary: The mechanism by which lightning perforates corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) at energy levels far below typical lightning strike energy remains unexplained.
verbatim: The yellow CSST pipe—it'll take a tenth of a coulomb to perforate the stainless steel. An average lightning strike has five coulombs of energy. So 1/50th the energy of an average lightning strike will perforate the yellow stuff.

summary: Resorbable synthetic polymers trigger inflammatory and immune reactions in the body, whereas silk does not—but the mechanism of silk biocompatibility is not explained.
verbatim: They have resorbable polymers, but they've got some problems made of synthetics, because they can cause inflammation and the immune system can react to them. Turns out silk is not such a big problem, and silk had been used in the body before.

summary: Develop ceramic toughening strategies that allow multiple-cycle loading, since intentional microcrack toughening in ceramics is exhausted after a single load event.
verbatim: In the 1980s the ceramics people went to town. They were going to start putting intentional little flaws in there to get these microscopic cracks. The problem with forming microscopic cracks for toughness is what happens the second time you load it. Now it's full of microscopic cracks, and they can't crack again.

summary: The strength-loss mechanism during welding of MP35N (a nickel-based alloy strengthened by twinning) remains unexplained and uncharacterized.
verbatim: I don't know that anybody — you lose your cold-work strength if you weld it. There's no reason why it's not weldable, it's basically just sort of like a nickel or stainless steel alloy. But you lose your strength because you lose your cold work.

summary: Cement is produced at 1.5 billion tons annually with no established recycling pathway, creating an unsustainable landfill problem.
verbatim: You want a problem to work on, figure out how to recycle cement. At some point in the next 10 or 15 years people are going to realize you can't keep landfilling all the cement.

summary: Why bismuth segregates to steel grain boundaries and causes embrittlement remains mechanistically unclear.
verbatim: Certain things you can't burn out — bismuth in steel goes to the grain boundaries and produces a brittle product.

summary: Water-vapor corrosion of ultra-thin glass substrates creates microscopic surface flaws that dramatically reduce strength over days, but the mechanism and kinetics remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: Glass is corroded by water vapor... those things will actually form little etched pits on the glass, microscopic — you can't see them... Just the humidity in there. Now, I've never seen this, but my thesis advisor, Bob Rose, used to do it.

summary: It is unknown whether ion-exchange strengthening actually reduces glass's sensitivity to humidity-driven surface pit formation and strength degradation.
verbatim: No, you don't. Well, you can, but now you've ended up with a compressive layer that's hundreds of microns deep, not angstroms — maybe 500 or a thousand microns deep.

summary: The genetic mechanism by which beryllium causes lung nodules in susceptible individuals remains incompletely understood despite clinical observation.
verbatim: If you're in the ten percent of the population that has a genetic predisposition to have your lungs react with beryllium, any beryllium compound that gets in your lung — whether it's metallic beryllium or beryllium oxide or beryllium chloride — will grow these nodules in your lungs and you will slowly suffocate.

summary: Investigate how the combination of high thermal conductivity and high thermal expansion coefficient in metals specifically defeats layer-by-layer 3D printing.
verbatim: Metals have one of the highest combinations of thermal conductivity and thermal expansion, and that's one of the things that kills you when you're trying to melt little pieces of metal on top of other pieces.

summary: Composite-to-metal adhesive bonding in cryogenic hydrogen environments remains poorly characterized, as evidenced by the X-33 tank failure during thermal cycling.
verbatim: They had a bad bonding problem. In one of my other lectures, and probably the joining course, I talked about how they had adhesively bonded this and how they made a mistake... it held. Everybody's sitting there, get out the champagne, we survived our test, we'll be able to fly this thing. And they start taking the hydrogen out, it starts to warm up, and then it goes pop.

summary: The mechanism by which paint on aircraft wings can focus lightning energy and reduce required strike energy to perforate the structure by a factor of ten is not explained.
verbatim: If you paint an aircraft and lightning hits it, the paint can actually focus the lightning energy, and it can take one tenth of the energy of a lightning stroke to perforate the wing on an aircraft.

summary: The cyclic behavior of artificially toughened ceramics after initial crack introduction is unresolved, limiting the viability of multi-phase ceramic design.
verbatim: That's true for the first loading. What happens on the second loading? After you've already introduced those little cracks, you can't crack them again.

summary: High-strength aluminum alloys consistently achieve only ~50% joint efficiency after welding, but the fundamental causes remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: High-strength aluminum alloys are very difficult to weld and get 100 percent joint efficiency. You make a little tensile bar and you put a weld across — 6061 aluminum, one of the most common, you might get 50 percent joint efficiency compared to the heat-treated properties.

summary: Carbon nanotubes are predicted to reach 3 million PSI but real specimens fall short; the role of thermally-induced point defects in reducing strength at practical temperatures is unquantified.
verbatim: They calculated the strength of carbon-carbon bonds and found these should be 3 million PSI... What's the probability of having a defect in a carbon nanotube? Pretty high... if you have some vacancies, you're going to find they're not as strong as you thought.

summary: Why do gold surfaces bonded in ultra-high vacuum fail at ~50% of bulk strength despite being atomically clean—is it residual surface roughness or something else?
verbatim: If the two surfaces are slightly curved, they don't really contact over the whole area. That's why you can take two extremely flat gold surfaces, polished to what we call an optical flat, and gold is somewhat soft, and you can squeeze them together in an ultra-high vacuum, and then you try to pull them apart, and they've got about 50 percent of the strength of a solid piece of gold.

summary: Ultrasonic welding of aluminum only redistributes rather than eliminates oxide contamination, leaving half the bond area with thickened oxide—the fundamental barrier to 100% joint efficiency needs investigation.
verbatim: Now what's the problem with an ultrasonic bond on aluminum? I didn't really eliminate the contamination; all I did was redistribute it. It's still there. Half of the bond area is still aluminum oxide twice as thick as it had been before.

summary: Linear friction welding for turbine blade attachment lacks the precision and process control achieved with circular friction welding, preventing adoption in jet engine manufacturing.
verbatim: One is linear friction welding. This is circular friction welding — it's nice and easy to build a machine that goes in circles, but they would love to do linear friction welding... they would love to be able to make turbine discs for jet engines, where they weld the turbine blade to the substrate.

summary: Linear friction welding of turbine blisk blades lacks sufficient quality control to be economically viable for production.
verbatim: If you can figure out how to get Six Sigma quality welds on linear friction welding, you could make a lot of savings for the airline industry and engine technology. But they never solved it.

summary: The minimum spacing between wire bond pad centers (4 mils) is constrained by tool head size and stiffness rather than electrical need, creating a bottleneck for I/O density in microelectronics packaging.
verbatim: When we get into designing microelectronics — how do you get more input and output bonds — you're limited to about four mils between each bond pad center-to-center because of the size of the head, the sewing-machine head. You go any smaller, you get the same stiffness problem we talked about with the tools that go into your knee.

summary: The mechanism by which explosion angle and detonation direction control bonding quality in explosive cladding remains unexplained.
verbatim: You put it at a slight angle — the tantalum plate to the steel plate, just laying on the ground — at a slight angle, you set off the explosive, and the explosive burns in one direction. You're forging these things together.

summary: The oxide-to-metal hardness ratio predicts cold-bonding ease, but mechanism by which oxide hardness controls whether deformation creates new surface versus merely smearing contamination remains unclear.
verbatim: If you think about it, the harder the oxide, the less you're going to smear the oxide across the surface... you might be creating new surface with your deformation, because down at 80% deformation you've increased the surface by fivefold, but all you've done is smear that layer of oxide thinner and thinner.

summary: Adhesive bonding theory lacks engineering treatment of realistic oxide-contaminated surfaces, starting instead from idealized clean-surface assumptions.
verbatim: On page six they start with the Lennard-Jones potential and bringing two atoms together — that's for a perfectly clean surface. They're not really starting where you need to on adhesive bonding, which is where you have an oxide surface, a dirty surface.

summary: Predict why adhesive joints under stress typically fail after 2-3 years despite theory suggesting 10+ year lifespans.
verbatim: If I get 10 orders of magnitude, this thing could last for 10 years. Many of you know adhesive joints under stress really don't usually last 10 years. They might last two or three years.

summary: The mechanism preventing brittle intermetallic formation when niobium is inserted between tantalum and vanadium remains unexplained.
verbatim: It turns out niobium does not form an intermetallic with vanadium, but tantalum does. So if you put a sheet of niobium in between and now do a diffusion bond, everything's fine.

summary: Isothermal solidification kinetics in transient liquid phase bonding—specifically the time, temperature, and alloy chemistry controls needed to achieve complete boron diffusion and eliminate the visible interface—are incompletely characterized.
verbatim: If you wait long enough you'll end up with a joint where the boron's diffused completely away, and you have a near perfect joint.

summary: Develop a predictive model for solder or braze flow across surfaces in the presence of flux, accounting for interfacial contamination rather than assuming clean surfaces.
verbatim: When you're talking about a wetting phenomenon spreading across the surface, I have never seen a really good model that can predict the solder flow or the braze flow across the surface in the presence of a flux.

summary: Develop a true ceramic solder that works below 450°C, a longstanding gap in joining ceramics to metals.
verbatim: If you can come up with a ceramic solder, the world will beat the path to your door. Because soldering occurs below 450° centigrade, you don't have as much thermal energy to drive these reactions.

summary: Lead-tin solders flow near their melting point with minimal superheat, but nobody understands the underlying mechanism well enough to design alternative lead-free systems with comparable wetting and gap-filling performance.
verbatim: Silver-tin and lead-tin are the two that flow close to the melting point without too much superheat... The spreading activity, the chemical reaction of these other things is not anywhere near as good as lead-tin.

summary: Plumbers report that tin-silver and tin-antimony lead-free solders fail to fill gaps of 3–4 thousandths of an inch reliably, causing 10% joint leakage rates versus near-zero with lead-tin, but the underlying wetting physics is not well characterized.
verbatim: If you talk nowadays to an old plumber... With the tin-silver or tin-antimony type solders they use today, tin is very fluid... typically if you're just talking about a copper pipe going into a copper elbow that's deformed to shape, they've easily got four thousandths clearance... When they solder up the whole system and go do the leak check, they may have 10% leaks.

summary: Why copper sulfide (vs. copper oxide) is uniquely resistant to non-activated rosin flux and how this selectivity manifests across different solder alloy systems.
verbatim: Since copper sulfide is more stable than copper oxide, guess what — a lot of the fluxes, and particularly a non-activated rosin flux, won't clean off copper sulfide. So small amounts of copper sulfide just destroy wettability. This goes not just for lead-tin alloys but for some of the other things we use in soldering.

summary: Erosion mechanisms of nickel-phosphorus, nickel-carbon, and nickel-boron braze alloys on nickel-based superalloy base materials remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: The types of braze alloys they like to use now are nickel-phosphorus, nickel-carbon, nickel-boron. These actually dissolve part of the base material when they first try to use them without any inhibitors.

summary: Extracting potassium from granite deposits and making it water-soluble for use as fertilizer in the southern hemisphere.
verbatim: People in Brazil came to Professor Allanore a couple years ago and said, we have tremendous granite deposits that actually have a fair amount of potassium in them, but we don't know how to extract the potassium and make it water soluble so we could use it for fertilizer. He's working on that.

summary: Understand the micromechanical toughening mechanisms in three-phase granite composites beyond microcracking.
verbatim: Granite is a three-phase composite — silica, feldspar, and something else; you can look it up, I can't remember what the three types of rock are, but you can see the three colors, it's speckled. Wilkening did his thesis, and that's one of his samples that he didn't test that I recovered. He found that you get microcracks at the tip of the crack, which gives significant toughening to stone composites — a factor of five or ten higher toughness than anyone had ever thought.

summary: The mechanism behind breakouts in continuous casting—when the solid shell fractures and releases molten steel—remains poorly characterized despite its massive economic consequences.
verbatim: Now if you have a breakout — if the liquid in the center of the shell of solid steel fractures the shell — you dump not 300 tons but a couple hundred tons of steel on top of your $100 million or billion-dollar facility, and it shuts you down for a few weeks, which is pretty expensive. So breakouts are important.

summary: Hydrogen loss during measurement of steel hydrogen content is rapid and incompletely characterized—the exact kinetics of rejection during solidification remain unclear.
verbatim: When you try to measure hydrogen content in steels — you weld the steel and then want to measure the hydrogen — if you don't quench it in liquid nitrogen within one or two minutes, you lose half your hydrogen, because it's coming out just like the foam in the soda.

summary: Aluminum welds consistently fail to achieve 100% joint efficiency (base-metal strength), unlike steel and titanium, and the optimal filler-metal matching strategy (undermatching vs. overmatching) remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: You go to aluminum and you're going to see we have some problems getting 100% joint efficiency. What's 100% joint efficiency? You weld the bar together and you pull on it and you get the same strength as the base metal. We're going to talk about, well, do you want the same strength, or what happens if you use undermatching filler metal so it would always fail in the weld metal, or do you want overmatching, and how much overmatching? It turns out the answer is, you do want overmatching for good mechanical behavior reasons.

summary: The mechanism by which inclusions trap hydrogen and protect against embrittlement remains incompletely understood despite prior research.
verbatim: There's a guy out at Colorado School of Mines who was elected to the National Academy because he showed that if you have slightly dirty steel it's better than if you have very clean steel in terms of hydrogen embrittlement. You want to have some inclusions to trap the hydrogen so it doesn't go all to the bad places.

summary: The precise time-temperature relationship for hydrogen release from different trap populations in high-strength steels lacks a fixed predictive formula.
verbatim: People have studied what temperature the hydrogen is released from the traps. Typically 375 Fahrenheit is the number that people use... In these types of steels, one hour at 375 is plenty. In higher-strength steels you might need a day at 375. There's not a fixed number, but I'm going to show you something that allows you to calculate all this.

summary: Water treatment additives (molybdates) chosen to prevent general corrosion paradoxically promote pitting and stress-corrosion cracking in high-strength steel; mechanism and mitigation unclear.
verbatim: They put molybdates [?] in the water, which some French researchers had shown — for the same type of steel and a great big generator rotor forging — they had a failure in France of a great big generator rotor forging in a utility, an electrical generating plant. It had stress corrosion cracking in the same type of steel with the same type of water treatment, because of pitting.

summary: Mechanism and kinetics of how different paint types trap hydrogen in welds, especially in high-strength steels, remain incompletely characterized.
verbatim: Some paints can actually keep the hydrogen in that would ordinarily be diffusing out, like the CO2 in my Sprite. Over a few days you can put paints on that will lock the hydrogen in. That's not usually a problem in lower-strength materials. In higher-strength materials, like 200 ksi steels, it can be a big problem.

summary: The mechanisms by which oxide inclusions in weld metal nucleate acicular ferrite and produce high toughness remain incompletely characterized, particularly at the transmission electron microscope scale.
verbatim: At the center of each one of these needles, if you look at it in a transmission electron microscope, will be an oxide inclusion... these are high-angle grain boundaries. When the crack tries to go through there, it's blunted, it changes its direction, and it gives you very high toughness, very high strength for the composition of the weld metal.

summary: Develop a predictive model or control strategy to prevent the chemistry-driven shift from acicular ferrite to martensite in high-strength steel welds, as exemplified by the Seawolf hydrogen cracking failure.
verbatim: The Seawolf was supposed to be welding HY-100, but they had a weld metal that was a little too rich in chemistry...the carbon was at the maximum of the range, the manganese was the maximum of the range, the chromium, everything was at the maximum of the range, and they were getting 130 ksi weld metal. It was more of a martensitic structure rather than acicular ferrite, and all of a sudden they ran into all kinds of problems with hydrogen cracking.

summary: Why 2219 aluminum has unusually good weldability compared to other aluminum-copper alloys remains unexplained.
verbatim: One alloy in the aluminum-copper series, 2219, has very good weldability. That's what the Space Shuttle main tank was made out of for many years, because you had to weld it.

summary: Why Marangoni flux enhancement works exceptionally well for titanium but poorly for steel despite identical welding physics.
verbatim: They wanted to make it work for steel. Doesn't work so well for steel; works great for titanium. The Soviets were doing it in the 60s.

summary: Develop a quantitative, objective method to assess titanium weld quality that doesn't rely on operator color perception.
verbatim: People have tried for years — you look at the color and you find out whether the quality of the weld is acceptable, and they go through all these colors and tell you what's unacceptable. White is when you've gone back to titanium dioxide. Gray, unacceptable. What's the difference between gray and silver? Well, you know what it is. But when you actually look at a piece of titanium it's not so clear. The US Navy had determined you can't use color to determine quality, because all it takes is someone like me that's colorblind, and they're all good, or they're all bad — who knows what they are.

summary: The kinetics of hot corrosion in the narrow temperature window (800–1000°C) where sulfur compounds condense on NiCrAlY coatings remain poorly understood.
verbatim: Pourbaix diagrams explain the thermodynamics of corrosion, but the real problem in corrosion is trying to understand the kinetics, how fast it occurs.

summary: The threshold chlorine concentration that triggers stress-corrosion cracking in Delrin remains poorly defined across different water chemistries.
verbatim: The problem with Delrin is a little bit of chlorine. How much chlorine? Ten years ago if you went to the DuPont website and looked at the materials it was resistant to... it said corrosion resistant. With an asterisk: less than half part per million.

summary: Understand why stress corrosion cracking occurred in 304 stainless steel reactor safe-ends at surprisingly low oxygen (1 ppm) and chlorine (0.1 ppm) levels.
verbatim: They got in and they found that they were getting stress corrosion cracking of stainless steels with about one part per million oxygen in the water and a tenth of a part per million chlorine.

summary: Galvanic corrosion mechanism at microscopic pinholes (holidays) in copper plating on stainless steel lacks detailed characterization of localized attack intensity.
verbatim: What happens there is now you get the galvanic reaction: this is your cathode, your anode becomes your stainless steel right here, and all the area driving the electrons is focused right on that pinhole.

summary: The composition and structure of the passive layer on stainless steel—whether amorphous or crystalline—needs clarification beyond the simplified Cr₂O₃ model.
verbatim: It's not really Cr2O3 — it's actually something much more complex, it's Cr2(OH)3. But if you actually analyze the surface of a steel that has more than 10 or 12 percent chrome, that top surface will be almost 100 percent chromium... it's maybe an amorphous layer, because it may only be 50 nanometers thick.

summary: The loss of corrosion resistance in activated stainless steel after plating and the role of surface iron contamination during the plating process should be systematically studied.
verbatim: In order for the stainless steel company to make this copper-plated tubing, they had to activate it to get the plating to adhere. Which meant that when you now have the little holiday, you didn't have a passive surface. Activated stainless steel will rust just like anything else.

summary: The practical knowledge of welding thick armor plate (14–18 inches) in multiple passes has been lost; modern welders lack the procedures to avoid cracking and residual stress in heavy weldments.
verbatim: We no longer know how to do that. I'll tell you the story of how we tried to weld that together unsuccessfully when the forging press broke after 60 years of service and some guys came in to try to weld it. They were very good welders — no defects in that weld — but lots of residual stresses.

summary: Hydrogen diffusion and trapping kinetics in welds remain incompletely characterized, particularly the rate and extent of hydrogen loss over time and conditions enabling re-nucleation.
verbatim: If this were a weld, there would still be hydrogen in there after an hour. There would be less hydrogen — I can't get as much as I had in the very beginning — but it's still there.
