summary: The growth kinetics of hydrogen cracks in the critical days after welding remain poorly quantified despite their catastrophic role in failures like Alexander Kielland.
verbatim: The hydrogen crack is going to grow within the first couple of days after welding, because remember the CO2, the Sprite example. But for the fatigue crack to grow, it was probably a year and a half — it's in the book.

summary: The mechanism by which phosphorus in primer paint causes solidification cracking in weld metal remains unsolved despite 50+ years of industrial attempts.
verbatim: You can't weld over paint because the paint will cause solidification cracking — in part because the paint has a lot of phosphorus in it for corrosion protection, and phosphorus causes solidification cracking. So one of my first projects was: "Tom, how can we come up with a weld metal that can weld over paint?" People had been trying to do this for 50 years, and I didn't solve it either.

summary: Hydrogen tolerance thresholds for ultra-high-strength steels (280+ ksi) remain poorly characterized—only fragmentary knowledge about critical ppm levels.
verbatim: Get to 300 ksi, and half a part per million hydrogen can destroy your steel in terms of hydrogen cracking.

summary: The mechanism by which TRIP steel transformation during deformation affects hydrogen cracking susceptibility remains unclear.
verbatim: We've known about TRIP steels for eighty years, but they're now starting to use them for very high strength steel in automobiles, where when you deform it, it transforms to martensite and becomes very hard.

summary: Sea Wolf submarine experienced hydrogen cracking in weld metal rather than HAZ—a departure from historical precedent that remains inadequately explained.
verbatim: except in the Sea Wolf, where it occurred in the weld metal, which was a big surprise, because it had always occurred in heat affected zone before. They didn't have such overmatching weld metal strength.

summary: Investigate why different carbon equivalent formulas (Ceq vs. Pcm) perform better under different hydrogen control regimes.
verbatim: However, the second method is hydrogen control, and they don't even use the same carbon equivalent formula. Why? Because this is the type of structural steels the Japanese started developing in the 1980s, and they came up with this Pcm, which is a cracking parameter... It's basically similar to the other carbon equivalent that we had.

summary: Submarine material engineers lack historical toughness data on HSLA steels comparable to the Pellini explosion bulge test work from the 1950s–60s, leaving them unable to confidently qualify these cost-saving materials for deep-hull applications.
verbatim: They believe that there's not enough history on the toughness of the HSLA steels. They don't have all the work that was done in the 50s and 60s on the explosion bulge test.

summary: The precise kinetics of hydrogen removal during post-weld heat treatment—specifically, how long is genuinely too long to wait before stress-relief baking without losing hydrogen—remains empirically unclear.
verbatim: Now you shouldn't wait too long to do your stress relief if you're going to get rid of the hydrogen. You can wait as long as you want for stress relief itself, but for hydrogen removal you can't wait too long.

summary: The mechanism by which severe under-matching filler metal causes catastrophic strain concentration and impact property degradation in plastically deformed joints—though empirically demonstrated—lacks a rigorous fracture-mechanics explanation.
verbatim: The reason has nothing to do with welding; it has to do with fracture mechanics. Think about it: if I have two very strong things held together by something very soft, and I now deform this in an underwater explosion or anything else, in the laboratory I'm going to concentrate all my strain in the weld metal.

summary: The mechanisms by which hydrogen remains trapped in frozen welds for months and then triggers delayed cracking upon pressurization remain poorly understood.
verbatim: You can trap the hydrogen in there, and if it's frozen for eight and a half months of the year you can still get a hydrogen crack. It had been pressurized 18 hours before at 188 PSI... It just let go 18 hours later.

summary: Welding thick steel (10+ inches) without post-weld stress relief—a capability lost after WWII that remains unavailable.
verbatim: We didn't know how to weld 10-inch-thick material without stress relieving it. We had done it for hundreds of thousands if not millions of tons of armor plate in World War II and before. But in 1980 we did not have the technology. We still don't have the technology.

summary: Understand why brittle fracture crack velocity differs dramatically between gas and oil pipelines, and how decompression waves interact with crack tip stress.
verbatim: In a gas pipeline, the pressurizing gas is always stressing the crack tip at the full pressure, and so in a gas pipeline you can run for 30 miles. But in an oil pipeline you're actually going to stop. This is important for you Coast Guard people. If you're going to build gas pipelines from Alaska, you need to understand the fracture mechanics. There's a difference between gas and oil in terms of whether you're stressing the crack tip.

summary: The transient thermal stress behavior during heating of thick components is poorly characterized and needs systematic calculation methods beyond existing formulas.
verbatim: I remember coming back from that first day of going up there, or actually the second day when I actually got to see the piece, I went back and told our administrative officers, beware the transient thermal stresses. This thing had been heating up for about an hour and a half, and something this thick — when you go through my fusion welding course I'll tell you how to calculate through the Einstein formula the rate of heating — but this was still in the transient, it was still being heated through the thickness.

summary: Why high-strength steels lose all fatigue benefit when welded, unlike in unwelded or stress-concentrated cases.
verbatim: If you put a weld in it and I load it transverse to a fillet weld, I get no benefit from strength in fatigue. Now this was sort of a shock to Ford in the mid 80s.

summary: Understand why sulfur preferentially segregates to austenite grain boundaries and how ferrite content mitigates hydrogen-assisted cracking in restrained stainless steel welds.
verbatim: They'd find that the sulfur would go to the austenite — which likes hydrogen but doesn't like sulfur — and it would crack at the austenite boundaries. This metal could be all austenite, or it could be a little bit of austenite-ferrite, which was good, they found. They'd like to have a little bit of ferrite — about three percent ferrite was good, because it essentially absorbed most of the bad sulfur.

summary: Arc instability mechanism at high pressures remains poorly characterized—why electron/ion temperature equilibration causes narrowing and convection-driven blowoff.
verbatim: It turns out the welding arc — shielded metal arc, gas tungsten arc — becomes unstable at 450 psi or greater. That's because as you increase the pressure above one atmosphere, you actually squeeze the arc into a smaller volume; you get it down so it becomes narrow enough that the gas flow in the arc becomes unstable and it'll get blown off to the side from the convection currents that are generated.

summary: Limited prior work on how pressure-driven changes in weld metal chemistry (carbon +40%, manganese/silicon +20–30%) affect mechanical properties and hardenability at operational depths.
verbatim: There's been some work — not a lot — on underwater welding metallurgy, but it does change the chemistry. Your carbon content, instead of 0.1, could be 0.14 — a 40% increase. Your manganese and silicon might go up by 20 or 30 percent. Your weld chemistry changes, and it changes to a more hardenable chemistry.

summary: The role of hydrogen saturation and escape kinetics in underwater wet-weld cracking at different temperatures, rather than cooling-rate effects alone.
verbatim: at lower water temperature hydrogen wasn't absorbing back into the water [inaudible] — it's getting into the weld pool at a very high saturation, but it's not escaping. That's the problem.

summary: Identify compositional or processing modifications that preserve the weldability advantages of niobium-based precipitation while maintaining the high-temperature strength of aluminum-titanium strengthened superalloys.
verbatim: There are some variations on it that use niobium rather than aluminum and titanium, and niobium is easier to weld in many cases... titanium substituting for aluminum gives you much better weldability, so you can only tolerate about one-half as much aluminum as you can titanium.

summary: Pitting initiation and fatigue crack growth in 5456 aluminum alloys under marine conditions remains incompletely characterized, especially regarding the relationship between alloy chemistry, pit depth, and crack initiation in thick structures.
verbatim: 5456 is more highly alloyed than 5083, which does cause pitting, and the pitting leads to fatigue cracks — those are the initiation sites.

summary: The mechanisms driving delayed fatigue cracking in thick 5000-series aluminum naval structures—why damage took 30+ years to manifest—are not fully explained and merit systematic investigation.
verbatim: The Navy has had a lot of problems with the 5000-series alloys when they started using them in the 70s and 80s on the superstructures. It took a few years for all the stuff to develop, so now you're living with what didn't show up for thirty years.

summary: Unclear whether matching-composition aluminum filler (4009) actually performs equivalently to overmatching (4145) in service; no long-term data comparing field performance of these options in aviation crankcase repairs.
verbatim: 4009 is matched composition, and 4010 and 4011 are very close. They probably give intermediate strength. So you can have low strength that you're being criticized for; overmatching, which you might actually make things worse with, in terms of creating a stress concentration at the higher strength because this is quite a bit higher strength; or you can match the composition, and people may not even know you made a weld if they're not really careful.

summary: Why aluminum alloys near eutectic composition show such poor weldability compared to other compositions remains unexplained.
verbatim: These are way out towards the eutectic in most cases, or if they have smaller amounts of copper they have larger amounts of something else: manganese, magnesium, or whatever. [...] If you look at the 2000 series, the best any of them do — except 2219 or 2218 — is arc welding with an A. Everything else is B and C.

summary: Hydrogen porosity formation mechanism in aluminum welds differs from steel hydrogen cracking, but the underlying solubility physics and why porosity results remains unclear.
verbatim: It looks like the same physical principle in terms of solubility of the hydrogen in the metal, but it looks like lots of porosity.

summary: Electroslag welding for heavy titanium sections (1–4+ inches) was used in Soviet submarine construction but lacks systematic characterization of weld quality, properties, and defect rates in modern Western practice.
verbatim: In electroslag welding, you use two vertical plates — heavy section plates, one to four inches thick; I've seen people do eight inches thick. You put two water-cooled copper dams on the side, to make a little vertical cavity.

summary: Friction stir welding fails for steel and titanium due to lack of high-temperature stirrer materials and reactive contamination, respectively—the fundamental material science constraints remain unsolved.
verbatim: The problem with steel for friction stir welding is you just don't have a stirrer rod with high temperature strength. There's really no good material that will go to the types of temperatures you need without just wearing away very rapidly. They have done it with titanium, but titanium is very reactive with a lot of metals and you can't tolerate the impurities that you get in there.

summary: Buried pipelines installed in the 1940s–50s lack verified material properties; developing rapid property assessment methods for aging in-ground steel is urgent but underexplored.
verbatim: the Pipeline Safety Administration of the Department of Transportation has now told the pipeline companies: you've got 45,000 miles of pipe buried in the ground for distribution of oil and gas in this country. Much of it was put in in the 1940s and 50s. We want you to prove the properties of this stuff that's in the ground, because they've had some ruptures.

summary: The fundamental mechanism of why martensite is most susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement remains poorly understood despite extensive study.
verbatim: I'm not sure anyone really knows exactly why martensite's the worst, but we've done plenty of studies — we have the worst type of structure, but it gives us some of the best toughness and some of the highest strengths.

summary: Understand why drawing lubricant on smaller-diameter welding wires causes higher hydrogen pickup compared to larger wires.
verbatim: I concluded it was drawing lubricant. Why? If it were inherent hydrogen in the welding process, the same argon in the shipyard no matter what the wire size — what's different about these? The smaller wires have a higher surface-to-volume ratio; it goes as 1/R.

summary: Eagar successfully solved a cracking problem by changing joint geometry to reduce restraint stress, but had no principled way to predict success beforehand—suggesting a gap in understanding or modeling how groove geometry couples to residual stress and cracking in restrained welds.
verbatim: I'd had no idea whether it would work... The only thing I could think of was how to lower the stress. It was sort of a shot in the dark, and it worked.

summary: The mechanism by which plasma spray with nitrogen gas introduces hydrogen into stainless steel and triggers delayed cracking in strain-induced martensite remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: they're using argon with five percent nitrogen as the gas for plasma spray... When it cools down quickly, it traps the hydrogen.

summary: Determining the optimal thickness range and weld balancing strategy for thin-wall steel ships to manage the competing effects of distortion and residual stress.
verbatim: The worst thickness of all, the most difficult to deal with, is about three-eighths of an inch or one centimeter. You get a fair amount of distortion and you can also get residual stresses. And now people are making eighth-inch steel ships.

summary: The interaction and relative severity of multiple stress-concentration mechanisms (geometric, metallurgical, and defect-based) at weld failure initiation sites is not well quantified.
verbatim: You've actually got several types of stress concentration. Geometric stress concentration at the notch — say it's a fillet weld, you've got geometric stress concentration at both corners. Metallurgical stress concentration because you have a different microstructure in the heat-affected zone. You can also have slight undercutting, or as the weld solidifies you can have microcracks, hot shrinkage — less than a human hair, but enough. When all these things line up at the same spot, it doesn't do you any good to weld.

summary: Hyzak discovered empirically that substituting titanium for some aluminum in nickel superalloys improves weldability, but the metallurgical mechanism driving this improvement is not explained.
verbatim: Hyzak found that if you replace some of the aluminum with titanium, it's much easier to weld. So he developed Inconel 718, and Inconel 718 is the workhorse today for nickel-based superalloys.

summary: The mechanism by which hydrogen from corrosion pits interacts with transient thermal stresses and poor microstructure to cause premature fracture toughness loss in service needs clarification.
verbatim: Corrosion like that produces hydrogen. So it was a form of hydrogen embrittlement, stress corrosion cracking — whatever you want to call it.

summary: The mechanism by which a thin paint layer (20 thousandths of an inch) on titanium surface dramatically increases weld penetration in TIG remains incompletely understood despite decades of modeling.
verbatim: when you put a very thin paint layer, only twenty-thousandths-of-an-inch thick, it's kind of like welding through paint, and you get a very deep penetration.

summary: The mechanism controlling the sharp 100°C-wide corrosion peak in hot sulfidation of turbine blades remains unexplained.
verbatim: In a very narrow range of a hundred degrees centigrade or so, you have really appreciable corrosion... Usually you're operating well up here. It's too hot for the sulfur oxide to condense on the surface... Over here the kinetics are too slow, but it can still occur. But in a very narrow range... you have really appreciable corrosion.

summary: Determine the surface finish and geometric tolerances achievable on internal non-straight channels machined in-situ during printing versus post-print machining.
verbatim: The place where I think hybrid makes a lot of sense is if you want to produce really intricate, highly tolerant, smooth internal features you couldn't access after the part is printed. In the case of conformal cooling, if you needed those channels to be super smooth, the only way to do that is to machine while you're printing, because once you've formed it you can't access these non-straight channels.

summary: Develop practical ultrasonic or optical stretch-measurement tools for divers to monitor bolt tension in underwater propeller maintenance without micrometers.
verbatim: If you're diving, it'd be a lot easier to use an ultrasonic tool than to get in there with a little micrometer trying to measure something in ten-thousandths. When you've got your gloves on and stuff, ten thousandths is sort of a joke.

summary: Develop or validate a practical forensic method to identify the mill origin of steel pipe using multi-element chemical fingerprinting.
verbatim: the steel composition is actually a fingerprint. We knew what the heat analysis was at the steel mill, as reported by the steel mill, for this amount of pipe they purchased. We compared that, and we showed that within one chance in a hundred million, this had been made at this plant and conformed to this heat that had been purchased by the oil company from the steel company.

summary: Quantify the safe length threshold for plastic gas piping under lightning strikes to refine design standards.
verbatim: These things are safe if the length is less than ten feet, which explains why all those other connections we've been using for fifty years are safe. It's the 100-foot lengths that are the problem. There's a length that goes into this L di/dt.

summary: Validate whether hydrostatic compression during a submarine's first deep dive actually provides complete stress relief equivalent to furnace post-weld heat treatment.
verbatim: You can't do that once you have all the equipment and the O-rings, the rubber and plastic and everything else inside the submarine. So how do they stress relieve it? The first deep dive — you've got hydrostatic compression and all those welds get stress relieved mechanically on the first deep dive.

summary: Identify whether reagent-grade acetone versus commercial-grade acetone affects porosity formation in electron beam welds of titanium.
verbatim: I told the engineer at General Electric, what are they using to clean it? He said acetone. I said, why don't you go get some reagent-grade acetone and have him start cleaning it with reagent-grade acetone?

summary: Soviet heavy-section titanium welding techniques using high-current gas tungsten arc with large electrodes achieved superior productivity; the underlying physics of this process deserves investigation.
verbatim: He would also talk about gas tungsten arc — what he called semi-submerged arc — in the open literature. They would use huge tungsten electrodes and a thousand amps of gas tungsten arc current. They could weld two-inch-thick titanium in four passes — better than submerged arc welding of steel in terms of productivity. They did it with some of the physics of this gas tungsten arc process.

summary: The specific mechanism by which pulsed current transfers drops via Lorentz force (the 'milking' effect) could be studied experimentally to optimize drop detachment.
verbatim: That's what we do many times with pulse current welding. The drops are coming off the tip of the electrode at about 100 hertz, and if we pulse with the right pulsing of current, we can use this Lorentz force to squeeze the drops off, just like milking a cow.

summary: Magnetic field control of cathode spot wandering in titanium welding to stabilize metal transfer.
verbatim: One of my ideas originally was to put a little magnetic field around it to force that cathode spot to wander around on titanium.

summary: A rigorous study of hydrogen diffusion rates through graphite composites at liquid hydrogen temperatures is needed to replace the suspect historical data.
verbatim: When he redid the test for the first time, the numbers were off by about three orders of magnitude for permeability.

summary: Develop non-destructive testing protocols to track sixteenth-of-an-inch crack growth in service submarine hulls, to validate safe operating limits without derating.
verbatim: What it means is, when these things come back for maintenance every year or every two years, you should go in and use non-destructive test techniques to see if those little sixteenth-of-an-inch cracks have grown.

summary: Correlate fatigue striation spacing with loading amplitude to quantify variable-amplitude fatigue history from fractography alone.
verbatim: because some of the fatigue cracks had different widths, telling you how fast it was growing... I could see the different striations and the variability

summary: It remains unclear whether hot isostatic pressing plus specialized heat treatment can fully restore mechanical properties of used turbine blades to new-blade specifications.
verbatim: We found that if you did hot isostatic pressing, you could take an old blade and rejuvenate it with a fancy heat treatment.

summary: Systematically measure and characterize residual stress relief in electron-beam or laser-built metal parts using shock-wave treatment at ~10^8 W/cm² (Grüneisen effect) to validate stress elimination across different alloys and geometries.
verbatim: We were going to use the laser or electron beam to send a shockwave through it — the Grüneisen effect. If you hit it with enough power, about 10 to the 8th watts per square centimeter, you can send a 400-ksi shockwave through it that eliminates the residual stresses, like a sharp stress relief. We proved you could do that — we showed you can get rid of the residual stresses.

summary: A systematic comparison of crack initiation and propagation behavior in friction-stir-welded aluminum and titanium alloys used in aerospace structures versus traditional arc-welded designs.
verbatim: There's a relatively new process called friction stir welding, invented at the British Welding Institute in the late 70s. Someone started a firm to build a small business jet by friction stir welding aluminum and titanium. I thought, I don't know if I'd like that, because look what happened to the Liberty ships.

summary: Systematic study of defect density in bulk-manufactured graphene and carbon nanotubes versus theoretical defect-free predictions to validate strength degradation.
verbatim: They're all saying, 'Oh, this is going to save the world. We will have things that are 10 times as strong.' Yes, *if* they are defect-free. They're not defect-free. So they're actually going to be one-tenth as strong, or one-fifth as strong, when we make them in high quantity.

summary: Determining the optimal porosity pattern and volume fraction in ceramic-metal joints for maximum strength across different material pairs.
verbatim: Based on that thought, back in the 1990s I had a student do her doctoral thesis, and she showed that you can actually get the strongest joint in ceramic-metal joints if you have about 10 volume percent porosity in the proper pattern on the interface.

summary: Develop a gold-nickel brazing system for copper-molybdenum joints that avoids brittle Ni₃Mo intermetallic formation while achieving diffusion bonding.
verbatim: If you could come up with a system with copper and molybdenum that wouldn't give you the brittle intermetallic but would give you a diffusion bond, you wouldn't have to have the high pressures for fixturing, you could do it faster — in a TLP joint you only need 5 psi, not 5000, for fixturing.

summary: Test whether strain energy scalar criterion predicts failure in dissimilar-metal bonds across different geometric scales and material combinations.
verbatim: The strain energy is just like a spring, dx, ½ kx². The bond energy goes linearly with the bond area... strain energy always goes one dimension higher than the bonding strength. Which means you can always bond small things, but you can't bond big areas, because strain energy will kill you.

summary: Systematically test whether patterned or tiled interfaces with controlled porosity can overcome the size limits of dissimilar-metal bonding.
verbatim: That's not to say there aren't ways around it. You can add porosity to the interface, you can pattern the interface, you can separate it so you essentially put a tile on there with spaces in between.

summary: Quantify the minimum time delay between hydrogen saturation in a weld and delayed cracking onset under realistic stress and temperature conditions.
verbatim: Even though this is nine months later, this is the oldest hydrogen crack from welding. You've got to remember, they froze it for the winter at minus 20. The hydrogen can't get out at minus 20... Then it warms up, and you stress it at the applied stresses, and wait 20 hours — I think it was 20 hours, more than eight hours — and then it ruptures.

summary: A systematic study of strain concentration and localization at undermatching welds under different loading modes (impact, bending, tension) could clarify the fracture mechanisms and perhaps identify protective design strategies.
verbatim: With undermatching weld metal, you concentrate the strain at the weld... a 1% strain gets concentrated in the weld. Now you start seeing 20, 25, 30% strain and the thing fractures. It doesn't really matter whether it's slow tensile failure, slow bending, or impact fracture.

summary: A systematic experimental study mapping crack sensitivity across composition ranges in the aluminum-copper, magnesium, and magnesium-silicon systems would validate freezing-range predictions.
verbatim: If you look at the relative crack sensitivity of different aluminum alloys — silicon, copper, magnesium, magnesium-silicon — you'll find this is composition of the weld of the alloying element.

summary: Test whether matching filler metal (4009, same composition as 355 base) actually improves fatigue life and residual stress behavior compared to under-matched 4043 in production parts, rather than relying on composition similarity alone.
verbatim: 4009 is an exact match for 355, so if someone comes afterwards and does an analysis they won't find a difference in composition. That's what the Canadian Transportation Board had said in his previous problem of last fall — you should have used matching filler metal. Well, if you've been doing it successfully for forty years on a hundred thousand parts, I'm not sure that's a good conclusion.

summary: Investigate why electroslag welding produces superior chemistry and weld quality compared to submerged arc for titanium.
verbatim: My first research contract on titanium at MIT was on submerged arc welding of titanium to get a good weld. They didn't have the best shape, but they had chemistry that was excellent... The reason they classified it is — to the best of our knowledge, that's one of the ways the Soviets built the Alpha subs. They didn't use submerged arc welding, they didn't use what the US Navy had spent millions of dollars trying to do.

summary: A systematic study comparing polybutylene and PEX fittings under identical stress and water conditions could clarify why PEX brass fittings suffer dealloying while polybutylene fails via stress-corrosion cracking.
verbatim: PEX tubing is fine. Some people are blaming the fittings. There's a billion dollars worth of lawsuits out in Las Vegas and the West Coast on PEX brass fittings, but that's another story. It's a corrosion problem called de-alloying.

summary: Develop a weld metal composition that tolerates phosphorus-containing primers without triggering solidification cracking, enabling direct welding over painted shipyard plates.
verbatim: What people have done is gone to different composition paints, but it still doesn't work very well. When I was in Japan in the 1980s visiting shipyards, they were trying to do it. About eight years ago up here at Bath Iron Works, they were trying to do it.

summary: Investigate the composition and microstructural mechanisms that allowed Japanese HSLA steels to eliminate preheat requirements compared to conventional alloy steels.
verbatim: That's why the Navy wanted to go to HSLA plate steels, and that's one of the reasons they sent me over to Japan in the mid 80s to see how the Japanese were making these steels.

summary: Validate the design and effectiveness of crack-arrester inserts (thicker, high-toughness steel sections) spaced hundreds of yards apart in pipelines to stop brittle fracture propagation.
verbatim: They were looking at using inserts in the pipelines to prevent the fractures. Every couple of hundred yards they were going to weld in a heavy wall, high toughness steel. So this would be your regular pipe, but they might put a 12-inch-long piece that they would just weld in there that was thicker and very high toughness steel.

summary: The mechanisms by which weld toe profile optimization and robotic control (torch angle, bead weaving, pulse current) improve fatigue strength in high-strength steels are not fully characterized or generalized.
verbatim: They have been able to develop welding procedures — changing the torch angle, whether they weave the bead, pulse current welding, lots of different things to try to control that shape, that profile, and get better fatigue strength.

summary: Develop quantitative criteria or a screening method to predict weldability limits for new nickel-base superalloy compositions before expensive full-scale welding trials.
verbatim: Some of them just aren't weldable, okay, no matter what you do. You can only use them as castings... One simple little test — you often don't have a lot of material, so they do a little circular patch test.

summary: Investigate submerged arc welding of titanium as an alternative to gas metal arc for heavy sections, building on Gurevich's 1960s publications.
verbatim: I had worked on submerged arc welding, and it turns out Gurevich had been publishing about submerged arc welding in the 1960s... We were curious about how they had built the submarine.

summary: Develop a rapid, non-destructive fingerprinting method to identify outlier steel plates with anomalously high toughness before they enter production, to prevent use as test coupons.
verbatim: When they found one outlier at 30 — and the other sheets coming from Sparrows Point averaged 20.5 foot-pounds, with 20 as the minimum — they'd cut all their test plates out of the 30 foot-pound plate, and that's what they sent to the lab to meet all the properties.

summary: Optimizing controlled cooling parameters and spray cooling uniformity for high-strength low-alloy steel production to achieve 65 ksi strength reliably without heavy alloy additions.
verbatim: You can't quench it in water, but if you spray it — more than a mist, like a garden hose sprayer, uniformly — you can cool it more rapidly. You can keep the grains from growing as big while it's red hot, and you can get 65 ksi.

summary: The critical flaw size in this vessel was much smaller than predicted (1 inch vs. 11 inches), suggesting a need to quantify how hydrogen embrittlement and microstructural degradation each reduce fracture toughness in service.
verbatim: When we actually got at the piece and found the original crack site, the critical flaw size was about an inch, not 11 inches, okay. Because the hydrogen reduces the fracture toughness, and the bad microstructure reduces the fracture toughness.

summary: Laser stress relief via pulsed shock waves shows promise but leaves surface damage; systematic optimization of pulse parameters and residual stress reduction is needed.
verbatim: We did some of that in the '90s, trying to use laser stress relief. You blast it, do little pulses, and all you do is leave a little divot on the surface, which you can grind off, but you hit it so fast that you send a shockwave through the metal, and that shockwave is a mechanical stress.

summary: Establish diagnostic criteria to distinguish corrosion-fatigue crack growth from stress-concentration pitting in high-stress components like helicopter rotor blades.
verbatim: Because if you look at the final size — the stress on the rotor blade has like a factor of 10 safety factor in stress, and the final ligament was not very big, so you knew how much stress there was. And you look at the size of the original flaw that everybody was pointing to — they thought it was corrosion pitting — did the fatigue crack even fit? No.

summary: Quantify the kinetic window for sulfidic hot corrosion in nickel-based superalloys across engine operating profiles.
verbatim: What we usually do at start-up — as you start the engine, you don't power it up right away, you let it warm up for a couple of minutes before you take off... they were starting their engines and going to full power for takeoff without warming up their engines properly. Instead of takeoff power getting them up out of this range where you don't have corrosion, they're getting a couple of minutes in *this* range — the corrosion range.

summary: Systematic characterization of critical flaw sizes and failure modes in ceramics versus metals for bearing applications.
verbatim: They're trying to make better ball bearings for jet engines. They want to make them out of silicon nitride because it's one of the toughest ceramics. The size flaws they've got to be looking for are five microns, because five microns will be a critical flaw size in fracture mechanics for a ceramic.

summary: Measure the residual thread fit degradation and micro-yielding damage after high-strength bolts are subjected to 75% yield preload plus service loading.
verbatim: If you do that and then put some service loads or excursions on top of that 75%, you'll often start to yield the threads. It might be micro-yielding, but now things don't fit up quite as well.

summary: The permeability of carbon composites to liquid and gaseous hydrogen was not characterized before the X-33 tank test, causing a critical failure.
verbatim: No one had checked the permeability of the carbon composite for liquid or gaseous hydrogen.

summary: The cold-start emissions problem in catalytic converters—quantifying the relationship between converter thermal mass, heat-up time, and pollutant breakthrough during vehicle startup.
verbatim: The catalyst isn't working when it's cold. When you start up the vehicle, all your emissions go right out the back until you heat up the catalyst and it starts working. If you've got a big thermal mass, it takes longer to heat up, and so it might be two or three minutes where you're spewing out all kinds of pollutants.

summary: Characterize the long-term recycling flux of US steel: quantify how much of the 5 billion tons of accumulated 20th-century steel has actually re-entered the scrap stream and when.
verbatim: Take 50 million tons times 100 years — that's 5 billion tons of steel. That has to be recycled, and in fact 70 to 80% of all the steel we produce is recycled.

summary: The thermal and mechanical stresses on the complex multi-layer wall structure (steel shell, welded rods, ceramic brick, water cooling) during cycling are not well characterized.
verbatim: The temperature gradient across the wall: 2,400°F on the inside, a couple hundred degrees on the outside. Sometimes they water-cool the outside steel shell — just a sheet of water coming down, a waterfall. They weld rods on the inside so the ceramic brick can be attached to the shell. It's a pretty complex structure.

summary: Lead contamination pathways in recycled aluminum—whether from highway dust, handling, or other sources—remain incompletely mapped despite known cases of scrap rejection.
verbatim: Finally they did a more extensive study. At the time — this was in the early '90s — the Mexicans were still using leaded gasoline, and they don't have five-cent deposit laws in Mexico. People would just throw their cans along the side of the highway. Other poor Mexicans would come along and collect the cans. But if you plotted the lead concentration from the side of the highway, it was very high right at the edge of the highway and within 200 feet on either side it dropped to very low values.

summary: Ultrasonic inspection sensitivity thresholds and detection protocols for thin cracks emanating from large internal voids in massive forgings need systematic study to avoid missing critical defects.
verbatim: The guy on his ultrasonics probably saw something here, but this was so thin when he's shooting from the far end that he didn't really see the crack. He only saw the big void. He could have turned his sensitivity up and he might have seen that crack, but his boss didn't even want to hear about the football-sized void.

summary: There is no clear engineering rule or measurement method for predicting when small ceramic coating gaps in high-power electric arc furnaces will allow arcs to breach water-cooled walls.
verbatim: But what happened is it jumped from the bundle to the wall because there was a gap in the ceramic coating, and that arc, which is supposed to be melting hundreds of pounds of steel a minute, worked on the pipe pretty quickly.

summary: The precise thermal distortion tolerances required during ship construction under variable solar heating have not been systematically quantified or modeled.
verbatim: You calculate what happens when the sun comes out from behind the cloud down at Ingalls, and the ship is changing its dimension as the sun heats one side of the ship and not the other. All of a sudden those things you just aligned within a quarter of an inch are now off by half an inch.

summary: Develop a technique to measure closed conformity defects in bearing assemblies after thermal cycling and deformation, when standard tolerance measurement becomes physically impossible.
verbatim: When it seized, it seized because it was generating too much heat. The aluminum housing — aluminum will absorb a lot of heat — when it crashed and landed, the heat started to soak back into the steel bearing. [...] we're supposed to go in there and figure out whether these things are accurate to 50 millionths of an inch. That's pretty much impossible.

summary: Aluminum fatigue behavior beyond 10^8 cycles remains unmeasured; the fatigue curve may or may not plateau at longer lifetimes.
verbatim: Fatigue strength: there is no fatigue limit for aluminum alloys. In aluminum alloys, the curve doesn't become horizontal, it just keeps going down. They've measured it out to 10 to the 8 cycles.

summary: Nobody had reliable data on how long running cracks actually propagate in gas pipelines before stopping naturally.
verbatim: They've had cracks in smaller pipelines, like a six-inch pipeline, run for 30 miles. You don't even store enough pipe for a 30-mile fracture, and how long would it take to replace 30 miles of pipeline?

summary: The crashworthiness and structural behavior of lightweight composite helicopter fuselages under impact is essentially unquantified, creating a safety design gap.
verbatim: The helicopter is sort of an anomaly: the shell where the people go is lightweight and probably doesn't have a safety factor much more than 1.5, but the moving components that keep you up in the air have tremendous safety factors. Because lots of things can go wrong in a helicopter, and it's not very forgiving.

summary: Lightning strike energy distribution remains poorly characterized; threshold data above 80 coulombs is sparse.
verbatim: There aren't a lot of lightning strikes more than 80 coulombs, so this is probably a safe product.

summary: Civil surveying techniques capable of maintaining 1 cm alignment tolerance over 4 km distances did not exist and had to be newly developed for LIGO.
verbatim: In order to run this thing, they had to align the mirror at one end with the mirror at the other within 1 cm over 4 kilometers. No one had ever needed to survey 1 cm over 4 km before. They had to develop new surveying techniques using GPS.

summary: Corrosion under insulation is a known failure mode but lacks systematic detection methods beyond manual inspection requiring expensive disassembly.
verbatim: There's something called corrosion under insulation, which is a big problem — moisture builds up. I've seen a number of failures because of corrosion under insulation. They go in with an ultrasonic thickness monitor and see how much wall thickness is left.

summary: The asymmetric beam modeling gap in 1980s bar joist design: computers could not simulate realistic small gaps between welded connections, leading to unmodeled shear loads.
verbatim: The problem was, you could model a perfectly symmetric system in 1985 — you could not model an asymmetric beam. In order to actually make the thing, there was a little gap. The computer program had all three of these things coming together at a point, but in fact one came in here and another came in here, and there was a shear load similar to the Hyatt Regency, and that's why the building came down.

summary: Quantify the stress-life relationship for aluminum beyond 10^9 cycles to establish design limits for long-service structures.
verbatim: People have gone out to 10 to the 8th or 10 to the 9th cycles — it takes a long time to get to 10 to the 9th cycles — but it just keeps decreasing.

summary: Quantify the protective mechanism by which mud seals corrosion holes in buried steel pipes and extends their service life.
verbatim: The U.S. Army did a study of 25,000 underground storage tanks, and they showed the typical corrosion rate: you'll perforate an eighth of an inch of steel in 5 to 25 years, depending on soil conditions, part of the country, amount of rainfall, pH of the soil, electrical resistivity of the soil because of the corrosion currents that can be carried through.

summary: Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) has been installed in over a billion feet across American homes since 1997, but systematic long-term field failure data and durability under real conditions remain undocumented.
verbatim: Between '97 and today, fifteen years, there's a billion feet of this stuff out there in American homes.

summary: Measure the actual grounding effectiveness of CSST installations to understand why manufacturers blamed improper grounding for lightning-induced failures.
verbatim: Up through about 2007 they were laying this off on the plumbers, saying you didn't ground it... they told you to ground it to *their* ground, and their ground means you have to ground it to one of their fittings.

summary: The friction coefficient behavior of glass lubricants at extreme forging temperatures lacks systematic characterization across material-temperature combinations.
verbatim: You spray on a glass frit, and people like Acheson Industries make different types of glass for different forging temperatures. You want a glass that's still viscous — more viscous than honey, but not so viscous that it's still brittle like glass.

summary: Improve end-region inspection techniques for seamless pipe to catch defects that automated eddy current cannot reach.
verbatim: The problem is, on the ends they couldn't do that because they had to grab it for the eddy current inspection. So the ends weren't inspected by eddy current, but they go in there with magnetic particle... They missed it.

summary: Measure how Poisson's ratio varies directionally in anisotropic sheet metals while satisfying volume-conservation constraints.
verbatim: Poisson's ratio still has to average out to a half, but it's not the same in all directions. They all have to work out so there's no volume change.

summary: Measure the actual tensile strength of freshly drawn glass fibers (claimed at 200 ksi) and track degradation over time as surface moisture exposure occurs.
verbatim: One of the secrets of fiberglass is they draw the fibers and coat them with epoxy or whatever plastic resin, and they keep the moisture away from attacking the surface of the glass, so those fibers maintain fantastic strength — 200 ksi if you could actually measure them.

summary: Quantify the actual heat transfer efficiency and boundary-layer dynamics when a flame heats a solid surface, since only 2–10% of theoretical combustion intensity reaches the steel.
verbatim: The combustion intensity is the theoretical amount of heat coming out of that tube, but only two to ten percent of that heat actually gets into the steel. Ninety to ninety-eight percent of the heat is just blown off to the side.

summary: Surface contamination from ambient dust and handling compromises weld quality in electron beam welding of high-value components.
verbatim: I notice there are little white spots that were not there when I looked 15 seconds ago... it's raining dust in this room. All you need is a little dust spot or a fingerprint.

summary: The exact split between conduction, convection, radiation, and electron-flow heating in welding arcs was measured by Metcalfe and Quigley but deserves re-examination or extension to different arc conditions.
verbatim: Of the total heat, conduction is about 4%, convection is about 2% — this is all out of that paper by Metcalfe and Quigley — radiation is 1%, and the electron flow is about 50% of your total heat in the arc.

summary: Quantify the field enhancement factor at rough metal surfaces during arc initiation to explain why surface roughness facilitates Paschen breakdown.
verbatim: If you study surfaces, they're actually very rough, and you get an enhancement of the field at the surface peaks. They found you could get easier Paschen breakdown with rougher surfaces.

summary: Quantitative relationship between electrode tip misalignment (skew angle) and weld nugget quality and electrode wear rate needs systematic measurement.
verbatim: The big problem was, not that you couldn't get a thousand if everything was aligned — but if this came in skewed at an angle, so you're really making contact right at the edge, you get a real hot spot. That was destroying things — if you didn't put the tips on square.

summary: No established method exists to remove bismuth from steel scrap through remelting, forcing a choice between contaminating the steel supply or abandoning bismuth-tin solders.
verbatim: You can purify it out of the ore, but you can't get it out by just remelting the steel. There is no way to do it.

summary: In-service inspection protocols for buried polymeric water and gas pipes are undefined, creating risk when replacing legacy metallic infrastructure.
verbatim: Once it's in the ground, are you going to maintain it, are you going to leave it in place? You don't want to have to dig this stuff up every five years to inspect it. As you substitute from one material to another, how are you going to inspect this over time to make sure it's still functionally and structurally sound?

summary: The mechanism and timing of solidified skin formation in continuous casting molds—specifically how thin the solid layer can be before breakout occurs—are not well characterized.
verbatim: You have water-cooled copper molds — the blue stuff or purple, whatever the color, I'm colorblind. It forms the solidified skin against the copper, and it's still pliable enough that you can actually bend it, rather than cooling it straight down.

summary: Measure the actual strength degradation curve of 3M epoxy adhesive over time at room temperature to establish reliable shelf-life data for composite manufacturing.
verbatim: The strength of the epoxy that hasn't cured is starting to cure at room temperature as soon as you take it out of the refrigerator... the curve looks like that. When 3M had their bullet point, they were talking about 10 percent of the remaining strength after 10 days. NASA had assumed that 3M meant 80 or 90 percent of the strength.

summary: Hydrogen permeability through graphite composite materials at cryogenic temperatures was measured with unreliable data; the original test conditions and methodology are unclear.
verbatim: They had done some tests of permeability of hydrogen through this graphite. Hydrogen diffuses through anything. They had done some tests at Stennis in Mississippi, and they had some numbers, but the numbers were fishy. When they went back to ask how they got the number, no one could tell them.

summary: Current NDT equipment cannot reliably detect cracks smaller than an eighth of an inch, creating a gap between detectable flaw size and actual critical flaw dimensions.
verbatim: Typically we can detect flaws an eighth of an inch in size or larger, with about ninety percent accuracy. So if critical flaw size is two and a half inches, what do I have to worry about a half-inch flaw for?

summary: Ratio analysis diagrams exist only for steel, aluminum, and titanium (driven by Navy submarine research); comparable diagrams for copper, nickel, and other materials have not been systematically constructed.
verbatim: You could do one for copper or nickel... These are only ratio analysis diagrams.

summary: Measure the permeability characteristics and long-term gas loss rates of multilayer plastic composites used in automotive fuel tanks.
verbatim: They still use those plastic composites now for gas tanks on cars, and they have a low enough permeability so people don't usually think about it. But you do have more permeability in plastics than in metals.

summary: The fatigue behavior of aluminum at very high cycle counts (10^8 and beyond) remains experimentally uncertain due to practical testing constraints.
verbatim: At one cycle a second on a fatigue machine, that's a year-long test. They've gone ten to the — well, they didn't do a hundred-year test, they go to higher frequencies. At 100 Hertz you can have machines that do it, but you have to start worrying about heating of the sample.

summary: Joint compliance—the distinction between hard joints and soft joints and how they interact with bolt tensioning methods—shows variability (±20–40%) that warrants systematic investigation.
verbatim: hard joint, soft joints, which is the compliance of the joint, plus or minus 20 to 40 — that's the plus or minus 30 I mentioned.

summary: Kinetics of dezincification in brasses used for plumbing fittings across different water types and corrosivity levels.
verbatim: What is eventually — a hundred years, a thousand years? These people are predicting a five-year lifetime in systems that are already 20 years old.

summary: The strength degradation curve of the structural adhesive over its ten-day shelf life was never fully characterized or communicated, leading to bond failures.
verbatim: When they actually looked at the data behind it, the strength of the adhesive looked like this: at one day it was 100 percent strength, and at ten days it was about ten or twenty percent strength. So they were out at seven days in some cases. The bullet point said ten-day shelf life, but it didn't tell you you only have twenty percent strength at ten days.

summary: Aluminum 2025, the world's toughest aluminum alloy, has only one known application (propeller blades) despite its exceptional fracture toughness; other uses should be explored.
verbatim: The toughest aluminum in the world is an aluminum called 2025... It's 15 times tougher than any other aluminum alloy, very low strength. I only know of one application: propeller blades.

summary: Quantify how moisture etching degrades fresh glass strength at the microscopic scale and timescale.
verbatim: freshly made glass, before it starts to get etched by the moisture in the air — it actually does on a microscopic scale, but it's so brittle these submicron imperfections destroy its strength.

summary: Systematically measure dynamic stiffness of modern high-performance aluminum bat alloys under actual collision conditions rather than static compression.
verbatim: They're still going to the best aluminum alloys. Get on the web — it will give you the history of the last 30 years of how Alcoa has been developing the highest-strength aluminum alloys for bats, not for aircraft.

summary: The discovery of stress-corrosion cracks in pre-shelf washers suggests residual stress relief procedures may not be fully effective or may be incomplete in production.
verbatim: They started looking and found these things sitting on the shelf in Navy supply depots with stress-corrosion cracks in them — never been put in service, just the residual stresses from the original manufacture.

summary: Characterize the fusion line microstructure and mechanical properties in continuously cast clad aluminum sheets, particularly the extent of mixing at the casting interface.
verbatim: For aluminum, the two fuse together. This is actually a fairly broad fusion line — a millimeter wide, and if you got in there you'd see a fair amount of mixing.

summary: The threshold concentration and kinetics of chlorine-induced decomposition in Delrin (polyacetal) are not documented; DuPont tested 200 solvents but never systematically characterized water sensitivity.
verbatim: The one solvent they didn't check — water. I'm not kidding. You read this paper, they never checked water. It turns out, if it's very pure water — in a nuclear reactor, water would be great, Delrin would last forever. But if it has half a part per million chlorine, it will start to decompose, and it will crack.

summary: The Westbrook plot's predictive validity has degraded over 10–15 years, raising questions about what structural and market forces have changed.
verbatim: I never have been able to quite reproduce this plot over the last 10 or 15 years, but the usage slope is steeper than the iso-market slope.

summary: Quantify the energy breakdown for copper extraction to isolate whether ore movement or chemical processing dominates the cost.
verbatim: Copper binds oxygen and sulfur less strongly than iron does — not much less, about the same. The bigger thing is just moving the rock, grinding and crushing it, and extracting.

summary: The mechanism by which acetic acid pre-treatment prevents paint flaking on galvanized steel remains unconfirmed; surface chemistry analysis is needed.
verbatim: I haven't done Auger or X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy — I haven't cut out a sample to see if I've got zinc carbonate or zinc acetate there. But I think it's zinc acetate.

summary: A quantitative survey of the actual leak rate and failure distribution in buried steel gas and water pipes would ground infrastructure planning and material selection.
verbatim: We always do, because whenever we start moving the dirt around we always uncover the holes in the gas pipes. We're leaking gas all the time.

summary: Measure or model how grain boundaries in ceramic materials initiate or propagate as microcracks, contrasting with ductile metals where grain boundaries rarely cause fracture.
verbatim: In ceramic materials the grain boundaries can become the crack. In metals with dislocations and movement and deformation, the finer the grain size the higher the strength of the metal — the reason is you get a pile-up of dislocations.

summary: The fundamental constraint preventing high-strength steel (>250 ksi) from wider use: critical flaw sizes drop below non-destructive testing detection limits.
verbatim: When we get into something like this, the smallest flaw you can reliably detect by non-destructive testing is about three millimeters. So we don't use steels in this region unless we're going to have a really tight inspection program.

summary: Nobody has systematically measured or characterized the surface-area dynamics and reaction kinetics between gaseous oxygen and liquid steel during BOF oxygen blowing.
verbatim: You're shooting the oxygen in there and there's so much surface area between the gas and the liquid that you get a very rapid reaction.

summary: The minimum ion-exchange diffusion depth needed to prevent catastrophic failure in chemically tempered glass under field conditions is incompletely characterized.
verbatim: So they have to make it 50 microns deep, and that's why it takes hours to do... But on a hard material like glass, it's hard to scratch it three thousandths deep. You can, but if you do you're in trouble.

summary: Eagar notes that ceramic flaw sizes are too small to inspect for reliably, making non-destructive evaluation impossible—a fundamental barrier to structural ceramic use.
verbatim: the critical flaw size is so small because they're so brittle that you can't even inspect for it.

summary: The mechanism and probability of electrical arc perforation in polyethylene-coated corrugated stainless tubing under lightning conditions has not been rigorously studied.
verbatim: The probability is very low. But in this case — I'll pass this around tomorrow — you can have a little holiday, a little tiny hole in the yellow coating. If the lightning strikes your structure, you'll blast a hole on the inside ten times the diameter of the little hole here.

summary: Ceramics fail catastrophically from microscopic flaws below the detection limit, making safe design impossible without a better inspection method.
verbatim: The thing is, you can't inspect things down less than a millimeter in size in general. So you have no way of knowing whether your structure is going to catastrophically fail on you — you just have to hope that it won't, and a lot of people aren't willing to risk their life on hope.

summary: Ice's fracture behavior and critical flaw sizes under realistic field conditions in Arctic structures are poorly characterized.
verbatim: Ice is a structural material. In the mid '50s, Professor Kingery in Ceramics had a big project to look at the strength of ice as a structural material. It didn't really become an important structural material until they started building the oil fields in Prudhoe Bay in Alaska.

summary: High-entropy alloys claim exceptional critical flaw sizes (40 inches) in published literature, but this vastly exceeds real-world materials; the measurement and validation of these claims needs scrutiny.
verbatim: They're claiming that would be a 40 inch critical flaw size. Here are their high entropy alloys... most of the metals are about four inches; that's the largest critical flaw you can get.

summary: Direct measurement of carbon nanotube tensile strength under controlled conditions remains unmeasured despite decades of theoretical claims.
verbatim: But who has ever measured the strength of a carbon nanotube? No one.

summary: Friction weld quality cannot be reliably inspected after joining; reproducibility is based only on process parameters and destructive testing of witness coupons.
verbatim: Once you've made that weld, it's very difficult to inspect it to make sure it's a good weld. All you really know is, did it collapse the right amount in the right amount of time on other welds that we made and destructively tested?

summary: Spot welds in ultrasonic aluminum joints are surrounded by non-welded material and cannot be inspected to confirm adequate joining.
verbatim: That spot weld in that ultrasonic joint in aluminum, it's not very inspectable. Just think about it — surrounded by a crack. You have two sheets together and you weld one spot; well, there's a non-weld shrouding it 360 degrees. How do you inspect that and know that you've got the weld you want?

summary: Quantify the time required for freshly fractured surfaces to become contaminated by atmospheric oxygen, CO₂, and moisture.
verbatim: Does anyone know how long it takes for air to contaminate a surface? If I were to break a piece of chalk, how long would it take that freshly formed surface to get contaminated by air and CO₂ and moisture?

summary: Quantitatively measure how interfacial energy varies with bonding type (metal–metal vs. metal–ceramic) to validate the claim that similar bonding types produce stronger bonds.
verbatim: Metal-metal bonds are going to be stronger than metal-ceramic bonds, whether covalent or ionic. I'm going to take advantage of that when I go into soldering and brazing, which is what we'll do tomorrow.

summary: Systematically characterize how phosphated steel surfaces retain lubricants compared to smooth surfaces, and measure the durability of calcium stearate films under cold-heading deformation.
verbatim: They would phosphate the steel and then put calcium stearate — you know it as soap — which is a lubricant. Now the lubricant is in this thicker porous phosphated surface, so you're not just putting on a film.

summary: Braze joint strength shows a dramatic thickness dependence (fivefold increase thin vs. thick), but the underlying triaxial stress mechanism needs mapping across joint geometries.
verbatim: Braze joints can have a fivefold increase in tensile strength if they're a thousandth thick as opposed to five thousandths thick. It all has to do with this triaxial state of stress you can set up in very thin joints.

summary: Degradation kinetics of hygroscopic tin and zinc chloride fluxes when exposed to ambient humidity—quantifying how quickly they lose fluxing capability.
verbatim: If you leave this flux out for 4 hours in Cambridge exposed to the air, it's no longer any good. It will pick up enough moisture from the air that the tin reacts with the moisture to form tin oxide and hydrochloric acid.

summary: Measure the rate of seal degradation in aluminum tube–brass ferrule connections under repeated heating cycles at commercial oven operating temperatures.
verbatim: This is an oven that operates at 500 degrees Fahrenheit — you've got a piece of stainless steel, and you've got an aluminum tube right beneath it with no insulation in between. This is in service for 12 years.

summary: Measure transformation kinetics below ~2 seconds, the current practical limit of quench-bath metallography.
verbatim: They really couldn't get things less than about 2 seconds because the thing won't quench that quickly. So that's the dashed line.

summary: The precise relationship between steel thickness, hydrogen concentration, temperature, and diffusion time to crack initiation has not been systematically mapped for practical weld geometries.
verbatim: Now, it's a diffusion process and it takes some time. How much time it takes depends on how much hydrogen is present, the thickness of the steel, and a number of other things.

summary: Quantify the relationship between ambient temperature and the thickness of surface moisture layers on steel, to validate the 50°F preheat minimum.
verbatim: There's a layer of moisture on that table as we're talking right now at room temperature. But as you get lower and lower in temperature toward the freezing point of water, that layer of moisture gets thicker and thicker. 50 degrees drives off enough moisture that they have found they don't get cracking by welding on steel that's above 50 degrees.

summary: Quantifying the actual stress state and fatigue limits in aluminum crankcase housings to establish whether the softness of 4043 filler is a genuine risk factor.
verbatim: No one's really done a big analysis on it, and they don't need to — these things are sort of proven by about seventy years of history.

summary: Optimal anodized aluminum thickness for laser absorption in surgical instruments lies between 6–10 microns but requires more precise characterization.
verbatim: somewhere between six and ten microns was the best. I actually calculated that from the wavelength of the light.

summary: Measure the quantitative relationship between oxygen/nitrogen/carbon impurity levels and titanium alloy strength and ductility across the full practical range.
verbatim: If you start looking at impurity elements, which is important in titanium — oxygen, nitrogen, and carbon — the strength goes up from about 40 ksi up to a hundred ksi with 2000 parts per million oxygen.

summary: The 1958 DuPont Delrin solvent-resistance study omitted water testing, leaving a gap in understanding how chlorinated potable water degrades polyformaldehyde under service stresses.
verbatim: The 1958 paper, the one solvent they didn't test the material in was water. They actually never tested it in water. They tested all these organics, and they figured the water wouldn't corrode it — this was the plumbing material of the future.

summary: Quantify how wet-dry cycling accelerates carbon steel corrosion as a function of chloride concentration and humidity cycling parameters.
verbatim: Wet-dry conditions can accelerate the corrosion. I told you the typical corrosion rate of carbon steel is about four thousandths a year, and it could be ten thousandths. This really depends on how many chlorides you also have around.

summary: The solubility difference between monatomic and diatomic hydrogen in steel is poorly documented and may explain why arc welding generates excessive hydrogen despite thermodynamic predictions.
verbatim: There is a plot — maybe I can find it in Kou's book — of the difference between the solubility of hydrogen as monatomic versus diatomic.

summary: Map the relationship between electrode moisture content, flux composition, and dissolved hydrogen levels across different welding processes and electrode types.
verbatim: You can have a wide range of moisture in the flux coating. Typically really good electrodes are 0.4 percent moisture, very extra dry electrodes are 0.2, and so you could easily get 5 or 6 parts per million hydrogen in typical mild steel welding.

summary: Quantitative relationship between wire diameter, surface contamination, and hydrogen absorption in shielded metal arc welding deserves systematic measurement.
verbatim: They had done all kinds of hydrogen tests on the wires — there'll be some residual high hydrogen. I plotted this, and I found the highest hydrogen in the smallest wire, next highest in the middle, and least in the largest.

summary: Quantify baseline hydrogen pickup during normal steel mill operations under realistic conditions (rain, wet scrap, furnace ingestion).
verbatim: I was at a steel mill once and it was raining outdoors. The magnetic crane grabbed about five or ten tons of scrap and was moving it indoors to put it into the hot furnace. Water was just pouring out of it into the steel furnace. Okay, so that's how you get three parts per million hydrogen in your steel.

summary: The precise relationship between heat source power density and distortion magnitude across different welding processes lacks systematic characterization.
verbatim: If you look at density of the heat source versus distortion, you'll find that it varies in that manner. Here's something else out of this book, looking at gas tungsten arc welding, which makes a very v-shaped weld, versus electron beam welding. The distortion angle alpha goes from near zero to very high values depending on the thickness of the material.

summary: No clear quantitative criteria exist to define the minimum preheat duration needed in high-altitude, cold, wet conditions before preheating becomes ineffective.
verbatim: They probably got their torch out and used their little template stick: oh, we got the outside to 150 degrees, which was their preheat temperature. That probably lasted all of four or five minutes once you took the torch away.

summary: The long-term service behavior of stainless steel filler in chromoly welds remains empirically unvalidated for high-temperature boiler applications.
verbatim: Found out from ten years before that if you weld it with stainless steel it'll be fine for the first ten years, then it'll crack, because you'll get carbides going into the stainless steel.

summary: Depth-dependent changes in weld pool geometry and thermal profile (broad at 1 atm, narrower at 20–30 atm) lack systematic empirical characterization below 100 feet.
verbatim: If you were to make a bead-on-plate weld at one atmosphere it looks like that; an underwater weld at greater depths might look like that, because the arc up here is much tighter. At one atmosphere it's broad; at 20 or 30 atmospheres it's narrower, and you get a different shape weld pool. If you get down 500 feet or so you actually start seeing differences.

summary: The boundary condition at which aluminum thickness transitions from distortion-dominant to residual-stress-dominant behavior (claimed to be around 3/8 inch) lacks experimental validation across different alloys and joint configurations.
verbatim: three-eighths is kind of the worst of both — the worst distortion. Very thin is not a lot of stress or distortion. Three-eighths is the worst distortion. Thicker than that, you've got lots of residual stress.

summary: No established method exists to apply mechanical stress relief (stretching or compression) to thin washer geometries to prevent stress corrosion cracking after reheat treatment.
verbatim: How do you stretch a washer to relieve residual stresses? Kind of hard to grip something that thick. What they could have done was a compression stress relief — a T-62.

summary: The hysteresis and energy loss mechanisms in baseballs during collision with bat materials need systematic characterization.
verbatim: The only problem in all this analysis is the ball has a lot of hysteresis because it's got lots of fiber and other stuff if you cross-section a baseball, and it's got rubber cores and things, and that stuff has a lot of frictional or energy loss. So there's a hysteresis in the ball. There's not much hysteresis in the metal — it's pretty much linear.

summary: The mechanical property variation within and across aluminum mill lots lacks systematic characterization as a function of processing parameters.
verbatim: One of the problems you have is the strength variation, both within a lot and among many lots. This high peak here is, say, 180 specimens from a single sheet of aluminum — a fairly narrow distribution of heat-treated properties. This is for 4300 samples from many sheets just coming out of the mill, a wider distribution of properties.

summary: Aluminum alloy fatigue and fracture data exist for bare material but systematic characterization of fatigue behavior in welded joints across thickness and product form is incomplete.
verbatim: There are tables after tables of stress intensity factors and fatigue curves. [...] They also give you the properties as a function of thickness of the material. It doesn't change a lot. But if you're trying to be really weight-critical, particularly on spacecraft, another one ksi — one or two percent — could make a difference.

summary: The relationship between weld color appearance and subsurface contamination (oxygen/nitrogen) in titanium needs quantification—color standards exist but physical basis for acceptability limits is unclear.
verbatim: They have acceptability of colors, which is what you'll find in the welding handbook — if you Google titanium welding. They have bright silver — you can see the ones I passed around, nice silvery weld metal with proper argon shielding. Silver, light straw, violet, blue, and white. This is titanium oxide — you just get a powder on the surface.

summary: Eagar identifies a critical gap in understanding how different rubber hose materials and permeability affect shielding gas moisture content during titanium welding.
verbatim: Different types of rubber hoses have different permeability for moisture, and if you just use natural rubber or neoprene or PVC, you're liable to get enough permeation of moisture right through your hose.

summary: Real-time thickness measurement across the full length of heavy aluminum plates during hot rolling is not standard practice; current single-point micrometer measurements miss the spatial variation.
verbatim: They measured the thickness by a guy bringing up a little wooden step stool with a micrometer, getting up there on the hot mill, and measuring the thickness with a micrometer while it's still hot... at one spot. Julie does a survey across the plate along the whole length — this might be 40 feet long.

summary: Quantify the relationship between solar heating-induced thermal distortion and welding tolerance requirements in large ships to improve predictive models for real-time compensation.
verbatim: And when the sun comes out, or a cloud goes in front of the sun, the whole ship changes shape from solar heating. And you have to weld these things so that there's not a bunch of mismatch.

summary: Establish fatigue cycle accumulation rates and inspection schedules specific to high-cycle regional operations rather than fleet-wide averages.
verbatim: Boeing had requirements for inspection after so many hours, increasing inspection requirements after so many hours, but it was for the fleet on average. They were taking averages for the whole world of 737s, not for Hawaii.

summary: Hydrogen embrittlement data at room temperature in notched tensile tests shows scatter that may mask real trends, and hydrogen-free baseline data quality is uncertain.
verbatim: I don't know if there's really good data for that. He may have actually had a little bit of hydrogen in the hydrogen-free samples. There's scatter around this curve, and I bet the scatter is as great as the slope.

summary: The kinetics and progression of delayed cracking in formed stainless steel (how cracks initiate and propagate over time under residual stress) would benefit from systematic measurement.
verbatim: The cracking occurs within a week. These cracks have gotten longer over time, because you've got the residual stress.

summary: Quantifying the magnitude and distribution of triaxial residual stresses in thick complex submarine structures to validate stress-relief requirements.
verbatim: In a complex three-dimensional structure you can have triaxial stresses. You can have HY-100 [steel] with stresses of 120, 130 ksi in a complex shape.

summary: No reliable measurement exists for predicting bolt loosening under combined field vibration and highway transport conditions in diesel engine assemblies.
verbatim: Everybody agrees, this bolt allowed the diesel fuel from the engine to get out, found an ignition source, and started a fire... The attorney for the defense of the manufacturer's theory is, when they put it on the flatbed trailer to move it down the highway, that's when the bolt vibrated loose.

summary: A systematic study of how prolongation test specimens capture (or fail to capture) the actual mechanical properties of large steel forgings used in pressure vessels.
verbatim: Later on, we found out the steel wasn't quite up to snuff, okay... But when you make a big forging like this, you can't go cutting pieces out of the big piece. So you use what they call a prolongation: the forging has a little end on it that you're supposed to cut off and make all your test specimens, so you know the properties of the steel are okay.

summary: Water chemistry conditions that promote pitting corrosion in high-strength steels used in pressure vessels remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: They were using some molybdenum oxide inhibitors in the recirculator for corrosion protection, and it turns out it pitted this steel. They didn't know it, because the whole thing was water-cooled in an outside jacket — no way to look at it.

summary: The detailed precipitation kinetics of aluminum-copper phases at room temperature over decades or centuries remain largely undocumented.
verbatim: They once did a study of the Wright brothers' engine, the one in the Smithsonian. Someone took a little sample off, ran it under the scanning electron microscope, and looked at how the aluminum-copper precipitates had grown over a hundred years.

summary: Characterize and reduce the property scatter in heat-treated aluminum alloys to enable tighter control of weld filler wire composition and avoid undermatching.
verbatim: Out of these specimens — 4,292 tests — forty percent of them had a very narrow distribution of yield strengths... because of the range of variability they got something more like an HY80 filler wire. They needed tighter hydrogen control, they didn't have that, and they welded up eighteen percent of the ship with a filler wire that was a little too low strength.

summary: Experimental characterization of how flux-coated surfaces alter weld pool convection patterns specifically in titanium (versus the well-studied stainless steel case) is lacking.
verbatim: There was a lot of research done on this for stainless steels in the early '70s... People started doing — they're doing research on this in the '70s, less about titanium.

summary: Powder bed additive manufacturing leaves behind defects after densification; the mechanism and severity of these defects need characterization.
verbatim: The problem with powder bed process is, it's 50 percent void, so it shrinks by 50 percent when you densify it. That leaves behind defects, so if you look on that broken piece you'll see the defects.

summary: Surface tension causes metals to ball up during laser or electron beam melting in additive manufacturing, creating difficult-to-remove defects whose root mechanisms remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: metals have a higher surface tension than any other material. It has to do with the chemical bonding. They have surface energies four times that of — sometimes ten times that of — most ceramics, and therefore they want to ball up. Once they start to ball up, it's very difficult when you're doing this laser surface melting or electron beam melting — it's very difficult to get rid of the defect.

summary: How to incorporate additive manufacturing into qualification testing without requiring full-scale tensile bars for every geometry.
verbatim: They have to have real tensile bars, they can't just do a hardness test and infer the strength. They haven't gotten that far on how to incorporate additive manufacturing into those things.

summary: Graphene production and stabilization methods remain unsolved—how to produce it efficiently and keep atomic-scale carbon sheets stable in processing without aggregating.
verbatim: Number one, it's difficult to produce. Number two, it's difficult to stabilize, because these little carbon sheets that are atomic size barely — they have a lot of surface energy and they don't want to be just little specks of two-dimensional carbon floating in some medium. So people have to stabilize them somehow.
