summary: Splat-cooled amorphous metals cannot be consolidated into bulk shapes or transformer cores—only thin flakes are achievable.
verbatim: The problem is, you couldn't make amorphous metal transformers, you couldn't make cores or anything of any substance from a splat-cooled metal. All you had was a metal splat.

summary: No one has systematically studied how to make carbon fiber precursors more efficient by reducing the raw material waste burned off during fiber production.
verbatim: Carbon fiber is extremely strong, but in order to get there you have to take a precursor and burn away half its raw material content. That would be one thing that you need to do to get the cost down.

summary: The wear behavior of integrated eyeglass hinges with rough surfaces has not been characterized despite widespread commercial adoption.
verbatim: We have a surface roughness like this — oh, we can put three parts together and turn it into one part, the hinge pin — and the article talks about how people won't have problems with it, it'll all be integrated together. But with a surface roughness like that, what do you think the wear properties of that hinge are going to be?

summary: Understanding why defects in triple-melted titanium alloys still control material properties despite the purification process.
verbatim: They triple-melt them to get rid of the defects, but the defects still control the properties of the thing.

summary: Surface roughness of powder bed fusion parts prevents tight clearances needed for precision mechanisms like eyeglass hinges; unclear whether post-processing or process changes could solve this economically.
verbatim: But do you think people really want a hinge with that surface roughness? It's got to be polished up, particularly if one of the hinge pins is this thing. You don't want it flopping around, and with surface roughness like that, you're not going to have the tight clearances you need for an eyeglass.

summary: Sintering of complex geometries produces non-uniform defects across different regions due to varying sintering rates, and no solution exists for this fundamental problem.
verbatim: They've never solved that problem. And we knew they never would when they invested the four hundred and twenty million dollars. When they signed those papers before they ever did the experiment, anyone who had ever worked on powder metallurgy or powder ceramics knew that part of the process was an Achilles heel. They have no solution for that.

summary: High surface tension effects in metals cause defects on sintered part surfaces, particularly preventing straight edges and fine surface details from being maintained during sintering.
verbatim: There are certain surface tension effects in metals, and remember, metals have higher surface energies than any other material, by about a factor of three. Those surface tension effects will lead to all kinds of defects in the sintered part on the surface.

summary: Molten metal spatter defects in directed energy deposition remain poorly characterized despite their obvious impact on surface quality and density.
verbatim: except you've got all this little spatter of molten metal drops that land on the surface and introduce defects. Should it be a hundred percent dense? You can get close to a hundred percent if you go slow enough. If you try to go fast, you start getting molten metal spatter all over the place.

summary: Heat transfer phenomena and process control in wire-fed directed-energy deposition remain understudied despite their relevance to large-scale additive manufacturing.
verbatim: If you go to directed-energy deposition, there's powder and wire deposition. My technical community where I got my tenure was welding. This is the types of stuff that I would do research on and look at heat transfer and whatnot.

summary: Binder-jetting powder shrinkage during sintering prevents precision aerospace applications, yet manufacturers claim automotive viability without solving this fundamental limitation.
verbatim: If I come to the conclusion that aerospace manufacturing is a sweet spot and I need ultra precision for the aerospace market, I don't think the powder shrink as a sintering process is any good for that.

summary: Compressor blade geometry control via binder jetting (shrinkage, balance tolerances for 30,000 rpm operation) remains unsolved compared to traditional casting.
verbatim: This really doesn't have great geometry control. I mean it looks good, but balancing this — because it's going to spin at 30,000 rpm — for something that diameter it's got to be balanced, folks, it's not going to be easy. Typically we cast these things; we don't do it by additive manufacturing.

summary: Composite repair methods in aerospace remain poorly developed despite widespread need in service.
verbatim: if you can figure out how to repair those composite structures, because that's one of the big Achilles heels for composites in aerospace. We can make them, but we sure don't know how to repair them very well, and they do get dinged up every now and then.

summary: Aluminum particle joining in additive manufacturing is fundamentally difficult due to surface oxide barriers.
verbatim: Because aluminum has an oxide and it's hard enough to weld. Try to take little particles of it and join them together is going to be extremely difficult.

summary: Internal residual stresses from thermal cycling cause parts to tear along layer lines and at weak fusion zones, but optimization of build parameters, orientation, and support design to prevent this remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: Parts manufactured with a lot of additive manufacturing processes will literally tear themselves in half, especially along layer lines where there may not be great fusion and strength. So this is a large factor when you're thinking about how to design parts for the process, how to orient parts within a build, how to support them, how to optimize parameters.

summary: Thermal management strategy for printing on cold substrates remains unsolved and is geometry-dependent.
verbatim: It's really hard to get good fusion to a cold plate with molten metal. So we're playing with ideas like, do you heat up the plate, do you heat up the whole chamber, to maintain that thermal environment and reduce the thermal gradients. It's something we're still figuring out, and it's very geometry specific.

summary: Residual stress and cracking behavior in larger parts printed via Joule heating needs investigation.
verbatim: When they started doing this about fifteen months ago, the big problem was keeping the heat in the metal. They weren't getting the diffusion, then we were getting porosity in the final layers... But you're going to have some problems with residual stresses eventually. They could not make that as a six-inch by six-inch part without getting cracks.

summary: Understand thermal dynamics and dimensional stability when machining freshly printed metal parts that are still cooling or thermally stressed.
verbatim: A lot of times you have to do a final machining step to get to really accurate tolerances, so doing machining to a somewhat hot part — you could have a molten metal part, so you have to wait for it to cool to a certain degree until you can machine it. But you're still dealing with all these thermal stresses, trying to machine in process. Then at the final part you're probably going to have to stress-relieve, and when you stress-relieve it's going to move, and you're going to have to machine it again.

summary: The mechanism by which rolling parameters cause centerline splitting in aluminum plate remains unexplained.
verbatim: This is a mistake in rolling. They rolled this half-inch aluminum plate, and because of the way they rolled it, it split right down the center.

summary: Why Carolina live oak was structurally superior to other oak species used in shipbuilding remains unexplained.
verbatim: It was Carolina live oak. There is now a society to preserve the Carolina live oak because it's stronger than any other oak in the world. That's why Old Ironsides survived and they said the cannon just bounced off — because it was the strongest wood.

summary: The long-term chemical stability of 19th-century borosilicate glass used in botanical specimens remains unknown, with field data suggesting significant degradation over a century.
verbatim: One of the things they didn't do was all the materials science to know whether the glasses were going to be stable over the next 100 years or whether they would decompose. Apparently only about 30% of them are still on display.

summary: Why do propeller bolts from certain vessels develop cracks under the head despite sophisticated Morgrip tensioning methods?
verbatim: This bolt, as I remember, came off an Israeli Corvette propeller. They were cracking — there are cracks right under the head.

summary: Why high-strength steels like HY-130 and HY-200 cannot maintain toughness while solving hydrogen embrittlement remains fundamentally unsolved.
verbatim: No one's ever really solved the hydrogen problems and been able to keep the toughness up.

summary: MP35N bolts cannot be manufactured in large plate or structural forms despite exceptional strength-ductility properties, limiting applications.
verbatim: You can make it into 2- or 3-inch bolts if you start with a 6-inch diameter rod, but you can't make it into plate.

summary: Achieving true multifunction materials that serve simultaneously as structural members and hydrogen containment vessels remains unsolved for single-stage-to-orbit spacecraft.
verbatim: To do it, you have to have multifunction materials. The tanks were supposed to be the structural part. They not only had to hold liquid hydrogen, they also had to provide the mechanical properties for the whole structure.

summary: Eagar identifies a fundamental gap: no structural material is made by vapor deposition despite its dominance in functional materials, suggesting an unexplored thermodynamic or kinetic barrier worth characterizing.
verbatim: I decided I'd do a calculation, because I couldn't think of any structural material that's made by vapor deposition... I did learn enough about vapor deposition that I decided I could prove why we don't use it to make structural materials.

summary: Why vapor-deposited coatings shatter when applied to bulk structural geometry (e.g., a full titanium-nitride drill bit) versus succeeding as thin films on steel substrates.
verbatim: If you made a titanium-nitride drill bit, the first time you drilled, you'd shatter it. As a thin film, it has very good wear resistance, which is what you're using it for.

summary: The Army has spent decades trying to vapor-deposit structural coatings inside gun barrels but defaults to electroplated chromium; identifying superior but cost-competitive materials for interior bore protection remains unsolved.
verbatim: The Army's been trying to do that for gun barrels for years... It's good if you're making gun barrels and selling them, but it's not good if you're the Army buying them... They know there are better materials than chromium, but there's nothing as cheap.

summary: Understand why private companies stopped building integrated steel mills after 1965, unlike government-backed efforts.
verbatim: We've had new steel mills built since 1965. POSCO, the world's largest steel company, in Pohang, Korea, built a steel mill in the 1970s. But POSCO Steel was not bankrolled by financial people — it was bankrolled by the Korean government. There have been probably a dozen steel mills built in the world since 1965 on greenfield sites, but not a single one has been built by a company that was risking shareholder money.

summary: Vanadium-attack mechanisms on stainless steel in high-temperature oil combustion remain poorly characterized despite decades of practical knowledge.
verbatim: Venezuelan oil contains vanadium, and vanadium forms an oxide that melts off the protective chromium oxide of stainless steel... Today the American Petroleum Institute has specs on getting the vanadium out. There is really only one alloy — a nickel-chrome alloy — that can survive vanadium.

summary: Thermal shock and erosion damage mechanisms in blast furnace refractory linings under cyclic thermal and pressure loading lack systematic study.
verbatim: You have to have abrasion-resistant walls. You have erosion all the way along. You have thermal shock from thermal expansion.

summary: Slag represents a massive waste stream (hundreds of millions of tons annually) with limited end uses; developing higher-value applications or reduction pathways remains an unsolved practical problem.
verbatim: One of the problems in the world is we produce a couple hundred million tons a year of slag which goes into landfills by and large.

summary: Rimmed steels produce superior surface quality due to carbon boil mechanisms, but the metallurgical reason for this advantage and how to replicate it in modern continuous casting is unclear.
verbatim: Rim steel gave excellent surface quality, whereas plate steels you end up with inclusions and other things on the surface.

summary: The mechanism by which thermal stress gradients during furnace heating cause brittle cracking in large steel ingots with internal defects remains incompletely understood and poorly documented across the metallurgical community.
verbatim: I will tell you that in the last twenty-five years, when I've met other metallurgists — not that I talk about this every day, but it could be a couple dozen metallurgists I've talked to and asked them if they know what a clink is — I've only found one metallurgist who knew what a clink was.

summary: The practical limits and qualification procedures for welding very thick stainless steel pieces (20+ inches) for high-reliability applications like fusion reactor components.
verbatim: About twenty years ago, the guys over here at the MIT Plasma Fusion Center came to me and they wanted to weld twenty-inch-thick by about four-foot-long stainless steel together... So every now and then someone wants to weld a piece of something that's twenty inches thick. Can it be done? Yes. But you can't make a lot of test welds and have them screw up.

summary: Undercooling and rapid solidification have been demonstrated for only one element (phosphorus); extending this to other materials remains unresolved.
verbatim: The more you undercool, you'd like to get to the point where if the heat of fusion is less than the heat capacity times delta T, you could undercool, nucleate, and solidify the whole thing all at once, instantaneously. They've done that, but only for one element in the periodic table: phosphorus.

summary: Steel band degradation mechanism in the Hazelett continuous casting process remains poorly characterized despite decades of industrial use.
verbatim: Every couple of days. They know approximately how long they last. It's actually a titanium-bearing steel. They've done a lot of work on these.

summary: The threshold thickness at which rapid-solidified iron-boron alloys transition from amorphous to semi-crystalline structure is known empirically but not well characterized.
verbatim: If you made it ten-thousandths of an inch thick — a quarter of a millimeter — that's too thick to get rapid solidification, and you wouldn't get an amorphous metal, you would get a semi-crystalline metal.

summary: Amorphous metal powders crystallize and lose their metastable structure when heated to modest temperatures, preventing the creation of ultra-fine stable structures despite decades of effort.
verbatim: The problem is these amorphous materials — even if it's an iron-based alloy, you heat them up to 400° centigrade and they crystallize, they transform. It's a non-stable structure, it's a metallic glass. People have been trying this for years to make ultra-fine structures.

summary: No established method exists for consolidating small rods produced by the Conform extrusion process into load-bearing plate geometry suitable for armor applications.
verbatim: The problem is, you can make it into rods because you're extruding it out, but how do you consolidate those rods into a plate? Usually you like your armor to be plate-shaped rather than rod-shaped.

summary: Understand why hydrogen solubility in aluminum alloys increases dramatically with magnesium content and how this affects degassing strategy.
verbatim: This is hydrogen solubility in different aluminum alloys as a function of temperature, and if you have lots of magnesium it's a lot worse. Magnesium will dissolve more hydrogen than aluminum.

summary: Develop practical degassing techniques for aluminum casting that match the effectiveness of chlorine gas but without environmental and safety hazards.
verbatim: How do you degas your aluminum now? [after chlorine gas was prohibited]

summary: The mechanism by which laser superheating vaporizes inclusions in weld metal remains incompletely characterized, despite Metzbower's empirical observations.
verbatim: He figured out that the superheating from the laser beam in the weld metal was vaporizing all the inclusions, and he got better properties in the weld metal than in the base plate because he was getting rid of those inclusion particles.

summary: The transient thermal stress failure mechanism in Navy heat exchangers that caused catastrophic failure in two minutes is not fully explained.
verbatim: They built it, and they found that it lasted not 100,000 hours but about two minutes, before it tore itself apart due to the transient thermal stresses. They fixed it, and I'm told now you actually do have ICRs in your ships. I remember I ended up being on what they call a Blue Ribbon panel, and we had to go out and look at it and say what was wrong.

summary: The assumption of perfect diffusion in the liquid during solidification does not match reality and needs investigation.
verbatim: They're assuming perfect diffusion in the liquid here, which is not really true — but in any case, you will actually sweep the concentration of the B component to the end of this thing if you solidify in one direction.

summary: Understand why HIP cannot eliminate segregation in bulk castings despite being effective for rapidly solidified powders.
verbatim: No, HIP will not do it, unless you start with something that's rapidly solidified powder, which has very small dendrites as a powder... HIP is used for a lot of powder processing. We get rid of the segregation by doing rapid solidification of powders, but then we have to weld the powders together.

summary: Eagar notes that metals have a strain-rate sensitivity exponent m around 0.2, compared to 1.0 for Newtonian fluids and 0.9 for glass, but doesn't explain the physical origin of this value or how to predict it for different alloys.
verbatim: A Newtonian fluid is when m equals one. For a typical metal, m equals 0.2. So if you have any instability in a metal where it starts to thin down a little bit, that instability will grow. It will neck down and break at the thin spot. A Newtonian metal — you can have a little neck in there and you can pull it out a hundred miles, if it really is an m of one. The only Newtonian fluid that we might work with typically is glass — may have 0.9. Metals typically have 0.2.

summary: The strain-rate sensitivity parameter m varies strongly with grain size in superplastic metals, but the quantitative relationship and underlying mechanisms remain incompletely characterized.
verbatim: Turns out m's a very strong function of grain size. If you get superfine grains, you can get extremely high abilities to stretch a material.

summary: Map the critical cold-welding threshold and surface strain limit that triggers surface crack initiation in multi-pass deformation.
verbatim: If you don't have enough lubricant, you start cold welding the material to the surface. If you get more than thirty percent local strain, it breaks. But if you deform it, don't break it, take it out, put it in another tool that's lubricated again, then you can start deforming again.

summary: The mechanism causing non-uniform plate thickness distribution (wavy edges vs. center) during hot rolling of thick aluminum plates with water cooling is not fully explained.
verbatim: So this hot aluminum plate is going through a little waterfall of water. It's not a heavy waterfall, but it's raining on the plate. [Context: This causes off-gauge conditions where thickness varies by twenty thousandths across a 3/4-inch plate depending on location.]

summary: A student explained 80% of plate thickness variation via cooling estimates, but the remaining 20% of unexplained variance in end-of-plate defects is unaccounted for.
verbatim: We could explain eighty percent of the variation they were seeing by our estimates of the cooling and how much increase in strength of the colder aluminum on the ends of the plates, depending on whether the water was on there.

summary: Under-deposit corrosion of cast iron in seawater remains a practical failure mode despite cast iron's normally excellent corrosion resistance due to its silica-rich passive film.
verbatim: Ordinarily the cast iron will last for a hundred years or more if you maintain it... But chlorides will eat through that when you start getting under-deposit attack.

summary: Why does 90/10 cupro-nickel perform well in erosion-corrosion service when 70/30 was theoretically expected to be necessary?
verbatim: I was being a little conservative when they said how do we solve this problem, I said you need to go to 70/30, because I knew from the velocity data that 70/30 would have had enough safety factor. Couldn't get it, used 90/10, and it's worked.

summary: Duplex stainless steel becomes problematic when welded, yet its suitability for critical structural applications with unavoidable welds remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: They said, well, can we use the duplex stainless steel? I said, sure, as long as you don't have any weld details. Can't weld this without real problems.

summary: The long-term durability of 2205 duplex stainless in a near-saltwater, hurricane-prone environment with stress-corrosion-cracking risk is unvalidated beyond the initial project outcome.
verbatim: I said, well, I don't know if you're going to make ten years on 316. Just shooting from the hip... there's something called stress corrosion cracking.

summary: The mechanism and kinetics of pitting corrosion in stainless steel under chloride attack vary sharply across alloy grades but lack a unified predictive framework.
verbatim: This is pitting of stainless steel... It's 304 stainless steel. That's a hundred and four millimeters per year... This is chloride pitting resistance versus chloride. This is 304, 316, 2205, and pitting... significantly better than 316 or 304.

summary: Seawater degradation mechanisms for syntactic foam resin systems remain inadequately characterized beyond empirical 10–20 year aging windows.
verbatim: It's basically little micro glass spheres — they can be lots of different sizes — encapsulated in a resin that will not be degraded by seawater over 10 or 20 years. All plastics get degraded by seawater over 10 years — that's the story of your rubber again.

summary: Why gas metal arc welding failed during the Sea Cliff hull fabrication at Mare Island despite prior development at David Taylor, while gas tungsten arc succeeded.
verbatim: They tried to prove out the welding technology that had been developed at David Taylor in Annapolis, gas metal arc welding, and they couldn't do it. They tried for six months and it just didn't work.

summary: CSST lightning perforation mechanism remains unexplained despite hundreds of documented failures.
verbatim: It's only happened about four or five hundred times... By 2001 they knew it was lightning — that there was perforating, holes in the pipe. And the bottom line story is it's just too thin...

summary: Why black iron pipe resists lightning perforation while CSST fails is poorly understood from a materials science perspective.
verbatim: No one had ever had a fire with black iron pipe because lightning had never perforated black iron pipe, so they didn't worry about it.

summary: Isotopic concentration errors in water standards limit temperature calibration precision; understanding and reducing these errors could improve accuracy beyond current millidegree limits.
verbatim: The errors in isotopic concentration are essentially what limits you to this thousandth of a degree accuracy. However, the calibration cell is good to 7 microKelvin.

summary: Understanding why different steel compositions produce distinctly different spark patterns during grinding remains empirically known but mechanistically unexplained.
verbatim: This is all a question of how the steel oxidizes. I can't tell the difference if you put two of these in front of me. But if you'd been doing it for thirty years, you could.

summary: The physics of spark formation during grinding—how oxidation state, carbon content, and alloying elements drive spark intensity and morphology—lacks a rigorous quantitative model.
verbatim: Stainless doesn't spark much because it doesn't oxidize well. This is all a question of how the steel oxidizes.

summary: How shipbuilders actually achieve millimeter alignment on 300-meter vessels when thermal expansion from cloud cover causes half-inch deflections remains poorly explained.
verbatim: If the sun goes behind a cloud, the ship changes shape by half an inch — and you have to align them within a millimeter... I said, 'Great big 100-ton jacks. They just squeeze them together.'

summary: The fundamental limits and practical strategies for controlling thermal distortion in large-scale ship assembly under real environmental conditions are underexplored.
verbatim: Shipbuilding ten years ago was the most precise — in parts per million or billion — manufacturing we did... If the sun goes behind a cloud, the ship changes shape by half an inch — and you have to align them within a millimeter.

summary: Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) gold assay remains ~2.5× less accurate than fire assay; closing this gap could displace a millennia-old standard.
verbatim: Twenty-five or thirty years ago I was given the job of coming up with a better process than fire assay. We couldn't do it then. We're getting close now with inductively coupled plasma — probably one part in 2,000.

summary: The root cause of closed conformity in the 40-inch Reali-Slim bearing remains unexplained despite evidence of its occurrence.
verbatim: Why was there a closed conformity? When you've got something as flexible as a 40-inch diameter ring that's only one inch high and even less in thickness, that's pretty flexible... The helicopter manufacturer manufactured that big aluminum housing themselves, and they just never bothered to look into the shape of that housing — and in fact they destroyed it.

summary: The practical limit of manufacturability for thin, large-diameter bearings with respect to runout and conformity control is not well characterized.
verbatim: You're heading in the wrong direction, which is one of the limitations on the ability to even manufacture bearings this thin and this small.

summary: Why do perfectly spec'd bearings fail in service after 30 years of reliable operation—a mystery case where government-inspected parts still seized in the field.
verbatim: They put some of these new ones in the field. These bearings were better bearings — none of the manufacturing defects — and they put them into the helicopters. They had to manufacture a thousand of these. All these things go out there, and guess what? Within two months one of them fails. One of the good bearings fails. But it was perfectly within spec, and these things have been flying for thirty years. What had happened?

summary: The fundamental mechanism by which lightning penetrates thin-walled CSST tubing while being stopped by thicker black iron pipe remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: The CSST, if it gets hit by lightning, creates a hole. It's just too thin. They didn't bother to read the NFPA 780 twenty years ago when they were developing the standards for that product.

summary: Understand why hydrostatic testing at 50% pressure (1,250 PSI vs. 2,500 PSI breaking strength) reliably detects defects that would cause in-service failure despite allowing flaws halfway through wall thickness.
verbatim: If you do the hydrostatic test, this pipe might take 2,500 PSI to break it, but you may only test it at 1,250. What does that mean? You probably could pass the pipe if it had a flaw about halfway through... That's why people have learned a hydrostatic test on every single piece of pipe is good enough.

summary: Statistical modeling of defect detection under partial inspection sampling has never been validated against real field failure data in structural welding.
verbatim: If you're only going to test ten percent, you're going to have to accept that if five percent of welds have defects, and you only test ten percent, you're going to still have four and a half percent defective welds out there... But the safety factors — which someone else will talk about — will hopefully take care of that four and a half percent. We've learned historically what to do.

summary: Understand why proper torque on a two-stage bolt assembly initiates cracks in the smaller-diameter section.
verbatim: It turns out the proper torque for this is just enough to start a crack in this... if your load path ignores this little shoulder and you don't grab it and keep it restrained, now your load path goes all the way through to the other nut, and all of a sudden you over-torque this thing.

summary: The safety factor used (1.67) for a dynamically loaded, fatigued connection was inadequate, but standards and practice for fatigue-loaded building connections remain unclear.
verbatim: It should have been a factor of 2 because it's dynamically loaded. This is not just a static building, this is something that could be swinging out there in the atrium, so it's fatigue loaded.

summary: Understand why mandrel fatigue cracks form and detach during seamless pipe piercing, creating rolling defects.
verbatim: The steel mandrel that pushed to make the tube probably had a fatigue crack on the end, and a piece broke off inside as it was piercing it, and just rolled that piece of cold steel into the hot steel.

summary: Thermal effects during high-speed fatigue testing (100 Hz) may confound results by converting room-temperature tests into heated tests; unclear how much this artifact affects measured fatigue strength.
verbatim: The problem with doing a fatigue test at 100 Hertz: you're putting enough elastic energy in there that you have to be careful you don't overheat your sample, and now you're doing a hot test rather than a room temperature test.

summary: No systematic study exists of why safety factors for Charpy toughness have escalated from 10 foot-pounds (critical threshold found in Liberty ships) to 20+ foot-pounds, or whether this creep is evidence-based or conservative.
verbatim: They found that all the ones with major failures had Charpy energy less than 10 foot-pounds. So what do you do? Put a safety factor on it. From then on they wouldn't build Navy ships and most other structures unless they had 15 foot-pounds. By 1960 the Coast Guard decided that wasn't enough — they made it 20 foot-pounds.

summary: The natural variability in steel toughness (15–30 foot-pounds across heats) remains unexplained despite known factors like sulfur content and grain size.
verbatim: There's natural variability — toughness going from 15 to 30 foot-pounds, you can still have that range of variability... When your mean was only half a foot-pound above your minimum, that's not good.

summary: Carbon fiber composite drive shafts fail catastrophically in engine fires, unlike metallic alternatives—the fire dynamics and failure mechanism remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: In the engine fire, the drive shaft burned up within seconds — it did try to transfer torque, but it tore itself in two. Afterwards they redesigned it and switched the drive shafts to titanium, increasing the safety factor against fire. It's not that they hadn't thought about fire — they just didn't particularly think of the engine becoming a fire-breathing dragon, which is essentially what happened.

summary: Sprinkler heads with Wood's metal sensors degrade prematurely when stored above 100°F, but the mechanism and creep kinetics of this failure mode are not well understood.
verbatim: It cannot be stored above 100 degrees Fahrenheit, because some of them use Wood's metal as the melting sensor at 160 degrees. If it stays above 100 degrees for longer than a certain time, it'll creep, and these things can fail at less than their rated temperature.

summary: Finding physical phenomena with oscillation frequencies higher than 10 gigahertz to improve the fundamental precision limit of atomic timekeeping.
verbatim: If you can find something that reproducibly and reliably gives you a higher frequency than 10 gigahertz, we can get one better than one part in 10 to the 10th. But that's our limit on time.

summary: Understanding why deformation transforms 302 stainless steel from austenitic to ferromagnetic, changing its crystal structure and magnetic properties.
verbatim: The reason I have 302 balls in there is because the more they're deformed, the more ferromagnetic they become. They transform on deformation to become magnetic.

summary: Why 302 and 316 stainless steels show different magnetism levels despite similar nominal composition—the mechanism behind partial ferromagnetism in 302 versus non-magnetic 316.
verbatim: You could actually have distinguished the 316 from the 302 by the level of magnetism.

summary: The root cause of bearing seizure in the MH-53 helicopter swash plate bearing under hover conditions remains unexplained despite multiple in-service failures.
verbatim: All of a sudden the bearing started to seize, the helicopter crashed, and the two pilots died... Over the next few months they did have more incidents — the Japanese Navy had one go down... they had a couple go down at other places.

summary: Understand why bearing wear patterns vary systematically by quadrant in a large flexible bearing, indicating non-circular deformation of the housing.
verbatim: They weren't all equal barrels. Some were skinny barrels and some were fat barrels. And they went in quadrants. First and third quadrant you had fat barrels, second and fourth you had skinny barrels. Why?

summary: Understand why bearing failures occur at steel-aluminum housing interfaces despite both components meeting individual specifications.
verbatim: A lot of times failures occur at the interfaces. We have the interface between the steel bearing made by company A and the helicopter swash plate made by company B. And if they don't fit together, whose fault is it?

summary: Design-to-manufacturing feedback loop is missing: we can now simulate geometry, stresses, and performance, but cannot yet predict how real manufacturing tolerances and QC programs will affect the final design.
verbatim: Now we have to get back, as Simone says, to manufacturability, and we're not there yet. You can't simulate everything... what's our manufacturing capability, what tolerances can we really control, what QC programs will we put in.

summary: Terahertz band generation and control remains underdeveloped for practical applications.
verbatim: There are little bands in here, like the terahertz band between infrared and radar, that really isn't used much. Some guys over in electrical engineering are trying to figure out how to do it. The hard thing is to control things — now we're talking about electrons moving several millimeters. In the terahertz regime you're talking about submillimeter wavelengths, and it's hard to figure out what to do. If you could develop devices that generate those rays efficiently — anyway, we use almost everything in that electromagnetic spectrum to observe materials in one way or another.

summary: How internal corrosion of aluminum tanks interacts with fatigue and weld defects to reduce service life and failure pressure.
verbatim: We go in and start looking at the tank. It was corroding on the inside, there was fatigue, lots of things wrong, bad welds in some of the originals.

summary: When multiple codes written by different committees conflict, there is no systematic method to resolve which code governs—currently handled ad hoc by consultants.
verbatim: But since they weren't all written by the same person — in fact they're all written by different committees — the codes have problems of conflicts. That's what keeps me in business to a certain extent. There's not a simple answer to what you do when there's conflict in the code.

summary: Understand why grinding swarf patterns indicate subsurface microcracking in submarine welds, and whether these submicroscopic defects pose actual structural risk.
verbatim: This grinder grinding the weld notices that the swarf — the little particles from grinding, called swarf, good Scrabble word, S-W-A-R-F — the swarf is lining up in little lines, less than a sixteenth of an inch in length. He says, I've never seen that before... They start investigating it, and the welds had a whole family, a cluster — they were full of these little micro-cracks.

summary: Determine the actual structural consequence of fillet weld measurement definitions (leg length vs. throat thickness) on joint strength and establish which metric truly predicts load-bearing capacity.
verbatim: The size of that fillet weld is defined in the United States as the leg length. The problem is there are two leg lengths... In Europe they use a more scientific definition, the throat thickness... The two should be related if it was a perfect triangle, which it's not... you have to say, what do I really want to measure? What you really want is some surrogate for the strength.

summary: Understand why a tool fragment wedged in pipe wall passed two successive hydrostatic tests but failed a third at lower pressure, possibly due to plastic deformation.
verbatim: I don't know if the plug came loose because of the previous hydro tests starting to give a little plastic deformation, opening it up so the wedge could fall out. When the wedge was no longer there, it wouldn't pass the hydro — it leaked.

summary: Investigate why the hydrostatic test failed to detect a 3–4 inch flaw at 80% wall thickness despite passing twice earlier.
verbatim: It passed the first hydro test because it had a plug in it — a V-shaped plug. It passed the hydro test at the mill, it passed the inspection because it was in a critical area that was not very well inspected.

summary: How to establish practical acceptance criteria for internal weld flaws that account for actual stress, environment, and corrosion allowance rather than relying on arbitrary code thresholds.
verbatim: You really need someone with engineering training to determine whether the flaw is acceptable or rejectable. That depends on the stress level, the environment, the wear allowance, the corrosion allowance.

summary: Bleach-induced stress corrosion cracking in stainless steel food processing tanks remains undetected until catastrophic failure occurs.
verbatim: What does bleach do to stainless steel? It corrodes it. And what happens underneath the insulation — if some of that bleach gets under the insulation, you've got corrosion going on that no one can see, and no one takes the insulation off.

summary: Long-term tension retention in cable-stay bridge cables under fatigue loading is not systematically monitored or understood.
verbatim: It's a fatigue-loaded situation, but the tension should stay fairly constant. Plus there's a big safety factor — safety factors are tomorrow's lecture with Dr. Belmar, and safety factors take care of a lot of mistakes. I don't think so. They may go back and check from time to time, but there's not a continuous adjustment every year. I don't know enough to say they don't check after five or ten years.

summary: Why don't buried steel gas pipes from the 1930s fail faster despite predicted 5–25 year perforation times?
verbatim: The pipe running down my street, water pipe and gas pipe, have been there more than 70 years. Why aren't they full of holes? Well, it is full of holes. Science is science. But it's surrounded by mud, and the mud seals it.

summary: Resolve discrepancy between calculated voltage (40 kV/m) and literature claims (2.5 MV) for arc initiation in plastic piping.
verbatim: I can show you a book on lightning that claims you can develop two and a half million volts, not just forty thousand. Same calculation, a little more sophisticated; they use two microhenrys rather than one.

summary: Lightning attachment and failure mechanism in flexible gas tubing remains incompletely characterized despite field failures.
verbatim: Part of it is people didn't think about the physics of a lightning strike. They didn't consider lightning... There's no engineering capability within these firms.

summary: Single-point versus multi-point grounding effectiveness for lightning protection in residential gas piping systems lacks rigorous validation.
verbatim: I pointed out that single-point grounding — one point in your house — is not good enough. The lightning, in the time of the lightning flash, can only see a distance of about ten feet in any direction. You'd have to ground it every ten feet.

summary: Why do iron whiskers achieve 2 million PSI strength while modern steels don't reach this theoretical limit despite decades of materials science.
verbatim: We grew iron whiskers in the 1950s that were a single crystal, all but a screw dislocation up the axis. They pulled those and got 2 million PSI strength experimentally, because if you don't have any mobile dislocations, you pull on a screw dislocation parallel with the axis of the screw dislocation, it won't move. It was like pulling a perfect crystal, and they got 2 million PSI strength for steel. We don't have steels at 2 million PSI.

summary: Understand why hydrostatic stress suppresses fracture in brittle materials during deformation processing.
verbatim: You can process by deformation some brittle materials, but under very special conditions. Anybody know what those conditions are? Those conditions are when you apply a lot of hydrostatic stress. You can suppress fracture if you have a lot of hydrostatic stress.

summary: Poisson's ratio and volume change behavior in foamed or porous materials under plastic deformation remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: If I deformed this piece of foamed aluminum, it's going to have different Poisson ratios. It's not going to have a zero volume change if I deform it, because I'm going to break up the pores.

summary: The transition from brittle to plastic deformation in rocks under deep confining pressure is not well characterized as a function of depth.
verbatim: So if you want to go study the fracture of rocks for earthquakes and stuff — it's a lot more complex than the simple fracture we have of rocks on Earth on the surface, because they're brittle and we can set brittle behavior. But the brittleness of rocks is a function of the depth in the earth.

summary: The yield criterion (Tresca vs von Mises) that governs deformation varies with crystallographic orientation and material class, but the boundaries are not systematically mapped.
verbatim: It's not always correct in crystalline materials. For a BCC metal or an FCC metal in the 110 plane in the 011 direction, the Tresca condition is correct, and I'll show you that later in the course.

summary: The relationship between hardness test pressure and uniaxial compressive strength appears consistent across materials, but the physical mechanisms underlying this 3× correlation remain underexplored.
verbatim: With work hardening, does anybody know what the rule is for a hardness test in terms of the pressure of the hardness test compared to the uniaxial compressive strength of the material, whether it's steel or aluminum or anything else? There's actually a correlation.

summary: Why multi-directional forging (three directions) suppresses internal centerline defects better than two-directional forging remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: If you actually forge from three directions, you can help suppress some of that. Or if you forge on an anvil die, which is what he's got here with three directions, you can suppress the tendency. Just forging from two directions is not as good as forging from three directions, in terms of suppressing the internal defects, depending on the delta operation.

summary: Grain size may control surface roughness and tolerance limits during deformation, analogous to orange peel formation.
verbatim: large grains don't deform uniformly at the surface and you will get a surface roughness that can be a lot more than that. It's called orange peel because it has the texture of an orange

summary: Characterize lubricant depletion and stearate retention under extreme sliding conditions in rapid cold-heading extrusion.
verbatim: If you just try to do oil all those extrusion operations, you have so much sliding against the workpiece, the oil would be gone. You have to have some peanut butter that has sticking power through long stretching of that.

summary: How lubricant films behave under the extreme pressures (3× yield strength) encountered in cold forming remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: I have some contact area K. From this I might be able to estimate some deformation zone geometry. The plastic deformation — this is a Delta equal to 10 type operation, high Delta operation, like a hardness test. But you will have a lubricant film which might get pushed aside under these very high pressures. I'm talking about pressures that can be three times the yield strength of the material. So the lubricant films don't always stay in place.

summary: The role of friction in determining deformation zone geometry during rolling and forming operations needs characterization beyond the frictionless-processing approximations in standard texts.
verbatim: What we want to talk about is the effect of friction. This is figure 8.1 of Backofen. Some of the science is: I've got some compressive pressure P that might be the yield strength, the local yield strength, I have some contact area K. From this I might be able to estimate some deformation zone geometry.

summary: The mechanism by which axisymmetric wire deformation reduces the inhomogeneity factor compared to plain-strain strip deformation—specifically why the 'plug' of undeformed material in the center creates less redundant deformation—deserves explicit analysis.
verbatim: Because I'm forcing the material to squeeze. The stuff in the center is hardly deforming at all. There's a big plug of material that doesn't get work-hardened very much. That plug of material that's not deforming — the redundant deformation is not as big.

summary: Understand why centerline cracks form in wire drawing and extrusion despite low strain (Delta ~1.5), when compressive forces fail to penetrate to the axial center.
verbatim: If I call this the axisymmetric line going down the center — this is a Delta operation of like 1.5. Not very high Delta. But look at that little arrow point right there. That's in tension. It actually started to slip and shear. All this stuff is in heavy compression, but as I get towards the center I actually get to tension. Because of the inhomogeneous deformation, the compressive forces don't reach all the way to the center.

summary: Characterize the stress state and failure mechanism in the Blackhawk helicopter washer to understand how residual stress and stress-corrosion cracking interact in aluminum alloys used for critical components.
verbatim: An Army helicopter in Arkansas was doing a night vision goggles training exercise, and it crashed and killed six Army soldiers and two pilots. It was because this aluminum washer was supposed to have been stress-relieved and was not. It had residual stresses in it, and it got stress corrosion cracking.

summary: Understand the physical mechanism by which orange peel surface texture forms in large-grain sheet materials during stamping.
verbatim: One of you asked me about orange peel. Here's a picture of orange peel — this is from Hosford's book too, probably chapter 16. I don't know what it is — looks like it might have been the bottom of a gas tank in the automotive industry — but it's a drawing from a stamping from sheet metal, and the surface looks like an orange. It's caused by large grain size.

summary: Why stearate molecules are such effective lubricants in metal forming remains unexplained.
verbatim: remember, soaps are stearates, and later we'll talk about why stearates are such good lubricants.

summary: The mechanism by which hydrostatic pressure allows metals to reach higher elongation without causing shape change needs clarification.
verbatim: It might allow it to go to higher elongation, but it doesn't cause the shape change. The shape change is due to shear.

summary: Understanding why superplasticity enables 400% stretch in nickel-base superalloys at 2200°F, and what physical mechanisms enable clay-like deformation.
verbatim: in superplastic forming you get material that, instead of taking a 30% stretch, will take a 400% stretch... You take the nickel-base superalloy up to 2200°F and it will deform like clay.

summary: Determine the physical basis for why Amtrak's trolley wire specification imposed an upper limit on elongation (8–14%) rather than just a minimum.
verbatim: Amtrak for some reason had a spec of between 8 and 14% elongation, and this stuff had 18% elongation. It had too much elongation. It was too ductile. It was too good. Ordinarily you have to meet a minimum, but they had given an upper limit. Why someone said the elongation should be between 8 and 14, I don't know.

summary: Understand why large grain size in drawn copper wire causes catastrophic surface degradation and sparking against pantograph brushes at operational speed.
verbatim: There really was nothing in the literature that said you couldn't do this, that the grain size should be a big problem. But it turned out it was essentially an orange peel effect, a large grain size effect.

summary: The mechanism by which non-uniform work hardening from inhomogeneous flow creates residual stress distributions remains underdeveloped.
verbatim: The last thing I listed was residual stresses. If I have non-uniform flow and some of it's shearing once, twice, three times, and other material is just shearing once to get the same shape change, in different parts of the part I've got different amounts of work hardening.

summary: Whether mechanical stretch or compression actually equalizes the residual stress distribution across a part, or merely smooths peaks and valleys.
verbatim: You compress it 3% — you pancake it 3% — rather than stretch it. Still mechanical stress relief. The parts that are high compression you will yield, and the places that are low compression, when you do that compression you will not yield, so when you're all done you've smoothed out all the peaks and valleys of residual stress going across the part.

summary: Dead zones form under specific friction and die-angle conditions, but the precise criteria for predicting when they occur remain unclear.
verbatim: If your die angle is not right, then nature will say that the easiest shearing plane may not be the frictional plane of the workpiece. There may be a lower-energy shear at some other angle, in which case you'll just shear the material — full frictional shear of the material.

summary: The recrystallization behavior of intermediate cold-work material (10–50% strain) is unpredictable and produces inhomogeneous grain sizes, unlike fully deformed or undeformed material.
verbatim: This stuff may or may not recrystallize, but if it does you're going to end up with a bunch of different grain sizes... The worst possible situation is some sort of intermediate or low level of work. You have to put a lot of work into the material to get a uniform product.

summary: The Conform process has material limits—steels crack the dies—but the fundamental mechanical reason for the strength ceiling across different alloys is not explained.
verbatim: The loads are so high that if you try to put steel through, all you're going to do is crack your steel dies. The steel is not strong enough to deform steel that much. You can deform aluminum because it's soft, you can sort of do copper, you can't do brass very easily — you'll crack your dies, almost no die life.

summary: How friction coefficient in ring tests varies with contact time and deformation rate at high temperatures remains unclear for nickel-based superalloys.
verbatim: The contact time — someone was asking how long — is a fraction of a second, measured in tens of milliseconds... The frictional shear factor as measured in a ring test was anywhere from 0.18 to 0.53.

summary: Understand what causes overlapping defects (forging laps) when material fills closed-die cavities during forging.
verbatim: In a closed die forging, when you're trying to fill some cavity, as you're trying to fill this mold, you will get situations where you actually get overlaps.

summary: Characterize the frequency and detectability of end-effect defects in forgings caused by metal flow stagnation near die exits.
verbatim: At the end you basically get a dead zone... it doesn't want to go too far in that direction and turn a 90-degree turn... in some cases that type of defect shows up in forgings, because people weren't careful about the end of the forging.

summary: Investigate the wear resistance mechanisms of indium tin oxide coatings under repeated mechanical contact, such as in touchscreen buttons.
verbatim: The problem is, it doesn't have great wear resistance. You ever go into an automatic teller, and down where they have the button in the same corner, and people hit it with their fingernail, and it wears out? So wear is a problem.

summary: Quantify how anisotropic texture in rolled sheet metal affects strength in the through-thickness versus in-plane directions, analogous to grain anisotropy in wood.
verbatim: Who says that the strength in the through-thickness direction of a thin sheet is the same as it is in the sheet, pulling in the direction of the sheet? And who says that pulling in the one direction is the same as pulling in the two direction, if one is the rolling direction of a piece of sheet, two is the transverse direction, and three is the through-thickness direction?

summary: Eagar notes that most metals have very low strain-rate sensitivity (m ≈ 0.01–0.02), causing necking, whereas superplastic materials achieve m ≥ 0.3; the mechanism underlying this wide range remains unclear.
verbatim: If you can get m up to 0.3, it will start to behave superplastically. Superplastic materials have large m values like 0.3. Most metals have m values on the order of 0.01 or 0.02.

summary: Understand why work-hardening rates differ between principal stress directions in anisotropic materials.
verbatim: But who says that the ellipse is going to grow with the same amount of work hardening in the one direction as the two direction? The ellipse doesn't have to be just a larger version of the smaller ellipse. You can have a change in your major and minor axis, if the material is not perfectly isotropic in the way it deforms.

summary: Why do hexagonal close-packed metals like alpha titanium achieve R values of 4–5 through twinning, while cubic metals max out at 2–3?
verbatim: And how can you get all the way up to five just because you're hexagonal close packed?

summary: Hydrogen embrittlement in high-strength steels may not always produce the characteristic intergranular fracture, making diagnosis difficult in ~2% of cases.
verbatim: Ninety-eight percent of the time you do, so these people are thinking, well, I don't see intergranular, it can't be hydrogen. You need to know about the other 2% sometimes.

summary: Brittle failures in high-strength steel elevator cables and aircraft-grade steels lack the expected intergranular fracture pattern even when hydrogen embrittlement is suspected, complicating failure diagnosis.
verbatim: One of the things you always suspect when you have brittle failures in steel is hydrogen embrittlement. He says, but we didn't see intergranular fracture... It's not characteristic in piano wire because you don't have grains that are well enough shaped to give you intergranular fracture.

summary: Eagar notes that plane strain conditions in cup drawing occur at two distinct locations but behave equivalently only in isotropic materials—the mechanisms differ fundamentally when anisotropy is present.
verbatim: A couple days ago I told you that this is plane strain and this is plane strain, and the two are equivalent. They are equivalent except when you're anisotropic. Here the strengthening is minor, here the strengthening is major.

summary: High-temperature superconductors show a critical-current anisotropy of seven orders of magnitude depending on field orientation, but published measurements typically only report the favorable parallel-field case.
verbatim: The people who are measuring it and telling you that they're getting 10-to-the-eighth amps per square cm are doing it with the field parallel, not perpendicular. If they measure it the other way, the critical current is not 10 to the eighth, it's 10 to the first. Seven orders of magnitude difference.

summary: Quantify the strain-rate sensitivity and recrystallization mechanisms in Conform processing across different powder alloys and temperatures.
verbatim: For these alloys, I determined, you end up getting what's called dynamic recrystallization. It comes out hot — you don't want to touch this piece of copper, because all the work that's gone into it brings it out at 400 or 500°. But at that 400 or 500° for this particular alloy, which has a little bit of silver in it, you get to the recrystallization range.

summary: Understanding why the 70% composition peak disappears in titanium superplastic alloys despite geometric predictions.
verbatim: In theory there should be. In this case, in titanium, it has to do with the diffusion of the different elements in one phase versus the other phase. If it were just simple geometry, yes, there would be one at 70. If you include the coarsening phenomena and the diffusivity in the different phases, that's probably why we get rid of the 70% peak.

summary: Why single-phase alloys cannot achieve superplasticity while two-phase alloys can, despite both having grain boundary sliding mechanisms.
verbatim: It's harder to get superplasticity in a single-phase alloy. It's easiest to get superplasticity when you have about 30% of one phase inside another, because that 30% phase is completely encapsulated.

summary: Why 304 stainless steel cannot be made superplastic while duplex stainless steels can, despite both being austenitic/ferritic systems.
verbatim: If we could make 304 stainless superplastic, believe me we would — it's the workhorse alloy. But you can't do it. You have to use a duplex stainless, because it's best to have that 30% concentration.

summary: The kinetics of delayed hydrogen cracking in drawn stainless steel—why cracks appear days later during shipping rather than immediately after forming—is not well explained.
verbatim: It's delayed cracking — it didn't exist when they put it on the boat; by the time it got off the boat in Japan, the hydrogen had done its dirty work.

summary: Why martensitic stainless steel exhibits transformation-induced plasticity with dramatically higher necking strains than conventional steels remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: For martensitic stainless steel, it can be 0.5 rather than 0.2, because this is a transformation-induced plasticity — remember I passed around the ferrite pot and the magnetism — it changes crystal structure, so you get increased plasticity.

summary: The microscopic mechanism by which stress state (triaxial vs. uniaxial) controls fracture mode in the same steel is not fully explained.
verbatim: The steel will change the fracture mode just by the stress state, whether it's triaxial or uniaxial... The material will change the microscopic fracture mode depending on the stress state.

summary: Understanding why grain growth during superplastic metal drawing would destroy superplasticity remains unclear and untested.
verbatim: You could probably do it, but it works really well with glass. And it's kept Corning a profitable company over the last 20 years... if you tried to do this very long time with super plastic metals, the grains would probably start growing, and then you lose your super plasticity.

summary: Whether non-uniform glass thickness in blow-molded black light bulbs leaves unrelieved residual stresses that cause catastrophic failure under thermal shock.
verbatim: When you have different thicknesses and you do the annealing process — you form at one temperature and at an intermediate temperature you anneal to soften the glass and relieve residual stresses, and then you cool it down — when you don't have uniform thickness, you may not get uniform cooling and therefore you may not have eliminated your residual stresses.

summary: The kinetics and mechanism of surface corrosion of freshly drawn glass fibers exposed to atmospheric moisture, and how it depletes the exceptional strength of virgin glass.
verbatim: Glass actually corrodes in the moisture in the air — it's a silicate, and it forms silicate hydroxides. The strength of glass will change dramatically within a few days after its manufacture.

summary: The heat affected zone in laser and electron beam welds is often claimed to shrink to zero, but Eagar suggests this contradicts handbooks and may be incompletely understood.
verbatim: A lot of people will say the size of the heat affected zone in a laser or electron beam weld goes down to zero, but that's not true. It says that in the welding handbook, but I've sort of made a career out of going to welding conferences and knocking what the welding handbook says is wrong.

summary: GE's electron beam welds of titanium compressor cases were plagued by porosity with unclear root cause despite extensive troubleshooting.
verbatim: They want to weld them together with an electron beam circumferential weld about a half an inch thick... they were getting porosity in their titanium welds. You're supposed to take two of these thirty-thousand-dollar units and weld them together; now it's a seventy- or eighty-thousand-dollar unit.

summary: Bimetallic bandsaw blades created by electron beam welding use high-speed steel tips on spring steel backing, but the tips have worse fracture and fatigue strength than the backing—the mechanics of this composite design gap are not explored.
verbatim: The steel on the tips has very good high-temperature strength, but it doesn't have the same fracture and fatigue strength as the spring steel. You end up with a composite.

summary: Understand why halogenated fire suppressants (like Halon) so effectively interrupt combustion by poisoning intermediate radical species.
verbatim: The chlorine or bromine or whatever the halide is poisons these intermediate reactions and stops the combustion process. It's very effective — it's just not good for global warming.

summary: Determine the quantitative relationship between torch orifice design, gas velocity, and flashback risk to optimize flame stability across different fuel-oxygen ratios.
verbatim: If you had too big a torch and not a big enough orifice, not enough gas, you could actually get flashback — once it ignites, the gas could burn faster going into the torch than coming out. So you have to balance the speed out with the burning velocity.

summary: Eagar notes that solid rocket motors cannot be turned off once ignited, and mentions that people are developing stoppable versions but provides no details on the technical barrier.
verbatim: There's a problem with solid rocket motors though. Once you turn them on, how do you turn them off? Basically you don't. You burn out until the fuel's used up. People are developing solid rocket boosters that can be turned off, but basically a solid rocket motor is just a mixture of oxidant and fuel and you have a controlled explosion going off.

summary: Titanium flame-cuts despite theory predicting it shouldn't; the mechanism of oxide dissolution into titanium metal at ~900°C needs systematic investigation.
verbatim: Titanium in theory should not be able to be flame cut, but in fact it can be... The reason it works is titanium will start dissolving its own oxide at about 900 degrees centigrade. As you get up to higher temperatures, this protective titanium oxide coating dissolves away into the titanium, and you expose fresh metal to pure oxygen — you get a very rapid reaction, like a flare.

summary: Plasma cutting produces rounded corners instead of sharp square corners when cutting at turns, an inherent problem whose root cause in heat-flow dynamics deserves investigation.
verbatim: When you get to corners and turn the corner, we have problems — we don't get nice square corners. That has to do with your turning and changing your heat flow direction. So that's an inherent problem.

summary: Molten copper jet cutting technology failed due to inability to maintain stable laminar flow and poor ceramic nozzle lifetime—fundamental engineering challenges remain unsolved.
verbatim: They could cut through steel with a liquid copper jet at 10 times the speed of plasma cutting or oxyacetylene. The problem was, how do you generate a nice stable laminar flow jet of molten copper?...their lifetime wasn't very good.

summary: Quantitative understanding of flame-straightening mechanics and optimal heating parameters for different material types remains poorly developed.
verbatim: This book has the potential to save the metalworking industry millions of dollars, which is in fact true. The difference between that book and the Maritime Administration books is, this one's quantitative. There's actually some science behind it. There's a lot of practical art behind the other one — the guy worked in the foundry and had to straighten things all the time.

summary: Unresolved debate over whether shape-charge penetration is driven by liquid-jet metallurgy or pure kinetic deformation mechanics.
verbatim: There have been debates on whether it is liquid copper, or whether it's just the kinetic energy of all that copper being mechanically deformed. That's what they do at Aberdeen Proving Ground — try to design these things and make better, more efficient ones. I saw some work — and I'm not telling you anything — where they believe they proved it actually is a liquid jet.

summary: The mechanism by which electrons penetrate the cold boundary layer in a plasma arc using voltage and kinetic energy remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: If I have electrons — if this is a plasma arc — and I have enough voltage across the cold boundary layer — the cold boundary layer may be on the order between 1500 Centigrade (the melting temperature of steel) and the free-stream temperature of three thousand or ten thousand. Out here let's just call it three thousand Centigrade. This is a non-ionized gas, too low a temperature to give off ions. So the electrons have to punch their way through with pure voltage and kinetic energy.

summary: The precise mechanism behind thoriated tungsten's electron-emission advantage and work-function reduction remains experimentally documented but theoretically unexplained.
verbatim: I don't know exactly why they started using thoriated tungsten, but thorium oxide is a very easy electron emitter. It gives up its electrons very easily, and it cools down the surface of the tip of the cathode by lowering the phi voltage — the work-function voltage.

summary: Arc plasma behavior under cooling remains counterintuitive and poorly mechanistically understood despite empirical observation.
verbatim: our electric arcs are very strange beasts in the sense that if you cool the outside, it gets hotter on the inside. If you cool the outside, you're condensing some of those electrons, turning them back into neutrals.

summary: Understand the mechanism by which electric fields pull liquid metal into peaks and overcome surface tension during arc initiation on liquid surfaces.
verbatim: It's most difficult to get Paschen breakdown or field emission on a liquid surface. Liquid mercury is harder because liquids don't have any peaks. But when you start getting to these voltages, even on a liquid surface, the electric field can actually create little peaks of liquid.

summary: The mechanism by which cadmium oxide dramatically increases current capacity in silver contacts remains poorly understood despite practical importance.
verbatim: Cadmium, for reasons that are still not completely understood, will double the amount of current. It's not the same thing as thoriated tungsten — thoriated tungsten will double the amount of current too — but the physics are a little different.

summary: The detailed plasma physics of how argon ions break up surface oxides during variable-polarity AC plasma welding of aluminum is incompletely understood.
verbatim: One of the theories is that the argon ions, when you're on the negative half cycle, will be thrown against the surface and break up the surface oxide. There may be some truth to that, but it's probably more complex. We don't have to get into all the details of the plasma physics and cathode spots.

summary: Plasma arc welding electrode tips degrade rapidly (lasting ~30 minutes); the mechanism and material science behind this wear is not well characterized.
verbatim: One of the problems with plasma arc welding is those little tips — the replaceable tips — last about a half an hour. When they first started coming out, they lasted about five minutes. That's one of the reasons plasma didn't just get picked up immediately. They've improved the cooling and the design, so now they get about a half an hour.

summary: Quantifying the current threshold above which plasma jet pressure causes weld pool gouging and humped bead defects in gas tungsten arc welding.
verbatim: once I get up to about 200 amperes, the arc force coming off this thing will actually start to gouge the weld pool. Above 200 amperes on a gas tungsten arc, I will start creating defects.

summary: Understand why the cathode spot remains stationary on flat titanium surfaces unlike other metals, causing upward plasma jets that disrupt droplet transfer.
verbatim: In titanium, that spot is stationary. It doesn't like to wander around. From the flat surface you'll get a jet shooting up from the surface that interferes with the metal transfer.

summary: Arc blow phenomenon lacks fundamental documentation and understanding despite being a common welding problem.
verbatim: There's almost nothing in the literature, even the welding handbook, about arc blow, other than that it exists. You have to do something to stabilize it, but there's very little in the open literature that really talks about it.

summary: Electromagnetic magnetic field effects on arc stability in dissimilar metal electron beam welding remain unsolved.
verbatim: We'll get to that also when we do high-power electron beam, because there are some problems that cannot be solved because of magnetic arc blow on dissimilar metals in electron beam.

summary: Experimentally determine which specific temperature threshold (melting point, critical transformation temperature, etc.) best defines the heat-affected zone width across different alloys and travel speeds.
verbatim: If you say a thousand degrees is my heat affected zone, you can find where a thousand degrees would be on that line. That will give you the width of the heat affected zone right there.

summary: Investigate zinc-copper alloying and high-resistance interface formation at galvanized steel spot-weld interfaces.
verbatim: They had problems because the zinc was alloying with the copper, creating a high-resistance interface.

summary: The effect of electrode tip geometry (angle and corner radius) on current concentration and weld quality in spot welding remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: They were using an angle here of about 15 degrees on the electrode tip. If your current is coming down through here, it has to come down like that, and if you think of flow lines, the current bunches up right at the corner. That's the same thing as a stress concentration. Mathematically, it's solving Laplace's equation.

summary: The discrepancy between electrode geometry (45° in qualification tests vs. 15° in production plants) causing premature electrode wear in automotive spot welding has not been systematically investigated or corrected across the industry.
verbatim: What were they using in the plant? A 15-degree angle. What were they using to run the test? Part of the Ford spec — 45 degrees. 45 gave you better electrode life, but then you go in the plant and use the angle that gives you lousy electrode life.

summary: The mechanism and design constraints limiting electron beam welding to ~0.1 ampere for proper focus—and whether higher-voltage machines (600 kV) achieved adequate penetration in thick steel—remain incompletely explained.
verbatim: The Japanese built one at 600 kilovolts and got 60 kilowatts, and were doing electron beam welds in four, five, six, eight inch thick steel. We'll talk about why that didn't work all that well.

summary: Competing constraints between heat efficiency (slow = wasted heat) and penetration depth (fast = shallow) make wire-feed additive deposition with thermal sources fundamentally inefficient.
verbatim: Because of the heat flow equation — distance goes as the square root of time — if you go slow, you're wasting a lot of heat, you're not getting efficiency. If you go fast, the faster you go the less depth you get of penetration, so you end up putting down less and less metal because you're just doing surface heating.

summary: Eagar flags the unresolved challenge of controlling laser beam shape: practical high-power laser cavities produce multiple diffraction modes that degrade beam uniformity, and achieving a true Gaussian beam costs over half the efficiency.
verbatim: Lasers have diffraction spots. If you want a nice Gaussian beam you lose a lot of your efficiency — over half your efficiency is gone. The laser mode cavity prefers to have all these multiple modes that degrade the beam, at least in terms of welding where you'd like a nice uniform peak Gaussian heat source.

summary: Non-uniform penetration in deep electron-beam welds oscillates at the bottom of thick sections; horizontal-position workaround exists but is not universally applicable.
verbatim: Non-uniform penetration — I talked about, in the vertical position, how the metal would slump down. In a big deep cavity, it's like you're almost drilling a hole and the metal's back-filling it. Every now and then it back-fills and you'll get a spike in your penetration. So the penetration depth is oscillating at the bottom. They never found a solution to that other than welding in the horizontal position, which worked for certain things.

summary: Electron beam welding demands prohibitively clean steel (doubling cost) because beam vaporization reintroduces oxides and nitrogen, causing porosity and embrittlement.
verbatim: Any oxides or nitrogen would come back into the steel and create porosity or poor fracture toughness. They had to get steel from the steel mills which was exceedingly clean. We could make it, but it was doubling the cost of the steel in order to get sound welds that weren't full of porosity.

summary: Understand why laser/electron beam welding in thick sections (>0.5 inch) encounters fundamental unsolved problems despite theoretical capability.
verbatim: Welding with lasers and electron beam — the theme is they're actually very different processes. You can get very thick sections in theory, but you have all kinds of big problems that people haven't really solved.

summary: Understand why rhenium became critical for turbine alloys and whether substitutes exist or can be developed.
verbatim: A lot of the alloys have six percent rhenium. It's one of the platinum group metals. It only goes for about forty dollars an ounce, and you can afford that in an aircraft engine. It's a little pricey, we don't like it, but it gives properties we can't get other ways.

summary: Scale and feasibility of carbon-free metal production when accounting for electricity source and total energy requirements.
verbatim: A number of faculty in this department have ways to do it with electricity. Except where do you get the electricity? You're going to burn coal to get your electricity. You can use hydroelectric or solar, but if you start doing some of these calculations, you find you've got a problem with scale.

summary: Ring vortex formation from large wind turbine blades and its hazard to aircraft remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: There's something called a ring vortex from these wind turbines, and planes will get caught in these. Some of these things have 100-foot, 150-foot blades, and they're not very fast, but they create a ring vortex. Some small planes have gotten caught in the turbine and can't get out.

summary: The mechanisms by which microstructure coarsening degrades GTD-111 superalloy properties after 30,000 hours of service remain incompletely understood.
verbatim: once it's served about ten years of service, 30,000 hours, it's no longer good for continued service because the microstructure coarsens and it no longer has the good properties

summary: Understand the mechanisms and economics of dewatering sub-bituminous coal from Wyoming mines to reduce transport losses.
verbatim: When I was there in the mid '80s, you could get it for $5 a ton. But you had to take it out of there by train, and you might be taking thirty percent of your weight as water. So there's a big deal about how to dewater that coal.

summary: Understand why thermal barrier coatings flake off and what controls the rate and extent of blade loss in turbine engines.
verbatim: If it starts flaking off very badly, you're going to lose your blade. But you can lose one or two blades and usually you don't lose the engine.

summary: Bismuth contamination in recycled steel scrap makes it brittle and unrecyclable, yet there is no known purification method short of returning to ore extraction.
verbatim: If you get 10 parts per million bismuth in a steel ingot, it's just a big paperweight. You cannot roll it — it's just brittle. The bismuth goes to the grain boundaries and there's no way to get it out. You can't oxidize it out. You have to go back to the ore.

summary: The mechanism by which ceramic armor defeats shaped charge copper jets remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: If you put ceramic in there, the copper doesn't react with the ceramic, and so it doesn't destroy it.

summary: Why tungsten carbide tips wear out unpredictably during eight-hour shifts in asphalt reclamation, despite being one of the hardest known materials.
