verbatim: The problem is the tips get a lot of abrasive wear, and the tungsten carbide, which is one of the hardest materials we have, basically wears out. You'd like it to last for an eight-hour shift, but they don't always.

summary: Sodium in waste streams destroys steel refractory materials, but the interaction mechanism and mitigation strategies remain unexplored.
verbatim: There's an element that will destroy steel refractories called sodium. Do you think there's any sodium in most of the waste streams? If you want to throw garbage, there's sodium all over.

summary: Chlorine gas in a steel furnace produces phosgene (a WWI chemical weapon), but the kinetics, conditions, and control of this reaction are not discussed as understood.
verbatim: There's another element called chlorine. You know what happens when you put chlorine into a steel furnace? You get phosgene gas, COCl₂.

summary: High-temperature superconductors have failed to achieve high critical current density perpendicular to magnetic field after 25 years, despite improvements in temperature and field strength.
verbatim: They had improved one property, temperature, and they got high magnetic field along with that, but they hadn't improved critical current density, and they still haven't today, twenty-five years later.

summary: The mechanism by which liquid hydrogen penetrates composite matrix pores and causes pressure-driven failure during warm-up remains uncharacterized.
verbatim: It turns out the liquid hydrogen got inside the pores, and as it warmed up and built up pressure, it blew up.

summary: Eagar notes that carbon fiber composites in BMW i3 production are lower quality than aerospace standards, suggesting an unresolved manufacturing or process control problem.
verbatim: He did his thesis on polymers, and his comment was the carbon fiber composites are junk. Maybe they're not made well. They're fine for just a shell on the outside of the vehicle, and it's lightweight, but the quality of the resin transfer molding would never pass the aerospace industry.

summary: The fundamental challenge of designing active cooling systems for hypersonic aircraft with extreme thermal gradients (thousands of Kelvin on one side, cryogenic on the other) remains unresolved, with inherent safety risks.
verbatim: On one side you'd have four or five thousand degrees Kelvin, and on the other side you'd have liquid hydrogen at 20 degrees Kelvin. As long as you didn't have a leak, everything was fine. If you ever had a leak, you have a big bomb.

summary: Quantify the mechanical coupling between primary bonds along polymer fiber axes and secondary van der Waals bonds between fibers to predict temperature limits and failure modes.
verbatim: Polymers are low-temperature materials, because they're not held together in a three-dimensional structure with covalent bonds, or primary bonds. They're held together with van der Waals bonds. Along the length, where the primary bonds are, tremendous strength... but you've got secondary bonds *between* the fibers.

summary: Embrittlement mechanisms in century-old cast iron pipes lack systematic characterization and prediction models.
verbatim: One of the things that happens with cast iron over time is it can become embrittled, and you can get stress cracking and issues just by it being so old.

summary: Quantitative prediction of stress concentrations and crack initiation in dissimilar-material assemblies (e.g., plastic-metal refrigerator shelves) under cyclic thermal loading remains unresolved.
verbatim: What was overlooked in this case was that when you have dissimilar materials joined together, you're going to create stress concentrations. The plastic is joined to the metal, and these things are expanding and contracting at different rates in service, and you get cracks over time.

summary: Thermal runaway initiation and propagation in high-energy-density batteries during charge and thermal stress lacks detailed mechanistic understanding and predictive design rules.
verbatim: With your battery, you want the energy density as high as possible... So you want to get the energy density up. Do you want to talk about some things you've seen in terms of fire protection or charging-discharging—

summary: The thickness threshold where materials transition from plane stress (high toughness) to plane strain (lower toughness) varies by material but lacks a predictive framework.
verbatim: The toughness is also a function of the thickness of the material. We haven't put the thickness on here, because where it goes from plane stress of high toughness to plane strain of lower toughness is a function of the toughness of the material.

summary: Rail steel lacks fracture toughness specifications despite known benefits, creating a measurement and design gap that persists because industry hasn't been forced to modernize century-old standards.
verbatim: Rail steel has very little fracture toughness in the specs. They don't put it in the spec, so they don't manufacture for it... A lot of the rail steel specs were developed in 1900 or 1920, and they don't want to modernize them.

summary: The Brazilian helicopter rotor failure initially attributed to surface grinding was actually caused by stress corrosion cracking in high-strength aluminum—a failure mechanism that was misidentified because typical flaw-size reasoning didn't apply.
verbatim: Fracture mechanics could not explain the failure with the typical flaw size you get from a grinding operation... they would have had to have an eighth-inch flaw. When you're sanding the surface of something, you don't get eighth-inch deep scratches... metallurgically, on the surface, it was stress corrosion cracking.

summary: Glass can match steel in strength if surface defects are reduced to nanometer scale with favorable compressive stresses, but the mechanisms controlling this transformation remain unclear.
verbatim: Glass in principle has very high strength; it just has very little toughness. If we can get rid of those defects, those little small flaws, and get them down to the nanometer size on the surface, and have favorable compressive stresses — we actually use ceramics in higher volumes than we do metals.

summary: Net-shape casting of structural beams succeeded at Chaparral, but the underlying mechanisms driving the one-third cost reduction and metallurgical limits of the hourglass-mold approach remain uncharacterized.
verbatim: Net-shape casting drove the cost down by one-third. Where people were building parking garages out of reinforced concrete, now using steel-frame buildings for parking garages became the cheaper alternative.

summary: Why do hot steel bars experience instabilities at high speeds (70–80 mph), and what is the physical mechanism?
verbatim: They tried for several months to run their mill faster, and it turns out there are lots of instabilities when you have hot steel bar at seventy, eighty miles an hour — it doesn't work very well.

summary: Characterize the actual pollutant emissions from cement kilns firing recycled foam to understand whether atmospheric discharge poses a genuine hazard.
verbatim: When they were firing the cement operations with the foam, some people found out about this and wanted to know what pollutants are you putting into the atmosphere from your cement kiln? They had all the data — they knew what was going up the stack in terms of CO and other impurities. They were trying to figure out how to explain this to the people in Midlothian, to the City Council, who wanted to regulate them.

summary: The mechanism by which sodium and potassium oxides in glass are attacked by atmospheric humidity, causing strength loss over time, remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: It turns out the problem is that the sodium and potassium oxides in the glass are attacked by the humidity in the air.

summary: Composite repairability and joinability remain fundamentally limited, with no established fusion-welding path for common structural composites like carbon-fiber laminates.
verbatim: Composites are not really very repairable. That's one of the things you give up. They're not very joinable.

summary: Composite tanks for cryogenic liquid oxygen storage remain problematic and poorly understood.
verbatim: there are real problems with holding liquid oxygen in a composite. There are problems with holding it in aluminum too.

summary: Why does ultrafine-grain copper develop excessive elongation, making it difficult to use for structural applications despite superior strength?
verbatim: That was the big fight, it had too much elongation. How can you have too much elongation for a structural material?

summary: Clean manufacturing methods for rare-earth extraction remain undeveloped after initial post-2010 research surge.
verbatim: there were all kinds of academics who started trying to think of a clean way to make rare earths. After about a year or so the Chinese, under pressure but also having achieved their objectives, started selling rare earths again to the Japanese.

summary: Nickel electroplating underlayers work well but pose toxicity and allergenicity risks; alternative base metals for gold plating need investigation to replace nickel.
verbatim: The reason is that nickel electroplates better than any other metal in the world. If you want to get a good gold plate, you put a nickel flash underneath it... Now, nickel is a little bit of a problem because it can be toxic. It is toxic in the human body, and some people are actually allergic to it.

summary: Why aluminum brake calipers fail thermally in automotive braking applications despite weight-saving potential.
verbatim: People have tried for years to replace cast-iron brake calipers with aluminum, but they had problems because brakes get hot, and if aluminum gets that hot it can distort and deform and your brakes don't work.

summary: Building codes ignored fracture toughness (energy absorption) criteria for 40 years after Irwin's work, until the 1990s Northridge earthquake—investigate why this institutional lag occurred and whether similar gaps exist in other industries.
verbatim: We never really worried about that a whole lot after the 1950s, when Irwin explained how important the energy of fracture was. We didn't change the building codes. So when the Northridge earthquake hit Southern California in the 1990s, buildings snapped in the earthquake and caused billions of dollars worth of damage.

summary: Why tin-silver solders leak more frequently than lead-tin solders, and whether this failure mode can be prevented.
verbatim: Then in 1978 you couldn't use lead-tin solder. You had to get the lead out, and you had to start using tin-silver solders, tin-silver-antimony solders. They're okay, but they tend to leak a little bit more.

summary: Characterize the brittle failure behavior of century-old cast-iron water mains and why mechanical disturbance accelerates failure in adjacent sections.
verbatim: One of the biggest problems in cities like Boston and New York is we've got hundred-year-old cast iron water mains, and every now and then one breaks. They're so brittle that when you work on it in this block, you know about five or ten years down the road the next block is going to have a leak.

summary: The exact mechanism by which biocide-treated steel pipe releases polymers that crack plastic sprinkler system components needs investigation.
verbatim: They put a biocide on the inside, they sprayed the inside of the steel pipe with something to keep the bugs and the corrosion down. It turns out that polymer they put on the inside of the steel pipe gets in the water, and it's stagnant water — it's not flowing through like in a potable water system, it just sits there — and it cracks the plastic.

summary: Manufacturing tolerance control for thin-walled turbine blades remains poorly understood despite billions in spending.
verbatim: If that core is off by two or three thousandths of an inch from its perfect position — and its perfect position is not just a center axis, it's the center axis in a twist — you're off by two or three thousandths over a couple of inches on something that's going to heat up to 1,300 degrees centigrade. It'll melt, and it's a piece of junk. All of a sudden, your manufacturability goes like that.

summary: Active cooling design for hypersonic vehicle skins using liquid hydrogen raises unresolved questions about thermal stress behavior and leak prevention in copper alloys.
verbatim: From minus 270 centigrade and 4,000 centigrade. I thought these were the Air Force's best designers, but they're actually people designing things to get money funding from Congress, so it has nothing to do with anything practical.

summary: Roman concrete remains durable for millennia while modern concrete fails in 1–2 centuries; the chemistry behind volcanic ash in Roman formulations is poorly understood.
verbatim: There's a lot of science behind Roman concrete and why it lasts for 2,000 years, when modern concrete typically doesn't last for more than 100 or 200 years. It has to do with a volcanic ash they used to make the concrete, and you get a certain chemistry. I don't know that much about it.

summary: The mechanism by which carbon diffusion distance differs from chromium diffusion during sensitization remains incompletely characterized, particularly the quantitative chromium depletion profiles across grain boundaries.
verbatim: the carbon diffuses from a larger distance, and it's a small atom and it does diffuse from a larger distance, and that denudes — makes the grain boundaries lower-chromium and therefore not as corrosion-resistant.

summary: Ceramics suffer environmental degradation in service, but the specific mechanisms and rates remain inadequately characterized compared to corrosion in metals.
verbatim: They were going to make high-temperature engines out of ceramics because they could go to higher temperatures and don't corrode. Well, maybe they don't corrode, but they do suffer degradation in different environments.

summary: Why aluminum lacks a fatigue limit while steel exhibits one—a fundamental materials difference that remains incompletely explained.
verbatim: Aluminum doesn't have a fatigue limit; aluminum keeps on going down, and they've gone out to ten to the eight cycles... You have a factor of safety and you're good. You shouldn't have a fatigue problem unless you have stress concentrations.

summary: The X-33 composite hydrogen tank failure mechanism during warm-up was not fully understood despite post-test investigation.
verbatim: They didn't want to cancel the program — it was a rush program in the early 90s to demonstrate rapid prototyping. So they just recalculated their safety factor and found out a 5 percent safety factor's good enough... They went back and found they didn't really have their 5 percent safety factor. This thing was a disaster from the initial fabrication.

summary: The mechanism by which lubricant on bolt threads reduces torque scatter and improves consistency is known empirically but lacks rigorous characterization.
verbatim: If it's lubricated, you'll get the same normal distribution, but the torque will be much less than if it's not lubricated and you've got dry friction. There's your plus or minus 30%.

summary: The production pathways and equilibrium conditions for phosgene and dioxin/furan formation when chlorine-bearing waste and plastics are processed in molten iron furnaces remain incompletely characterized.
verbatim: in the presence of chlorine you form this compound COCl2. That's known as phosgene... You also had dioxins and furans, which are fairly toxic themselves, that were produced in the bath from putting plastics in there.

summary: Whether diamond impurity fingerprinting can reliably distinguish blood diamonds from Angola by geological region.
verbatim: You look for the impurity content in the diamond. You analyze the impurities, and certain diamonds you can fingerprint to what geological region of the world they came from.

summary: Roman concrete outlasts modern concrete, and researchers have identified volcanic rock composition as a key factor—but the full chemistry and replication pathway remain incompletely understood.
verbatim: There's actually a recent article, in the last two or three weeks, in *Science* magazine about how the Roman concrete is so much better than our concrete even today. It's lasted better. Some people have been researching this and found it's because they used a particular type of volcanic rock with certain properties. Now they're trying to improve concrete today based on what they've learned about the chemistry of Roman concrete.

summary: Dezincification mechanisms in brass fittings under specific water chemistry conditions remain poorly characterized despite massive litigation.
verbatim: some material scientists on the West Coast have determined that this type of brass — the leaded brass we've been using for about a hundred years — is defective... they get some dezincification... in certain waters that are pretty corrosive, like Las Vegas, Colorado River water

summary: Recycling of concrete and other high-volume man-made materials remains unsolved despite their massive production scale.
verbatim: The most used man-made material is something we don't recycle, and we make one and a half or two billion tons a year. It's going to be a bigger and bigger problem. If you can figure out how to recycle it, you'll become a rich person.

summary: Whether lightweight metal catalytic converter substrates could reduce emissions during cold-start, when ceramic converters remain inactive.
verbatim: At one time they were looking at a lightweight catalytic converter substrate, which in this case could have been a rolled metal like that, because most of your emissions occur on startup before the catalytic converter — this big heavy one — gets to temperature.

summary: The mechanisms by which ceramic knives avoid crushing cell walls and releasing onion juice, unlike metal blades.
verbatim: Because they don't crush the cells and let out all those juices that make you cry. The ceramic knives stay sharp, slice the cell, and don't release as much of the juice, so you don't cry as much.

summary: Friction welding of titanium blades to engine discs failed despite promising weight savings, and the root causes remain unclear.
verbatim: The Air Force had a big program to do friction welding of blades to discs, great big ones, and it never worked out. You can take my welding course and I'll tell you more about it.

summary: Why brittle materials sometimes exhibit a shear lip on the compression side while showing brittle fracture in the center—the mechanics of mixed-mode fracture geometry.
verbatim: If you look carefully, you will see a little what we call a shear lip on the compression side — a positive shear lip on the compression side, and a brittle fracture in between.

summary: Understand why fracture toughness plateaus around 200–300 MPa√m even in optimized material systems, and whether this is a fundamental physical limit.
verbatim: You'd like to be up in this corner, as far up there as much strength and as much toughness as possible. But you kind of poop out at a toughness of about two or three hundred megapascals per square root of meter.

summary: Ceramics show an unusual toughness-strength relationship where strength gain correlates with toughness gain due to critical flaw size effects; the mechanism deserves investigation.
verbatim: Ceramics are sort of interesting. They actually get strong — as they get stronger they actually get tougher. That's because ceramics are full of critical-size flaws.

summary: Edge-defined film growth for silicon solar cells is too slow to be economically viable, but nobody has systematically characterized the growth rate limits or explored whether faster pulling speeds are possible.
verbatim: One of the problems with this edge-defined film growth — I was out there at that lab, and they have nice machines and it works, but it's really slow. When you're pulling something that thin and that light, you don't make very many pounds per hour.

summary: The stiffness-modulus relationship determines bolt spacing in gasket seals, but the cost trade-offs of tighter bolt spacing in low-modulus materials versus material cost are not well characterized.
verbatim: The modulus, the stiffness of the material, determines how closely you have to put the bolts in order to get the seal. If there's a rubber gasket in between, the thing's just going to bow and you're going to lose your seal. So I just doubled the cost of my bolts — I don't know if they included that.

summary: Copper contamination and surface 'copper checks' occur during continuous caster startup despite oxidation layer formation; the mechanism and prevention remain incompletely solved.
verbatim: Yes, you can sometimes get a little copper contamination before the thing starts oxidizing and forming a little slag layer on the initial startup. That can cause what they call copper checks on the surface.

summary: Understanding why titanium alloys spontaneously ignite above 900°C in jet engine compressors, causing catastrophic failure.
verbatim: Titanium, you get above 900 degrees and it just will go on fire like a flare. They've burned out engines because the compressor blades are made out of titanium.

summary: Materials capable of surviving sustained Mach 17 flight in atmosphere with frictional heating approaching 3000°C.
verbatim: The problem is, when a spacecraft at Mach 17 is coming into reentry, what happens? They have to have these carbon tiles that absorb the heat. The frictional heating will give temperatures of 3000 degrees centigrade.

summary: The mechanism by which zirconium oxide's thermal expansion coefficient (roughly twice that of other ceramics) prevents spalling in ceramic-metal bonds remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: The reason they use the zirconium oxide is because it has a coefficient of thermal expansion about twice that of most other ceramics, which comes closer to matching the metal. One of the problems of trying to make ceramic-metal bonds is the difference in coefficient of thermal expansion. When you heat them up you don't want them spalling off.

summary: The relationship between bonding potential asymmetry and material properties like Poisson ratio remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: He pointed out that this curve is actually steeper than that curve. If you blow up this region right here, it's actually asymmetric, not a nice symmetric parabola. He talked about how you can explain Poisson ratio because of the energy potential.

summary: Understand why plastic composite truck beds show superior resilience to denting compared to steel in real mine operations.
verbatim: The coal companies didn't want to give back the resin mold composite beds, because they didn't crack — they were resilient. The steel dented and you couldn't close the tailgate, if you're dumping things into a pickup truck and abusing it like they do in a coal mine.

summary: Why rust flakes off steel while magnetite adheres—the physical mechanism behind the volume-change-driven spalling of Fe₂O₃ versus Fe₃O₄.
verbatim: Magnetite has a volume ratio and coefficient of thermal expansion such that when it forms on steel, it will adhere. Rust on the other hand, when it forms, can have a four to ten times volume change depending on how many H2Os are in it and how much chlorine might be around, and it will flake off.

summary: Why cast iron with silicon forms a glassy protective layer while plain steel does not—the mechanism by which silicon composition affects oxide adherence and corrosion resistance.
verbatim: Some of them are cast iron, and cast iron has a lot of silicon, and it forms a glassy silicon layer, so it grows less. Cast iron grows less.

summary: Iron-chrome intermetallic phases in duplex stainless steels cause embrittlement, but the mechanism and prevention conditions are not fully characterized.
verbatim: If you're not careful with duplex stainless steels — you have higher chromium and lower nickel, and the ferrite can get hydrogen in it. But the real problem is you can get iron-chrome intermetallic phases that embrittle it.

summary: Quantum mechanical understanding of hydrogen embrittlement in body-centered cubic metals remains incomplete despite multiple competing theories.
verbatim: Frankly it's still a matter of opinion among metallurgists what causes hydrogen embrittlement. There are four or five theories — strain in the lattice — I suspect when we get really good at quantum mechanics on a larger crystal, rather than just a few atoms, we might be able to figure out what hydrogen does in terms of embrittling the body-centered cubic structure.

summary: The mechanisms controlling pitting resistance differences between 304 and 316 stainless in chloride environments warrant systematic investigation, given dramatic real-world failure differences.
verbatim: They asked me to figure out why... that 2% molybdenum went from something that would look stainless for 15 or 20 years or more in this environment, to something that could only last a couple of weeks. That's the most dramatic example I've seen.

summary: The protective oxide layer on stainless steel fails to reform in marine chloride environments even though it reforms readily inland—the mechanism underlying this difference is unclear.
verbatim: In a chloride environment, the protective scale did not reform like it would inland. But right there on the coast.

summary: Investigate the stability and chromium carbide formation behavior of chrome nitrides (formed by nitrogen) versus chrome carbides in low-carbon, nitrogen-alloyed stainless steels.
verbatim: Nitrogen doesn't form chrome carbides — it forms chrome nitrides, but they're not as stable.

summary: The Navy abandoned non-magnetic submarine hulls made from super-austenitic stainless steel; the technical barriers and failure modes deserve systematic study.
verbatim: The US Navy about 10 years ago was interested in building submarines out of this material. Why? Because they're not magnetic. The problem with magnetic submarines is, if you've got a superconducting quantum interference device up there in a satellite, you can see 100 feet down, and you can see this long magnetic hot dog in the ocean. But they finally gave up.

summary: Aluminum alloys gradually soften at operational temperatures after heat treatment, degrading strength over decades—the mechanism and rate of this coarsening process needs systematic study.
verbatim: One of the problems with aluminum alloys: they melt at low temperatures, but they will also soften. You can heat-treat them and get 10 to 12 times the strength of pure aluminum, but they can degrade over time at relatively low temperatures.

summary: The mechanism by which scandium grain refinement enables higher strength in extruded aluminum bats compared to other grain refiners remains unstudied in detail.
verbatim: It's got scandium as a grain refiner, which is better than titanium or zirconium or the other things we typically use on the bigger alloys. You can get extremely fine grain, extremely high strength that will hopefully last long enough that you won't get too upset.

summary: The relationship between bat wall thickness, dent accumulation, residual stress buildup, and fatigue failure in high-strength aluminum baseball bats has not been systematically characterized.
verbatim: The product insert that came with this basically said on the warranty card: rotate bat one-quarter turn at each at-bat. You don't have to worry about hitting it with the grain — you've got to worry about distributing the dents, or not building up residual stress. I haven't studied that in detail.

summary: Quantify how hysteresis in ball material affects the stiffness-matching principle for optimal momentum and energy transfer.
verbatim: The ball has a lot of hysteresis, which complicates things, but nonetheless. We took one of our bats and pushed on the bat, measured its stiffness, and lo and behold, they were the same within 30 or 40 percent.

summary: Understand why stress corrosion cracking initiates from the outside surface of thin-walled 7075-T6 aluminum cylinders under high hydraulic pressure.
verbatim: The problem was, these things were exploding when they failed. It was a little stress corrosion fatigue crack starting from the outside. He brought me this thing and wanted to know, what do we do about it?

summary: The genetic basis and penetrance of berylliosis susceptibility remains incompletely characterized despite the disease's discovery in the 1940s.
verbatim: They showed through contaminating rats — it wasn't until years later that they learned there's a genetic predisposition. I think one of the students in this class did a presentation on berylliosis once, and that may have been where I found out it was only ten percent.

summary: Understand why aluminum passivates under certain water conditions and loses its sacrificial anode properties, unlike magnesium.
verbatim: The problem with aluminum: if you have certain ions in your water, the aluminum can form a passive scale on the surface, and all of a sudden the aluminum becomes non-anodic, becomes cathodic.

summary: Stress-corrosion cracking mechanism in fusion-welded magnesium alloys triggered by atmospheric humidity remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: when you try to weld it, the humidity in the air will almost crack it right behind the weld. Not quite that fast — you come back two days later after fusion welding magnesium alloys, if you haven't stress-relieved it, just the humidity in the air will cause stress corrosion cracking.

summary: Why sheet-rolling of magnesium is difficult compared to casting, blocking automotive applications, is unexplained.
verbatim: You can't roll sheet very easily, and automobiles are made out of sheet. You can make castings, but I have yet to figure out why they do all this.

summary: Understand why magnesium's hexagonal close-packed crystal structure limits its deformability and causes cracking during shape changes.
verbatim: One of the problems with magnesium, aside from the fact that it's hexagonal close-packed and you can't roll it very easily because it doesn't have enough deformation systems — when you learn about dislocations, they only work in certain materials like cubic metals, and magnesium is not cubic, it's hexagonal close-packed. It deforms by twinning, and you will crack it if you try to give it a general shape change.

summary: Titanium engines catastrophically catch fire above 900°C when the metal dissolves its protective oxide—the exact mechanisms and prevention strategies need clarification.
verbatim: If you get above 900 degrees centigrade — it's very corrosion resistant, it has reasonably good oxidation resistance up to 900 degrees, but above 900 degrees it will dissolve its own oxide, and all of a sudden it catches fire. It's like a great big magnesium flare.

summary: The chemical and physical separation of naturally co-occurring zirconium and hafnium ores presents an unresolved industrial challenge.
verbatim: These things right here in these columns of the periodic table tend to be found together in nature. If you have a zirconia ore, it's going to have lots of hafnium, or vice versa.

summary: Delrin's chlorine tolerance threshold is poorly characterized across different water chemistries and chlorine concentrations.
verbatim: A half a part per million chlorine would cause the stuff to decompose... Cambridge water is like 5 ppm chlorine — ten times what Delrin can support.

summary: Roman cement durability mechanisms remain incompletely understood despite 2000-year performance.
verbatim: The Romans used Portland cement, and the Roman cement is some of the best cement in the world — two thousand years later it's still there. The aqueducts, the Appian Way, made out of cement. Volcanic ash certainly has certain advantages for making cement, but I don't understand all the reasons.

summary: Develop recyclable composite materials to replace non-recyclable multi-layer juice box construction.
verbatim: Composite — what do I mean by composite? Juice boxes — seven layers of material, plastic, aluminum foil. If you try to peel these things apart, you can't, they're bonded together. The Achilles heel is recyclability. You either burn them or you put them in a landfill, that's it.

summary: High-temperature turbine blade alloys have plateaued despite decades of development; fundamental barriers to further temperature increases are not well articulated.
verbatim: They're graduates of this department, or assistant professors who went off to [Pratt &] Whitney or General Electric and developed these alloys. But they sort of ran out of steam, literally.

summary: Understanding why diamond tool performance degrades catastrophically when machining steel due to carbon diffusion, despite diamond's superior hardness.
verbatim: At 1000°C, the diamond starts diffusing into the steel. So what they use is cubic boron nitride, which is actually between diamond and silicon carbide... if the wear mechanism is chemical — basically dissolving the carbon into the steel — diamond's pretty lousy.

summary: Long-term degradation mechanisms and failure modes of PEX plastic pipe under realistic home water supply conditions over decades.
verbatim: Most PEX is rated for about 200 psi pressure, which is much more than you need for conveying water in a home. So much of the water in homes is now plastic.

summary: Why nickel precipitates in magnesium anodes preferentially corrode instead of protecting the steel substrate remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: Because if you had a nickel precipitate, it would become cathodic, and the magnesium anode would just eat away itself. It won't protect the steel — it'll protect the nickel, the impurity within it, because there's a shorter electrical circuit path.

summary: Magnesium's fundamental corrosion mechanism in the presence of chlorides remains unsolved despite decades of automotive and naval interest.
verbatim: No one's ever solved that problem, except for the people who use it as a corroding material — using it as an anode.

summary: The metallographic behavior of magnesium-carbon composites under aqueous polishing—specifically why water-based solutions cause accelerated corrosion—deserves systematic investigation.
verbatim: Ron Latanision, a professor here a number of years ago, said that when you tried to polish that metal metallographically, if you used a water-based polishing solution, it would corrode faster than you could polish.

summary: The timing and kinetics of zinc hydroxide formation on hot-dip galvanized steel and its effect on paint adhesion lack quantitative characterization.
verbatim: One of the things I've since learned is that if you hot-dip galvanize your steel, you have to paint it within a few hours, before the zinc hydroxide is really formed. Because if you get zinc hydroxide under there, the paint will not adhere.

summary: Why pitting corrosion occurs selectively at anodes in high-voltage electrochemical applications remains unresolved, with material options severely limited.
verbatim: They started with stainless steel, and the tips were pitting — terrible pitting on the anode, because that's where the corrosion occurs. The cathode was cathodically protected, no corrosion. They said, we need a better material.

summary: The mechanism by which UV light degrades PEX in real outdoor conditions deserves systematic study, given that UV energy is theoretically sufficient to break C–C bonds.
verbatim: Ultraviolet will break down primary bonds. Ultraviolet gives you a sunburn because it breaks down the primary bonds in your skin.

summary: Why cast iron water pipes degrade after ~100 years despite their silicon oxide protective layer remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: But after about a hundred years, depending on the quality of the water, that starts to break down too.

summary: Why titanium oxide cannot be soldered despite flux treatments, unlike stainless steel chromium oxide.
verbatim: You can't solder to titanium. It's got this protective oxide. There is no flux that will eat away the titanium oxide.

summary: Steel gas pipes installed in the 1920s–30s are leaking throughout the country, yet the mechanism and rate of corrosion failure remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: We've got pipes that were put in in the 1920s and '30s, and they are steel pipes leaking gas in the ground… They have to go around once a year and put those cool probes in the ground and go sniffing for gas to find the leaks.

summary: The dramatic difference in service life between cast iron (150+ years with minimal pitting) and steel (30–40 years) gas pipes lacks a systematic explanation.
verbatim: cast iron might last for 150 years and pit some; steel lasts for thirty or forty years.

summary: Stress concentrations arise from modulus mismatch between implant materials and bone, but the quantitative relationship and design guidelines remain unclear.
verbatim: If I have a composite material with two very different moduli, I end up with effectively a stress concentration. I get cracking and all kinds of problems... a high modulus material next to a low modulus material in a structure gives you a stress concentration. Not because of a notch, but just because of the differences in the materials.

summary: Understand the mechanism by which molybdenum carbide precipitation hardens steel at high temperature (700–800°C) rather than causing the softening typical of most materials.
verbatim: They found that if you put molybdenum in the steel you get very good high-temperature properties — at about seven or eight hundred degrees C, the steel would not just soften, it would actually get a little bit harder. You start getting some precipitation of molybdenum carbides that would actually precipitation-harden the steel at high temperatures.

summary: Fatigue crack initiation and growth in cast iron gas pipes under pressure cycling after mechanical damage remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: A backhoe had damaged the pipe about a quarter of an inch deep, and just the pressure cycles had caused a fatigue crack. When it finally got to critical flaw size, the whole thing went, and they had a 600-foot flame in the air at eleven o'clock one night.

summary: Understand how granite's three-phase composite structure creates crack-toughening mechanisms at notch tips that boost fracture toughness 2–3× above predictions from single-phase constituents.
verbatim: granite's a three-phase material, three different types of rock in there, and you actually form little cracks at the tip of that notch that toughen the material. If you measure the fracture toughness of granite, because it's a composite material, it has about two or three times the toughness you would predict from the toughness of silica, or the toughness of feldspar, or the other one.

summary: Map the minimum elongation threshold below which leak-before-break behavior becomes unreliable in thin-wall aluminum structures.
verbatim: You don't have to have twenty percent elongation — two percent elongation is usually enough, as long as you never fall below that.

summary: Why composites cannot achieve the fracture toughness-to-strength ratio needed for aircraft landing gear, despite their weight advantages.
verbatim: Because you can't get the strengths with the critical flaw sizes in anything other than steel. So even though it's exceptionally heavy, you still use steel for a landing gear on an aircraft because it's the only thing.

summary: Why cold-worked MP35N achieves exceptional toughness remains unclear, despite its widespread use in critical applications.
verbatim: Now, one of the things that makes it so tough — there's now a standard specification for it, an ASTM spec, and this goes back to 1978... This stuff really does stretch.

summary: Aluminum recycling streams are contaminated by alloy diversity, making mixed scrap unusable; new separation methods are needed.
verbatim: The aluminum alloys are so different in their classes that if you try to mix them all together you end up with a mishmash that you can't use for much of anything. People are working on new ways to separate the alloy content out of the aluminum alloys.

summary: Composite repair processes are difficult and uneconomical despite the material investment, undermining their practical advantage.
verbatim: This is one of the Achilles heels of all your fancy composites. How do you repair them? You went to all this trouble and processing and extra expense to make this fancy material, and then you have a hard time.

summary: Continuous caster breakouts, though rare, remain costly and inadequately predicted; control algorithms and casting speed limits lack mechanistic grounding.
verbatim: If you're not careful about the radius of curvature and the casting speed, you can have a breakout — all that liquid steel falls down through everything else — probably a hundred-million-dollar loss. They've got control algorithms and everything else. A lot of incentive to run it as fast as possible but not too fast.

summary: The metallurgical mechanisms underlying the quality improvement that occurred when Chaparral Steel slowed rolling speed while splitting rebar remain unexplained.
verbatim: The quality actually went up — that was another benefit. They proved that with I-beams in less than a year, and that's the rest of that story.

summary: The fundamental adhesion problem between glass and steel during cooling remains challenging despite workarounds.
verbatim: Steel and glass don't like each other. As it cools down, thermal expansion causes them to separate at the interface. It's a problem to try to bond glass to steel — we can do it, but we have to put an inner layer like titanium or something reactive in there.

summary: Optical fiber manufacturing requires strict moisture control during drawing, but the threshold moisture content and its effect on optical properties in graded-index fibers is treated as proprietary by Corning rather than published.
verbatim: The water content — they actually have a drying step before they do everything... The glass can pick up moisture — sodium hydroxide, silicon hydroxide, potassium hydroxide — you can get OH ions in there and it will screw up some of the optical qualities of optical glass.

summary: The depth to which ion exchange penetrates glass during chemical tempering and how it affects long-term durability is not well characterized.
verbatim: You take a glass — in this case they took a sodium aluminosilicate glass — and you do an ion exchange with potassium. You put it in a salt bath with potassium, and just because of entropy effects the sodium exchanges with the potassium. Potassium is a larger atom. You're doing this at relatively low temperatures, below any viscous diffusion, for hours.

summary: The tin-side surface of float glass is demonstrably less flat than the air-side when measured at atomic resolution, but the root cause and practical implications remain unclear.
verbatim: if you go in there with an atomic force microscope and measure the flatness, the tin side is nowhere near as flat and as perfect as the air side.

summary: Humidity attack on soda-lime glass forms subsurface hydroxide pits only tens of nanometers deep, but the kinetics and depth-limiting mechanism are not well characterized.
verbatim: Some of those sodium atoms will hit the surface, and when sodium sees moisture it might form sodium hydroxide, might form a little pit. It won't keep forming the pit forever, and depending on the composition and network structure, the silica is fairly immune to moisture corrosion, but the sodium and potassium are not.

summary: Why do thin-walled scandium-aluminum baseball bats crack after just one or two hits despite achieving 100+ ksi strength?
verbatim: they're getting so thin in the wall that some of these things you can take about one good hit before you start getting cracks in your bat. Who wants to pay 150 dollars for a bat and use it once?

summary: The geological process by which manganese-rich nodules nucleate and grow on the deep ocean floor remains poorly understood.
verbatim: They were formed by some geological process — these vents in the middle of the North Atlantic Ridge. They're just sitting there on the bottom. You have spewing up of minerals into the water from the vents, and somehow they're nucleating and growing, sort of like hail falling onto the surface of the ocean.

summary: Custom one-of-a-kind printed circuit boards have never been successfully 3D-printed despite industry interest from Cisco and Motorola.
verbatim: They wanted to be able to customize one-of-a-kind printed circuit boards. I was also working with Motorola — they had a little operation down south, and another here on Route 128 — and they were trying to do the same thing. It never worked. People would still love to do this.

summary: Understand why thermal conductivity limits productivity in laser-based metal 3D printing, and whether the Langmuir effect truly prevents scaling to higher power.
verbatim: If you try to go to higher power, the Langmuir kicks in and you start evaporating, you start forming welding fume in the atmosphere. So you have a thermal-conductivity limitation on your productivity.

summary: The actual strength degradation mechanism in carbon nanotubes from thermodynamic defects remains poorly quantified experimentally.
verbatim: In that perfect little carbon nanotube there's going to be a missing carbon atom. At any temperature above absolute zero, thermodynamics — the entropy — tells us we're going to have a vacancy. That's a defect, and it will create a stress concentration and be much weaker, maybe ten times weaker.

summary: Understanding why manganese-aluminum-bronze wetting and surface-tension balance works better than other alloys for 3D printing, while most metals suffer surface-tension defects.
verbatim: Manganese-aluminum-bronze has a better wetting and surface-tension balance than some other things. You can see we were reasonably successful with that, although we're still going to end up with tremendous residual stresses.

summary: Carbon-free metal reduction methods are being developed to eliminate CO2 from metal production, but a major challenge is identifying reliable large-scale renewable electricity sources beyond hydroelectric power.
verbatim: Professor Sadoway said, well then we should be the ones to figure out how to clean it up, and get away from carbon-free metal reduction. So Professor Allanore and Professor Sadoway and a number of other people in the department have various schemes to generate metals without using carbon. In general they're going to do that by using electrons, and today where do most electrons come from? The utility, which burns coal.

summary: Concrete recycling is virtually nonexistent despite 2.2 billion tons annual production, creating an urgent waste-disposal problem.
verbatim: What's concrete recycling? Almost nothing. And it's 2.2 billion tons. You want to solve a world problem that's coming up? What are we going to do with 2.2 billion tons when it comes back after useful life?

summary: Titanium combustor fires in jet engines remain inadequately understood and prevented despite documented incidents a decade ago.
verbatim: There have been a number of combustor fires in jet engines where the titanium ignited. It's exactly like a sparkler going off; it's exactly the same thing as a flare... There were a number of fires about ten years ago in aircraft engines.

summary: A lightweight replacement material for jet turbine disc roots could enable major collateral weight savings in engine design, but no viable candidate exists for high-temperature combustor service.
verbatim: People have been trying for years to make a jet turbine disc that does not have to have the big heavy flange and the mechanical attachment... If we had a material that was lighter weight, we'd love to use it.

summary: Ceramic core positioning tolerance in single-crystal blade casting is a hard limit preventing thinner cooling channels.
verbatim: The problem is the ceramic core inside that you grow the single crystal around, very slowly. If it shifts by one or two thousandths of an inch, you've got junk, because you can't afford two thousandths out of seven. So you really can't get them any thinner than they're already making them.

summary: Identifying failure modes and design solutions for organic fiber reinforcement in concrete, given that natural fibers decompose over time.
verbatim: Natural fibers tend to decompose — organic fibers rot. But we've been using them to make bricks since the days of Moses and before. Can't make bricks without straw. But what are the issues if we want to use it for concrete?

summary: Why does titanium welding porosity mysteriously recur even after successful cleaning protocols are established and followed?
verbatim: Then they called me up two weeks later and said, we're failing twenty-five percent again. I said, have you changed your cleaning? No, we're doing the same thing.

summary: Lightning-induced perforation of corrugated stainless steel gas tubing coatings lacks systematic characterization and mitigation strategies.
verbatim: In a lightning storm, you'll have an arc, and the arc can perforate the polyethylene coating, which is good for 30,000 volts — not a problem for household current, because it's insulated. But 30,000 volts is nothing compared to the millions of volts of a lightning bolt. To the lightning, the yellow tubing is not there.

summary: How paint on aluminum aircraft wings changes lightning strike behavior and damage patterns compared to bare aluminum remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: I know a lot about what happens when you hit an aluminum wing that's bare, or a painted aluminum wing — the two things are different. Just putting a coat of paint on it makes a big difference in how the lightning attacks it.

summary: Root cause and prevention mechanisms for rapid wear failure of asphalt reclamation tool bits, and optimization of sintered diamond tip geometry for extended service life.
verbatim: You ever been driving on the interstate late at night and they're reclaiming the asphalt? They have a great big machine. This is the tool that's on the wheel that's beating up the asphalt and throwing it back into a trailer to be recycled. And you can wear out these tools in three or four hours, in which case you have to stop the machine.

summary: Understand why pad conditioners become clogged during electrochemical polishing of semiconductor wafers and how to optimize their design.
verbatim: They get clogged up just like any sponge with all the grinding swarf. So they come in with pad conditioners, which are basically diamonds, and they eat the junk out of the holes in the polishing pad. It's a complex process...

summary: The mechanism by which microcracks at crack tips absorb energy in brittle materials remains incompletely quantified across different loading conditions.
verbatim: At the tip of the crack you actually get little microcracks, and those microcracks absorb more energy than anyone ever thought they would in terms of fracture behavior... but the dynamic fracture toughness was greater than they had assumed.

summary: Investigate why duplex stainless steel centrifuge discs experienced brittle fracture when improperly heat-treated, and establish robust heat-treatment protocols to ensure consistent toughness.
verbatim: They had one of them let go in France, almost killed somebody but didn't, and then they killed someone in China... they didn't heat treat the steel properly.

summary: Understand the mechanism by which Silly Putty transitions from superplastic (slow strain) to brittle (fast strain) behavior.
verbatim: Silly Putty is almost a Newtonian material — it stretches hundreds of percent strain if you pull it slow. But the interesting thing about Silly Putty, because as a polymer it has some very interesting mechanical properties — I can pull on Silly Putty slowly and it stretches. What happens if I pull it quickly? Nothing — if I pull it quickly and it's small enough in diameter for me to break it, I get a brittle fracture. No deformation. That's a brittle fracture. So Silly Putty is very strain-rate dependent.

summary: The relationship between shear lip width (plane stress fracture area) and material toughness lacks a quantitative model despite observable correlation.
verbatim: The size of that 45 degree fracture, the plane stress area, is another measure of the ductility — an indirect measure of the toughness of the steel. I have seen big fractures and explosions where I have shear lips that are three or four inches wide. That's some of the best material that's up here, with a four-inch wide shear lip in plane stress, is going to be really tough material. It's not a measure of fracture toughness, but there is a correlation.

summary: Necking geometry in tensile specimens varies with specimen geometry (flat vs. round, gauge length, size), but the predictive rules for how these factors control necking angle and morphology are incompletely characterized.
verbatim: Necking or distortion — I just passed around some samples to show necking, and the necking is different in a flat specimen than in a round specimen. It's geometry dependent. The way you measure it depends on the length of the specimen and the size of the specimen.

summary: The mechanism by which nickel sulfide inclusions in glass create defects and compromise integrity remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: Little pieces of nickel sulfide — you shouldn't have a lot of nickel sulfide floating around, but nickel sulfide inclusions are bad for glass and create defects.

summary: The long-term strength degradation of glass fibers in humid environments is incompletely understood—whether corrosion continues slowly under protective coatings or halts.
verbatim: That doesn't mean the glass continues to corrode — maybe it does, but it slows down so much that glass has been there for a hundred years now, some of it, and it's weaker than when it was first put in, but it's not that much weaker.

summary: The tin-side imperfections in float glass (nanometer scale) degrade strength, but the mechanism and optimization remain unclear.
verbatim: The tin side has some imperfections — we're talking about imperfections on the order of many nanometers, but it affects the strength.

summary: Why do continuous welds allow cracks to propagate all the way around a structure, whereas riveted joints arrest crack propagation before circumferential failure?
verbatim: Cracks tend to run all the way to the end of the plate, and if you have a weld that's continuous, the crack goes all the way around. There's nothing to stop the crack once it starts to run. Most of these cracks started at welding defects.

summary: Welding two large forgings (3–4 foot square welds) for generator rotors to bypass the capacity constraints of specialized heat-treatment facilities is an unsolved manufacturing challenge.
verbatim: They wanted to know, could we take some of our smaller plants and weld two forgings together? Now you're talking about welding two pieces that are like three or four foot square weld. It's not an easy problem.

summary: The creep-fatigue interaction mechanism in titanium welds under combined stress remains unsolved, as evidenced by Soviet submarine failures.
verbatim: Titanium has this problem: if you put it under continuous compressive stress, even at room temperature or seawater temperature, it will start to slowly creep. Then if you flex it, there's an interaction, and the cracks grow ultra-fast... The US Navy asked me, 'How did the Soviets solve the creep-fatigue interaction of the titanium?' I said, 'I don't know.' It turns out they didn't.

summary: The mechanism by which fretting in ultrasonic welding breaks aluminum oxide and achieves metal-to-metal contact remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: That microscopic motion — there's something we call fretting corrosion or fretting wear that can break up those surface oxides and get rid of my surface contamination locally and cause true metal-to-metal contact.

summary: Understand the fundamental physics of how ultrasonic vibration sweeps surface contaminants (oxides, oils) away during cold welding to enable full contact.
verbatim: ultrasonic welding is a cold welding process that tends to leave behind little gobs of surface contamination all over the surface, but if you're clever you might be able to sweep it away, which is what they did.

summary: Understand why graphite transitions from lubricant to abrasive in space environments, a phenomenon discovered during early Mercury missions.
verbatim: I will tell you about how graphite is a lubricant on Earth and an abrasive in space. That was a big surprise at the beginning of the Mercury program. Some of the first space shots, things quit turning.

summary: Wire bonding speed is fundamentally limited by mechanical inertia and stiffness of the bonding head, preventing faster than ~7–10 bonds per second despite economic pressure.
verbatim: You run into the same stiffness and vibration problems limiting how fast you can go. You can try to run it faster, but the mechanical inertia of all these parts moving up and down — you have to make the sewing-machine heads lightweight because of the inertia.

summary: Ultrasonic wire bonding sacrifices throughput (1–2 bonds/second vs. 7) to improve quality, suggesting an unresolved trade-off between speed and bond reliability.
verbatim: You can improve this problem if you do it with ultrasonics. You can't make seven a second if you're doing ultrasonics at the same time. You might make one a second, or two a second.

summary: Understand the mechanism and control of crevice corrosion at the interface between tube sheets and inserted pipes in large heat exchangers.
verbatim: For each of those 10,000 pipes going through the tube sheet, you need a joint between the tube sheet and the pipe so you don't get water leaking out. If you don't get a good seal, you get crevice corrosion over time.

summary: The surface energy differences between liquid metals and how strongly impurities bond to them in vacuum merit detailed investigation.
verbatim: Surface energy becomes important in all this cold welding. How strongly bonded are the impurities to the surfaces?

summary: Why metallic surface energies are 2–3× higher than ionic/covalent materials remains incompletely explained despite the electron-range hypothesis.
verbatim: Why are metallic surface energies so much higher? For ionic and covalent, the surface energy comes from just the top two layers — more than two atomic distances away, that curve drops off. For metallic, these free non-localized electrons give us bond contributions from greater distances. The number of electrons involved in the surface energy is greater by a factor of two or three, and therefore metals have surface energies two or three times higher.

summary: Polymer chain diffusion across plastic interfaces remains fundamentally limited, causing persistent weak demarcation lines even after successful surface extrusion during welding.
verbatim: That's the problem in joining plastics in general: you can't get polymer chains going across the interface. They don't diffuse — they're too big to diffuse — and so you always end up with a strong demarcation which is just van der Waals bonding.

summary: Impact resistance of polyethylene gas pipe welds remains poorly characterized despite decades of field deployment; creep behavior under sustained tension also needs investigation.
verbatim: If you do a tensile test you can set parameters such that you'll probably fail in the base material, or you'll fail at a substantial fraction of the yield stress. But impacts are still a problem. Creep too, if you put this under tension.

summary: The interplay between surface roughness and joint thickness in type-one adhesive bonding needs systematic investigation to understand when roughness enhances versus degrades bond strength.
verbatim: There are times when having a little bit of surface roughness even in type one, as long as you don't destroy the thinness of the joint, increases the surface area and can enhance the effective surface energy of the joint.

summary: The competing requirements of anodized aluminum surface preparation: porosity needed for adhesive bonding versus sealing needed for corrosion resistance.
verbatim: But if you're going to use it for an adhesive-bonded prep surface, you don't want to seal it. You want to leave it nice and porous. So it's mechanical interlocking.

summary: Understand why cyanoacrylates bond strength degrades dramatically when switching from thin films to thick, high-viscosity formulations used in structural anchoring.
verbatim: I just gave up two or three orders of magnitude on bonding strength, because I started out with something I'm not going to get this thin — I'm not going to use the thinness of the Stefan equation there.

summary: Investigate the specific hydroxy radical chemistry that explains why cyanoacrylates bond preferentially to basic vs. acidic substrates (paper vs. wood).
verbatim: Crazy Glue sticks better to paper than it does to wood, because paper is slightly basic... Crazy Glue doesn't work as well on most woods because woods are slightly acidic.

summary: The exact source of hydrogen contamination in plasma-sprayed stainless steel coatings and its role in delayed cracking remains unclear.
verbatim: I said, well, that could be the source of hydrogen. And it turns out it was. They were trying to get a rough surface... [but] I just don't know where the hydrogen came from.

summary: Moisture and road salts attack adhesive bonds in automotive door panel assemblies after 5 years, causing structural failure, yet the precise degradation mechanism remains unexplained.
verbatim: After about five years the adhesives were attacked by moisture — road salts, rainwater splashing up in there — and these door panels were just rattling.

summary: Understanding why adhesive bonds degrade over decades in service, particularly corrosion migration at the interface.
verbatim: Over time you get some corrosion at the interface as things migrate in. [Boeing] were using adhesive bonding — but then they were putting rivets in. He says, well, why are you doing that? They said, oh, just to be sure, because in thirty years adhesive bonds are going to get weaker.

summary: The mechanism by which water vapor deposits inside surface asperities on Teflon under thermal gradients, enabling wet adhesion.
verbatim: If you could deposit the water on the inside like this — and you can, if you vapor-deposit in a temperature gradient. So if I had steam up here and I cooled my surface and I vapor-deposited, I would end up depositing water inside these asperities.

summary: Understand whether Teflon coating prevents ice buildup in carburetors, conditional on the icing mechanism (rain droplets vs. frost from humidity).
verbatim: Then the question is, should you put Teflon on your carburetor or not? The answer is, it depends on what's causing icing... If it's water droplets because you're flying in rain... Teflon would be great. But what if it's just the humidity in the air, and that's cooling and depositing on the walls of the carburetor, and you're getting frost buildup that you can't get off with a sledgehammer?

summary: Why aluminum and magnesium cannot be diffusion bonded despite being common metals remains unexplained beyond the oxide stability issue.
verbatim: Among the common metals: iron, titanium, and nickel, and in particular titanium. But the things that can't be bonded very easily are aluminum and magnesium. Why? Because they form very stable oxides that won't dissolve into the base material.

summary: The mechanism by which titanium oxide is consumed by titanium above 900°C and the conditions that trigger spontaneous combustion in engines needs deeper investigation.
verbatim: In titanium — our poster child for diffusion bonding — above 900° centigrade titanium will consume its own oxide. In fact that's been a problem in the titanium jet engine business. They've actually had titanium fires in the engine if they run the engine improperly and they get above 900° centigrade.

summary: Why exactly does grain growth and stage-three porosity occur above 0.8 of absolute melting temperature, and what is the precise relationship between grain boundary motion rate and interface porosity?
verbatim: Above eight-tenths of the absolute melting point... you have to stay far enough below — or close enough to — the recrystallization temperature of the metal, so that you don't start getting lots of grain growth... if they do and the grains get too big you get to stage three too early and you're full of porosity at the interface.

summary: The physical mechanism by which tin diffusion into copper during transient liquid phase soldering leaves behind lead-rich material with dramatically improved high-temperature strength needs investigation.
verbatim: The tin diffused into the copper, leaving behind a very rich lead, which is what they had intended to get anyway.

summary: Whether industrial solder joints in circuit boards actually operate via transient liquid phase diffusion bonding rather than conventional solder mechanics remains unclear.
verbatim: I started thinking about it and realized that a lot of the joints they were making — they might have been making solder joints with the same old lead-tin solders with copper or gold, but in fact what they're really doing is transient liquid phase diffusion soldering.

summary: The thermal expansion mismatch problem when joining silicon or gallium arsenide chips to substrates via transient liquid phase diffusion needs investigation.
verbatim: we actually worked on transient liquid phase diffusion soldering, to try to join silicon, or in his case gallium arsenide chips to the substrate. Big thermal expansion problems.

summary: Determine the dominant failure criterion for dissimilar-metal joints when stress and strain are multiaxial tensors rather than scalars.
verbatim: You have a problem if you want to do stress or strain... What strain do you use? People have been worrying about this for years, not just in dissimilar-metal joints but in a biaxial tensile test — what do you use for the criteria for failure?

summary: Why larger computer chips crack during bonding despite advances in integration—thermal strain limits remain poorly understood.
verbatim: If they tried a centimeter and a half on a side, they couldn't bond it to its substrate without it cracking, just from about a 30° centigrade temperature differential that you have to carry the heat out of the chip.

summary: Develop a kinetic (non-equilibrium) extension to Young's equation that accounts for temperature gradients and actually provides new physical insight.
verbatim: People have tried to take Young's equation and develop a kinetic equation of wetting from it, but I've never seen a model that really works or gives you new insight.

summary: The wetting kinetics of lead-free solders versus traditional lead-tin solders under transient non-equilibrium conditions has not been systematically characterized despite massive industry investment.
verbatim: nothing wets as well or as fast as lead-tin solder. Hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent by industry and government.

summary: Understanding why gallium arsenide cracks during room-temperature bonding despite no thermal cycling.
verbatim: gallium arsenide will crack just from bonding even at room temperature. You don't have to worry about the thermal cycling.

summary: Investigate why abietic acid rosin flux loses chemical activity at high copper tarnish levels and whether additives can restore performance.
verbatim: Abietic acid will form a copper abietate. You actually clean the surface of the copper oxide, but it's not a very strong acid... At high tarnish, there's not enough activity to clean the surface.

summary: Why certain metals like beryllium and titanium remain fundamentally unsolderable below 450°C despite flux chemistry advances.
verbatim: Beryllium and titanium, they're just not solderable. Below 450 C, you don't have enough temperature to break down the titanium oxide or the beryllium oxide.

summary: Predicting and preventing long-term corrosion of fine solder joints on printed circuit boards from residual halogenated flux.
verbatim: If you're talking about very small solder joints, such as you have on a printed circuit board where your joints are very small, it doesn't take more than a year's worth of corrosion — because the joints are so thin and so small — and all of a sudden you've corroded away your joint.

summary: The mechanisms by which specific trace contaminants (Al, Mg, Zn, S, Cd) degrade solder wettability and joint quality remain incompletely characterized.
verbatim: If you pick up very much contamination, you find that 50 parts per million of aluminum, magnesium, or zinc — zinc could be in a lot of things, we use it for corrosion protection, but it would easily get into that solder bath — will form intermetallics. Those intermetallics start to act like sand in the solder bath.

summary: The mechanism by which tungsten prevents copper interdiffusion into silicon remains poorly explained and could be rigorously studied.
verbatim: IBM announced they had come up with this mystery bonding layer or inter-diffusion layer that would prevent inter-diffusion of copper into the silicon, so it wouldn't destroy the semiconductor properties. The mystery material turns out to be tungsten.

summary: Understand why solder ball connections begin to fail due to thermal expansion shearing around 2,000 connections per chip.
verbatim: You can get up to 2,000 theoretically before you start running into thermal expansion problems, of these things just shearing themselves apart.

summary: Understanding how to safely volatilize zinc contamination from vacuum brazing furnaces without redistributing it to cooler regions where it becomes trapped.
verbatim: The outside is water-cooled; you can put your hand on the wall of the vacuum furnace when it's running. So all they did was move the zinc into the cooler regions.

summary: Characterizing and controlling erosion mechanisms in high-temperature brazing of complex multi-metal heat exchangers.
verbatim: In brazing, you can have erosion of 50 or 100 microns or even more.

summary: The mechanism by which cadmium oxide suppresses arcing in electrical contacts at high amperage is presented but not mechanistically explained.
verbatim: If you put a tenth of a percent cadmium oxide in there, you can get 15 amps. Then you can break a circuit at 15 amps without creating an arc — it will suppress the arc.

summary: The exact failure mechanism of the Thresher's seawater piping valve—whether it was the braze joint itself, material defect, or design flaw—remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: They think it was a sea water piping valve, where they brazed a steel pipe where the seawater came in to help cool the nuclear reactor, and it let go.

summary: The mechanism by which gas expansion in the ballast valve caused clogging during emergency blow procedures is not well characterized.
verbatim: when you expand gases, they clogged the valve and they didn't blow the tanks completely.

summary: Helicopters failed in desert conditions due to sand ingestion causing engine abrasion, but the fix (engine particle separators) was developed under time pressure—understanding the fundamental erosion mechanisms and optimal separator designs remains unclear.
verbatim: The helicopters were failing because they would ingest dust and sand from the desert, and within three minutes they would just abrade away the whole engine. They had to develop things called engine particle separators and stuff. They worked around it, but they realized they were working very fast to solve problems.

summary: The cost reduction pathway for powder metallurgy 3D printing from $1,000/pound down to $2/pound automotive pricing remains unspecified—a significant gap between demonstrated and viable manufacturing economics.
verbatim: You've got kind of a little hurdle from $10,000 a pound to something that's automotive, which is going to be selling for on average about $2 a pound. You better have some really good ideas of how to reduce that. So what are they doing? They have multiple print heads. They have like twenty print heads. That could reduce the cost by a factor of ten. Ten into 10,000 and you're down to 1,000. You only need another factor of 500. So what's your next idea?

summary: Frosty welds appear consistently when welding galvanized steel, but the underlying mechanism and mitigation strategies deserve systematic study.
verbatim: Well Bill, you always get frosty welds when you weld steel through galvanizing because the zinc vaporizes. He says, well yeah, but I need to fix it Tom.

summary: Statistical process control fails at low sigma levels due to multiple concurrent failure modes, but the precise transition point and how to diagnose multiple root causes remains unclear.
verbatim: At three Sigma, I'm producing seven percent defects, and there are multiple reasons. When you've got that many problems, there are multiple reasons. Trying to apply statistics, which tends to home in on one, is going to give you lousy statistics because you've got too many variables.

summary: Beyond Six Sigma, defect rates drop too low to gather statistically significant samples, making further process improvement difficult to quantify.
verbatim: But many companies would use SPC and get to five Sigma and have this goal to get to Six Sigma, and they really couldn't do it. The reason was, at Six Sigma there's not enough defects to give me good statistics.

summary: The underlying cause of submarine piping conflicts and cascading inventory failures—how to model or predict spatial interference and material constraints during design—remains systematically unaddressed.
verbatim: But this piping had to use this metal and that piping had to use that metal, and they were always out of inventory, because when they had a problem, someone would steal from inventory that had already been ordered, which might be a nine-month lead time. They'd get that problem solved, but all they did was create other problems for the future.

summary: Cable-stayed bridges require extremely precise strand length tuning (within 1/4 inch), but the mechanics of stress redistribution after individual strand failure is not well characterized.
verbatim: they have to basically pull those strands within about a quarter of an inch of being all at the same length, otherwise you have too much stress on one of them. One strand of the wire rope snaps, and then another one snaps.

summary: No one had previously attempted to forge ultra-high-purity alkali halide crystals (potassium chloride, potassium fluoride, cesium chloride) with zero dislocations or voids for high-power laser windows.
verbatim: No one had ever tried to make very high purity, low imperfection — no dislocations or voids — things of potassium fluoride and potassium chloride and cesium chloride. No one had ever tried to do that before.

summary: Recent structural failures have resulted from the transition from ASD to LRFD design methods, with specific failure cases warranting investigation.
verbatim: There have been some interesting failures because of this stuff, and I'll talk about that on Tuesday. There are some interesting failures that come about because of canned programs.

summary: Understand the fundamental kinetics of why molybdenum shifts the C-curve nose by an order of magnitude and whether this effect is predictable from first principles.
verbatim: molybdenum is just changing the nose of that C-curve over from a second to thirty seconds, twenty seconds. I can slow the reaction down by a factor of twenty by adding half a percent moly to the steel.

summary: Understand why bainite has dramatically different toughness than martensite despite similar strength, despite both being hard quenched phases.
verbatim: Bainite in the as-quenched condition, you can bend it into a U, and it has almost the same strength as the martensite. It's because of a different type of transformation.

summary: The hydrogen embrittlement mechanism in electroplated high-strength steel and its interaction with fatigue crack initiation remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: When you electroplate the steel, you introduce hydrogen. The steel's embrittled. If that thing gets shipped to him and whoever did it didn't bake out the hydrogen, the steel's embrittled, and it starts getting stressed. Within a few days or a few weeks, you have a brittle material, and it can start a crack.

summary: Develop a practical method to determine welding procedures for old steels of unknown composition, which arises frequently in bridge and building renovation.
verbatim: They'd say, 'We're redoing something' — like Dr. Belmar [?] said, they're redoing something like the Longfellow Bridge. They've got this old steel in this old building, and they want to know how to weld it... 'We don't know.' And I'd say, 'Then I can't tell you, because I need to know how much carbon, how much alloy content is in the steel.'

summary: The mechanism by which hydrogen atoms preferentially accumulate at crack tips during stress—while intuitively explained by lattice strain—lacks quantitative experimental validation under controlled welding conditions.
verbatim: Why is that? Well, hydrogen is an interstitial atom. It likes to strain the lattice, and if you strain the lattice, the hydrogen will go to the lowest energy state where the lattice is already expanded. That's at the crack tip.

summary: Eagar notes that early HY-80 submarine welds experienced delayed hydrogen cracking 8 hours after welding due to poor hydrogen control, but the precise mechanism of hydrogen diffusion to crack tips over this timeframe isn't fully characterized.
verbatim: Some guy welding at night would hear this piece that had been welded during the day, and it'd be a big boom, like a rifle shot. A crack — a hydrogen crack — just ran through the part they had made that day, 8 hours earlier. Delayed cracking. The hydrogen diffused to the crack tip during those eight hours.

summary: The mechanism by which hydrogen embrittlement reverses when steel is heated without cracks forming remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: Hydrogen that gets into steel is reversible. If I have a piece of steel and I embrittle it with hydrogen, I stick it in an oven to get the hydrogen out, and as long as no cracks formed in the meantime — say I had no stress — I get rid of the hydrogen, there's no more embrittlement, and it goes back to being a ductile piece of steel.

summary: The exact mechanism and critical temperature window for hydrogen stress corrosion cracking in welded steel is incompletely characterized—the minimum time-to-failure is empirically observed near room temperature but the underlying physics deserves investigation.
verbatim: This is time to failure versus temperature. These are real data points in hydrogen sulfide, and it shows that the minimum time to failure is right around 25 degrees centigrade, and lo and behold it's just over an hour.
