summary: Delayed hydrogen cracking in high-strength steel occurs on a time scale (hours to days) that makes early testing misleading—the physical mechanism and kinetics remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: It could have formed afterwards, after your one hour. You have to wait. The US Navy waits seven days before testing for cracks.

summary: The threshold strength level at which hydrogen cracking becomes a serious risk in bridge welds is not precisely defined; the jump from 70 ksi (safe with care) to 100–120 ksi (requires post-weld testing) lacks a clear mechanistic explanation.
verbatim: With 70 ksi, I can use almost any electrode with a little bit of care and I won't get enough hydrogen. With 120 ksi I could get cracking.

summary: Local stress relief on pressure vessels risks unintended tempering embrittlement in intermediate temperature zones, but failure mechanisms and steel-type dependencies are not well characterized.
verbatim: There are all kinds of rules on local heat treatment, because local heat treatment somewhere on the part is going to get into this intermediate range where you get temper brittleness. You could damage your steel, depending on the type of steel, by doing local stress relief.

summary: ASME code tables (UCS-56) for stress-relief requirements vary by weld geometry at marginal thicknesses, but the physical basis for these geometry-dependent cutoffs is not clearly explained.
verbatim: Some welds at an inch and a quarter you don't have to stress relieve, some at an inch and a quarter you do, at 1-1/2 inches you pretty much always have to. So it depends on the geometry as well, and they have these rules.

summary: Determine whether incomplete preheat, combined with frozen conditions and subsequent loading, has measurable effects on hydrogen diffusion kinetics that could explain the nine-month delay before failure.
verbatim: They didn't preheat properly, and it had a hard microstructure because they didn't preheat properly... It must have been preheated to 100 degrees... they didn't bother to shovel the snow off the inside... they're not even drying the stick electrodes.

summary: The metallurgical consequences of re-heat-treating large forgings with stand-in material samples that cool differently than the actual component remain poorly characterized.
verbatim: But that doesn't cool exactly the same way as this piece. This one's 200 tons; this one might be two tons, and they cool differently, they get different grain sizes.

summary: Why the heat-treated pressure vessel lost toughness despite passing small Charpy samples remains unexplained.
verbatim: They took Charpys out — it failed. So they redid it, and this little piece passed, and that little piece had enough toughness. But when they went out to test this thing after it exploded... the crack ran right from that corner stress concentration, and it just ripped off a piece about a third of the way around.

summary: The hydrogen source causing stress corrosion cracking in this large heat-treated vessel is not clearly identified.
verbatim: It's partly a hydrogen cracking story. It's not a welding story, but it's a hydrogen cracking story... you have to have a source of hydrogen, and you'll get stress corrosion cracking.

summary: The mechanism by which hydrogen causes strength reduction (up to 75%) in high-strength steel under complex stress states remains incompletely explained.
verbatim: If you looked at hydrogen, well, I could explain all kinds of things with hydrogen. I can get up to 75% reduction in strength if I have a lot of hydrogen.

summary: The mechanism preventing larger single-chip assembly due to cracking from residual stresses in soldering/brazing remains understudied in the electronics-welding interface.
verbatim: you couldn't join something more than about one centimeter on a side without it cracking due to residual stresses from the soldering or brazing operation.

summary: Fracture mechanics predictions of weld defect significance need validation against real service data across different loading and material conditions.
verbatim: Well, first of all, do fracture mechanics and see if the pore makes a difference, and I will tell you that 19 times out of 20 those little imperfections — fracture mechanics will tell you they're insignificant... through experience they've seen these bridges last 80 years with no problem, no fatigue cracks. They know what size imperfections are permissible at the design stress levels that the codes allow.

summary: Despite decades of Navy-funded research, the conditions under which undermatching weld metal might be safely used remain unresolved, with every large-scale structural test revealing brittle failure at the weld.
verbatim: The Navy and other people have spent millions and millions of dollars over the years trying to see if they could use undermatching weld metal... But every time they've done it, they've had to weld up whole structures and shoot at them with ballistics if you're the Navy... every time the result has been failure.

summary: Understand why repeated attempts over 25 years to use undermatching filler metal in high-strength steels have consistently failed despite theoretical advantages.
verbatim: about every 15 years, someone would go out and spend millions of dollars trying to find out if they could use undermatching filler metal. The advantage in steels is, you get this acicular ferrite that will give you strengths up to 120 ksi, which means you can weld steels with base metal of 100 ksi, and you'll be overmatching.

summary: Why weld notches produce identical fatigue strength regardless of base-material strength, unlike stress-concentration behavior in non-welded holes.
verbatim: If you put a weld in there, you get no advantage for high-strength steel in fatigue if it's welded. The reason is the weld produces a notch. It's a stress concentration. And it turns out, in terms of fatigue, that notch is going to give you the same fatigue strength whether you're a low-strength steel or whether you're a high-strength steel.

summary: Understand why closure welds around plate overlaps catastrophically reduce fatigue strength despite adding no structural benefit.
verbatim: It doesn't really add any strength. In fact, it tremendously reduces the fatigue strength.

summary: The mechanism by which large freezing ranges in aluminum alloys produce hot tear cracks during solidification deserves deeper investigation.
verbatim: In the heat-affected zone you'll actually melt some of the grain boundaries — some of the inter-dendritic spaces — and you'll get liquid. Because aluminum has a 6% volume change on solidification, you get big internal stresses.

summary: The metallurgical mechanisms controlling residual stress relief via controlled stretching and multi-stage aging in thick aluminum alloys remain inadequately characterized.
verbatim: You can't heat treat it to relieve the residual stresses for various metallurgical reasons... they have this huge hydraulic jack that can take a six-inch plate by about 10 or 12 feet wide and just stretch it one percent... you may do a double age. You may age it to get strength, and then you stretch it, and then you might age it again to get even more strength, or overage it to get corrosion resistance.

summary: Long-term fatigue and stress concentration behavior of aluminum pressure vessels with unreinforced port holes under cyclic loading.
verbatim: The boiler and pressure vessel code said, hey, if you've got a hole in a plate, you've got a stress concentration factor of three, you have to use a doubler plate... he says, D.O.T. doesn't regulate me... so we'll just keep building these things without any doubler plates, without any reinforcements where the boiler and pressure vessel code requires them.

summary: Why do compressed air tanks blow up even when built to ASME standards, and what causes their failure modes?
verbatim: they do blow up every time, even if they're built ASME. This one wasn't built ASME.

summary: The mechanisms behind corrosion-assisted failure in aluminum pressure vessels after multiple repair welds.
verbatim: One of them comes back for about its third time being welded on, because it started leaking... It was corroded, but it was basically an overload failure.

summary: Investigate why aluminum oxide skin behavior during welding differs fundamentally from the melting point prediction, given the large temperature gap between oxide melting (~1500°C) and aluminum alloy melting (550–660°C).
verbatim: That aluminum oxide skin is actually a hydrated aluminum oxide, so it doesn't really melt at 2,000 °C — maybe it only melts at 1500 °C. Given that the aluminum alloy melts at 550 to 660 °C, depending on how pure it is or how highly alloyed it is, that's a big temperature difference.

summary: Whether under-matching weld metal (softer filler than base) actually causes fatigue failures in aluminum crankcase repairs, or if investigators are confusing correlation with causation.
verbatim: For thirty years, every now and then someone would investigate one of these and find their weld metal was softer than their base metal, and say that's the cause. They didn't go through any fracture mechanics and determine what the stresses were.

summary: Why do helicoil and double-helicoil inserts show the same strength as base metal at 204 inch-pounds despite their larger thread area, when theory predicts they should perform better?
verbatim: with the stud into the base metal, half of them failed at 204 inch-pounds. With the stud into 4043 weld, half failed — with helicoil and with double helicoil.

summary: Establish why 4145 weld metal showed dramatically higher strength than 4043 in the same stud-pull test, and whether this translates to practical fatigue performance in service.
verbatim: They also made one into 4145 weld metal and got a really big increase in strength.

summary: Whether under-matching filler metal actually improves fatigue strength in thin welds remains unclear and deserves systematic study.
verbatim: I think you might prefer in many cases to have under-matching filler metal, because this is not an impact-loaded situation, and you can get a little better fatigue strength of softer material.

summary: The mechanism by which palladium improves crevice corrosion resistance in caustic solutions remains unexplained in Eagar's treatment.
verbatim: In very caustic solutions, like pH 10 or greater, you improve the crevice corrosion resistance. There are only a few situations where titanium will corrode, but at very high pH in crevice corrosion.

summary: The mechanism by which compressive stress promotes fatigue crack initiation in titanium at room temperature remains unexplained.
verbatim: If you have it under a big compressive stress, it would fatigue very readily. That's what they call the creep-fatigue interaction.

summary: Why gas metal arc welding fails for titanium despite extensive US Navy investment remains unexplained.
verbatim: The US Navy had been working on it, and they never really got it to work very well. I was doing research on it and I couldn't get it to work either... The US Navy had been working on a process that the Soviets had determined a long time ago didn't work. I won't go into the reasons why it doesn't work, but the Soviets used electroslag, and another process they used was gas tungsten arc welding.

summary: The relationship between shielding gas dew point and hydrogen absorption in titanium welds is empirically known but mechanistically poorly understood.
verbatim: This is dew point of the argon shielding gas versus hydrogen content. Here's 60 parts per million. If your dew point gets very high, all of a sudden your hydrogen goes up, your hardness goes up, your minimum bend radius — you lose mechanical properties.

summary: Understand why the Soviet Alpha-class submarines developed widespread fatigue cracks and became noisy within two years of operation despite advanced titanium construction.
verbatim: I told you how the Soviets ended up mothballing these things. Two years later they were noisy, they were full of fatigue cracks.

summary: The protective patina on native copper is complex (copper oxide, sulfide, and other phases) but its composition and formation mechanism are not fully characterized.
verbatim: It's not just straight copper oxide — it's a copper oxide sulfide and other things. They call it a patina.

summary: The fundamental reason why single-cell batteries are thermodynamically limited to ~1.5 volts despite theoretical possibilities remains underexplored.
verbatim: typically it's very difficult to get more than about one and a half volts out of a battery... It's almost impossible to get a voltage of two volts in a simple single-cell battery.

summary: Understand why titanium spontaneously ignites above ~900°C and consumes itself in jet engines.
verbatim: Above about 900 degrees centigrade — I have to check, I think it's 900 — it will dissolve its own oxide. And so they've had jet engine fires due to titanium catching on fire.

summary: Characterize the conditions and mechanisms of under-deposit corrosion attack on titanium in heat exchangers.
verbatim: You get what we call under-deposit corrosion attack, and titanium can corrode under some of those conditions, and it did.

summary: Investigate why niobium and tantalum leap from low thermodynamic nobility (ranks 33–34) to top practical nobility (ranks 2–3).
verbatim: Niobium and tantalum were thirty-three and thirty-four; they shoot up to two and three. Why are they so good? It turns out these things have practical nobility because they form a protective oxide skin.

summary: The mechanism by which titanium reacts with anhydrous ammonia to cause stress corrosion cracking and explosions remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: Titanium will react with anhydrous ammonia and cause stress corrosion cracking, and they had some really exciting explosions. They were using some of this with the rocket programs early on and blew up some of the launch pads.

summary: Why replacement baffles made of certified 316 stainless steel failed rapidly in a hot chloride steam environment while the original material survived.
verbatim: It's supposed to be made out of 316 stainless steel. And it was made out of 316 stainless steel, but over time they had to replace the parts, or they put some new baffles in. All of a sudden within a few weeks, stuff is cracking and falling apart.

summary: The distinction between stress-corrosion cracking and stress-assisted cracking remains ill-defined, with real consequences for engineering and insurance liability.
verbatim: The fundamental question for the insurance carriers was: if all the damage was done in a half an hour, was that a slow process? Was that corrosion? ...if they called it stress corrosion cracking, the insurance company was going to deny the thirty million claim. If they could change the name and call it stress-assisted cracking — well, what cracking is *not* stress-assisted?

summary: Identify the chemical mechanism responsible for extreme corrosion rates (40–80 thousandths/year) observed in the Arizona warehouse sauna environment.
verbatim: They were getting forty thousandths of an inch per year. I've never seen anything that rapid before. In fact when they told me, before I went out there to see it, I said no, you've got to have something else going on, because the fastest you ever get is ten or twenty thousandths.

summary: Quantify the corrosion mechanism driving exceptionally high carbon steel degradation rates in hot-arid diurnal cycles with condensation.
verbatim: That's the fastest carbon steel corrosion rate I've ever seen. You could do sewage, you could do chlorides, you could do anything you want — this was the best, and it was in Arizona.

summary: The mechanisms and detection of microbiologically-induced corrosion (MIC) in underground tanks remain poorly characterized, with over-attribution now clouding diagnosis.
verbatim: There's a certain type of corrosion we now call MIC — microbiologically induced corrosion — which we really didn't recognize... Now you read a report on corrosion in a tank, and half the metallurgists in the world say, oh it must be MIC. So now everything is MIC.

summary: Prediction of underground storage tank failure time from soil properties lacks reliable quantitative models; leaks vary wildly (6–40+ years) across similar tank geometries and soils.
verbatim: The quickest leaks were in six years... But some of them last 30 years, and they've had some tanks last 40 years... They had a regression formula that took some of these things into account, so you get the cross effect.

summary: The mechanism and kinetics of pitting corrosion in stainless steel at the splash line (oxygen concentration gradient) in chloride solutions remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: At the splash line where I had extra oxygen, I could perforate — that was about half-millimeter-thick stainless steel, about 20 thousandths — I could pit right through it in 24 hours in warm water.

summary: Whether mildly acidic passivation solutions like citric acid can achieve the same corrosion protection as stronger acids in high-chloride environments remains unclear.
verbatim: Milder solutions than nitric acid that can passivate are citric acid and phosphoric acid... I think they ended up using the citric acid, and they did do it in place. But it's not as strong and it didn't work quite as well.

summary: The source of chloride contamination in deionized water used for rinse cycles in pacemaker case manufacturing is unidentified despite being a known cause of corrosion.
verbatim: But in fact, there's some data that says their deionized water, which was supposed to be like 10 megohm — their deionized water had a pH of three... where do the chlorides come from in the cleaning solution.

summary: Quantify the mechanism by which suspended solids in seawater abrade protective oxide films on copper alloys at different flow velocities.
verbatim: At certain velocities, those solids in the water going by will just eat away that oxide skin, just abrade it away.

summary: Characterize the under-insulation crevice corrosion attack mode in austenitic stainless steel when exposed to chloride disinfectants in food processing environments.
verbatim: Under-insulation attack. Same thing as crevice corrosion — you actually get an acidic condition underneath the crevice, and get preferential corrosion underneath something else on top of it.

summary: Oxide layer loss under erosive seawater conditions in cupronickel/Monel alloys remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: And that's because of the erosive conditions and losing the oxide skin.

summary: HY-130 steel cannot be welded reliably across the varying thicknesses and conditions required for full-size submarine construction, despite fifty million dollars in development.
verbatim: If you weld only a certain thickness under certain conditions you can weld it, but a real submarine has to have different thicknesses, and not necessarily under those conditions. So from a practical point of view, HY-130, you can use for specialized applications, but you couldn't build a whole ship out of it.

summary: Steel-aluminum transition joints in marine environments corrode catastrophically and perforate, but the mechanism and mitigation strategies are not well characterized.
verbatim: It was at a steel-aluminum transition joint where there's tremendous corrosion. He just picked this up out of the scrap yard and took it home... I have a little piece that we polished and you can see the corrosion — it just corroded through the steel like mad.

summary: Hydrogen trapping in frozen steel can extend crack formation timescales from days to months, but the conditions and mechanisms remain poorly understood.
verbatim: I'll tell you a story one of these days of where it lasted for nine months. But it was frozen in the High Sierra mountains in the winter — so you can trap it if you freeze it.

summary: Fine grain size simultaneously improves both toughness and strength, but the mechanism and optimization remain unclear.
verbatim: Fine grain size is one of the only things that improves both toughness and strength at the same time. Usually you add alloying elements and things get worse in terms of toughness.

summary: The mathematical relationship between hardness and tensile strength in work-hardening materials remains incompletely characterized—Eagar notes it should be exactly 2.57× in non-work-hardening cases but observes ~3× empirically due to work hardening, without explaining the discrepancy.
verbatim: It turns out some of the tests are actually one-third or three times the tensile strength. If you take my deformation processing course you can prove it mathematically that in a non-plastic, non-work-hardening material it should be exactly 2.57 times, but because it work hardens it's about three.

summary: Understanding why HY-180 is nearly impossible to weld, despite Navy development—a fundamental weldability limitation that remains unresolved.
verbatim: The Navy developed that, it's almost impossible to weld. Even the Navy doesn't use it — they built a couple of little prototypes and decided it's too difficult to weld.

summary: The mechanisms by which high-side chemistry in weld metal (e.g., carbon at 0.15, chromium at 0.29) causes cracking in high-strength steels like HY-100.
verbatim: Every heat of steel that they made the welding wire out of for the first 18 percent of the vessel was on what we called a high-side chemistry, and it was really more like an HY-130... and that's why they got cracking.

summary: The specific peening strategy and stress-relief protocol for very thick welds (14+ inches) to prevent mid-weld cracking remains incompletely documented or understood.
verbatim: When you get very thick, that thing took two days to weld up with 600 passes. And they were only doing short links. So you may have to stress relieve as you go, which means you go in there and pound it with a hammer every now and then.

summary: The intermediate plate thickness range where distortion is worst—between thin flexible sheet and rigid heavy plate—lacks systematic characterization.
verbatim: The absolutely worst situation for distortion is somewhere in between. No distortion when you're thin, because the plate or sheet is flexible. No distortion when you're very heavy.

summary: Quantify how weld sequencing and restraint geometry jointly control residual stress magnitude in thick plates.
verbatim: Up to about an inch you may only get 80 percent of the residual stresses. It depends on the weld sequencing and how much other restraint is around it, whether it's the last side on a six-sided box or the fourth side. You'll have different amounts of restraint.

summary: Determine why vibratory stress relief fails to reduce residual stress despite decades of commercialization attempts and large Navy and British Welding Institute studies.
verbatim: The U.S. Navy spent over a million dollars trying to prove whether vibratory stress relief works. They don't use it. So what do you think they concluded? The British Welding Institute spent several million dollars for the oil companies trying to verify it.

summary: The mechanism by which drawing lubricant on small-diameter wire concentrates hydrogen in the weld metal needs investigation.
verbatim: Now why would they have dirty wire as a function of diameter? Which one has the highest surface-to-volume ratio? Smaller diameter wire, more surface to volume. So dirty wire has more surface, and what's on the surface? Drawing lubricant.

summary: Eagar identifies a lack of understanding about the long-term behavior of small welding defects (sixteenth-inch cracks) under submarine operating conditions.
verbatim: You may have to do a little more inspection when they come back in port for inspections, but those little sixteenth-of-an-inch-long cracks, how fast are they going to grow?

summary: Map the relationship between temperature and notched tensile strength in hydrogen-containing steel to explain why room temperature is the worst condition.
verbatim: A hydrogen-free specimen — no brittleness, no hydrogen embrittlement. If I have a hydrogen-containing specimen, it turns out the worst condition is right somewhere down here around room temperature. Higher temperatures, it diffuses out just like the CO2 coming out of my Sprite or the hydrogen bubbling out of the weld that you saw the video of.

summary: Room temperature (~20°C) is the worst-case condition for hydrogen-assisted cracking kinetics, but the mechanism behind this peak susceptibility window is unexplained.
verbatim: Where is the shortest time, and what time is it? It's just over one hour at room temperature, 20 degrees C. We live in the worst possible temperature for hydrogen cracking.

summary: Understand why different hydrogen cracking tests (Prooftstform, Tekken, implant test) all partially work but also partially fail to predict real welding behavior.
verbatim: There are literally dozens of these little laboratory tests to try to simulate the restraint that you get in a real welding situation. They all sort of work, but they also all sort of don't work, right?

summary: The source and transport mechanism of hydrogen into cookware during plasma-spray coating with Ar–H₂ mixtures remains incompletely characterized.
verbatim: I said, you've got martensite, you've got your residual stresses from the forming operation — I don't know where your hydrogen comes from.

summary: Understand why Japanese shipbuilding steels required no preheat while equivalent alloy steels needed 200°F preheat—a cost-saving innovation whose metallurgical basis wasn't fully explained.
verbatim: The Japanese were making commercial steels for shipbuilding at the time that required no preheat. They might have one-inch-thick plate that in the old days, with an alloy steel, you had to preheat to 200 degrees — now they didn't have to preheat it at all, at least during the summer in Japan.

summary: The metallurgical mechanism of temper embrittlement in carbon steels in the 600–1000°F range is avoided empirically but lacks clear explanation, especially relative to alloy steels.
verbatim: We tend to avoid for metallurgical reasons 600 to a thousand, because you get something called temper embrittlement, which is another problem in carbon steels — not so much in alloy steels, but we try to avoid that.

summary: The mechanism behind hose instability in high-energy electron beams in atmospheric conditions remains poorly characterized and limits welding applications.
verbatim: The only problem with that high-energy electron beam: it worked great in a vacuum, but unfortunately the ocean is not in a vacuum, it's got air above it. They ran into something called a hose instability. You could shoot what should have been a straight beam coming out, but then the atmosphere would cause those electrons to whip around like the end of a garden hose that wasn't restrained that had water flow.

summary: Why do some shipyards successfully weld stainless-to-chromoly transition joints while others consistently fail under identical procedures?
verbatim: People had been making this joint in other shipyards for years. So I said, why don't you just machine the joint prep a little differently... The reason other people had probably been successful, I don't really know, is that these guys were probably butting things up tight, and other people may not have had things quite so tight, or they were putting in a bigger weld.

summary: Understanding why thick-section welds fail catastrophically after successful repair attempts despite increased preheat.
verbatim: They decided, well, we need more preheat. They came in with heating blankets and heated up just locally... They heated locally, and this time they successfully made the weld, put it back on its post, and on the first shot to forge something — big bang, cracked again.

summary: Laser marking and engraving techniques introduce hydrogen or create brittle high-hardness zones in high-strength steels; optimization of non-melting laser methods is incomplete.
verbatim: They went to laser scribing, where you melt the surface. All they're doing is a super rapid cool in a high strength steel, and they would end up with high hardness, not necessarily a hydrogen crack, but just very high hardness. The thing would start a brittle crack and they would start fatigue cracks. So now they actually have some laser engraving techniques that don't melt the surface.

summary: Fillet welds at stress concentrations (like rigging blocks) initiate fatigue cracks in large structures; design rules for preventing this failure mode need clarification.
verbatim: The cracks started at a fillet weld where they had little blocks... they decided we don't need to take that off. Well that became the stress concentration, that was the beginning of the fatigue crack that caused the thing to fracture.

summary: Investigate why the IMT hot isostatic press vessel failed via brittle fracture despite supercomputer design—specifically, the role of transient thermal stress from internal heating and external water cooling.
verbatim: They designed this on a supercomputer. In the mid-1980s, the supercomputer was not quite as good as a PC of five years ago. They had assumed everything was steady state heat flow — but you have this thing heated on the inside and you have to water cool the outside to keep it from getting too hot. They had this brittle fracture.

summary: Why do some high-toughness steel plates occasionally arrive at 30 foot-pounds while the average hovers near 21, and what causes this unexplained variability in normalized plate properties?
verbatim: But every now and then one of the plates would come in at 30 foot-pounds... Most of them were down around 15 to 19 on the first normalize, and they'd have to second normalize some of them, even triple normalize.

summary: The physics of why arcs cannot run in parallel remains incompletely understood despite practical workarounds.
verbatim: You can't run arcs in parallel. From basic physics, an arc is not a resistive element — it actually is a negative-resistance element. If you try to run two arcs in parallel, from a physics point of view one will snuff out the other and you'll carry all the current in one arc.

summary: The mechanisms controlling plasma conductivity scaling with current in multi-arc systems need investigation.
verbatim: The conductivity of the plasma becomes much greater with more current. So if you have fifty percent of your current here and fifty percent here, one of them will take a hundred percent of the current and starve the other.

summary: Mechanism of fatigue crack initiation at saddle attachments on tanks due to localized stiffness changes under dynamic sloshing loads.
verbatim: They had a saddle arrangement. And right there you have a change in stiffness. So as the liquid is sloshing around in the tank, that change in stiffness, you're going to get a fatigue crack right there at that location.

summary: The interaction between strain localization caused by undermatching filler metal and the geometric stress concentration at the weld toe in fatigue loading needs clarification.
verbatim: If you try to undermatch this, you're localizing the strain. You actually have here a weak material and a strong material... undermatching could localize the strain in the weld metal, and you could get more plasticity, and so it probably makes things worse.

summary: Sulfur inclusions in stainless steel cause both solidification cracking and pitting corrosion initiation, but the mechanism linking these two failure modes is incompletely characterized.
verbatim: It wasn't hydrogen cracking; it was eventually tied to the little bit of sulfur in the steel. It would also cause pitting corrosion — you'd have a little sulfur inclusion and then you'd study where your pits are, and they're right there at the sulfur inclusion in the steel. They found that on solidification, a lot of times the steels would crack.

summary: Quantify the competing effects of zero ferrite (non-magnetic requirement) versus cracking susceptibility in super-austenitic stainless steel welds, particularly the phase transformation behavior under constraint.
verbatim: The problem is, with the super-austenitics, you can have zero ferrite, because that was what the Navy wanted. They wanted super-austenitic; it had zero ferrite so it wouldn't be magnetic. I showed you what would happen with that, my little Farberware pot. It was like five or ten percent ferrite down at the bottom.

summary: Long-term behavior and failure modes of welded martensitic stainless steel (410) threaded rods under sustained tension in high-chloride environments, including delayed cracking mechanisms.
verbatim: Delayed cracking. Rings a bell, right? High-hardness martensitic stainless... They hung it in August, and the thing came down a couple of days later.

summary: Duplex stainless steel's stress corrosion cracking resistance at high tensile stress in seawater environments lacks definitive guidance.
verbatim: You might be able to use a duplex stainless, but I'd have to look it up and research it, see if it'll be good enough at these stress levels in this environment.

summary: The mechanism of chloride stress corrosion cracking in austenitic stainless steels remains incompletely understood—Eagar describes it as 'a chemical reaction' that is 'not necessarily hydrogen exactly, but similar,' suggesting the precise failure mode is unresolved.
verbatim: If you test in boiling magnesium chloride — which is a standard ASTM test for looking at chloride cracking resistance of stainless steels — we have things that will fail within an hour. It is a chemical reaction. It's not necessarily hydrogen exactly, but it's similar — you're eating things away.

summary: Ferritics show promise for chloride resistance but are hindered by grain growth and poor impact toughness—understanding how to overcome these trade-offs would expand material options for corrosive environments.
verbatim: Or if you go to the ferritics. But the problem with ferritics and martensitics is, the martensitics will hydrogen crack, and the ferritics have grain growth and impact toughness problems.

summary: Understanding why atmospheric pressure changes alter weld pool shape and arc characteristics, as observed when PIGMA welding was developed to compensate for Denver's lower pressure.
verbatim: It turns out the atmospheric pressure there is about 0.82 atmospheres. So it didn't work the same — the shape of the weld pools wasn't the same when you lost 20 percent of your pressure... the arc characteristics changed enough — pressure does affect arcs.

summary: Unclear why molybdenum content raises critical pitting temperature in stainless steels, and how welding segregation lowers it.
verbatim: This is a function of molybdenum content... When you weld it, because of segregation in the welding zone and changes in the microstructure, you'll get pitting at a lower temperature.

summary: Long-term formation of brittle topologically close-packed phases in nickel superalloys remains incompletely understood as a practical failure mechanism.
verbatim: If you hold some of these alloys at temperature for a long period of time, you'll end up with that structure. This also happens in some of the stainless steels. The times we're talking about are tens of thousands of hours. Okay. That may have been one of the problems we had with my chrome-moly tube over at the Boston Navy Yard... the stainless steel probably, after ten thousand hours, formed this brittle phase, and the things would crack. So it's a general problem.

summary: The mechanisms and solutions for creep-fatigue interaction in compressed titanium submarine hulls were not well solved by Soviet designers and remain a significant engineering barrier.
verbatim: It turns out that if you compress titanium and hold it under compression, fatigue cracks grow really fast. Well, guess what a submarine hull is — it's held under compression when you're down deep... the people from NRL were asking me about, how did the Soviets solve the creep-fatigue interaction — is that they didn't. They just built the ships and then they found out about the creep-fatigue interaction.

summary: Why some liquation cracks in nickel alloys self-heal while others remain as persistent voids is unexplained.
verbatim: They call this a self-healing crack. Well, this one might be self-healing here, but these two weren't self-healing, they're still voids. So it's not a great situation.

summary: The relationship between weld profile geometry and solidification cracking susceptibility in nickel alloys lacks systematic characterization.
verbatim: So the weld profile makes a difference — not just for fatigue. This would be a good profile for fatigue; this is a worse profile for fatigue, with a higher stress concentration at that corner than this one. But this is lousy for solidification cracking.

summary: Understand the mechanisms of coarsening in nickel superalloy gamma-prime phases during long-term service and how heat treatment parameters influence the rate and reversibility of this degradation.
verbatim: The problem is, there's something called coarsening in metallurgy: if you have fine structures — these nice rectangular blocks because of the crystal structure — over time they will get larger... The bigger bubbles steal molecules from the smaller bubbles, and so the little bubbles pump up the big bubbles.

summary: Eagar observes that stop-drilling cracks works differently in sheet metal versus thick plate, and the mechanics of this difference in 3D are poorly understood.
verbatim: Stop-drilling cracks. One of the problems is, if you're not careful, you think the crack goes to here and you put the hole here, but in fact the crack went deeper and you can't always see it — then you didn't do anything to stop the stress concentration. It works in sheet metal. It doesn't work so well in plate, because if you start thinking of the other dimension, how are you going to stop-drill it? The crack is not necessarily just perpendicular to the surface, okay.

summary: Why 5456 aluminum—a Navy workhorse alloy—exhibits cracking behavior that differs from other 5000-series alloys.
verbatim: [Section title references '5456 cracking' as a distinct phenomenon; Eagar notes 5456 is a Navy alloy with good weldability and joint efficiency, yet the title flags cracking as a specific issue]

summary: Understanding why scandium grain-refinement works better than titanium in aluminum alloys remains unexplained.
verbatim: We use titanium in some aluminum alloys as a grain refiner — you get titanium nitrides or titanium borides that form as low precipitants and keep the grains from getting large, so you get fine-grained aluminum. But scandium works even better.

summary: Magnesium stress-corrosion cracking in welds remains unsolved and blocks automotive adoption.
verbatim: That's why I said magnesium is the metal of the future in automobiles — always has and always will be — unless someone solves the stress-corrosion cracking problem, okay.

summary: Practical methods to eliminate cracks trailing behind the welding arc in magnesium are unknown.
verbatim: If you go to the welding handbook they will tell you how to do it; they just won't tell you how to get rid of the crack that follows behind your arc.

summary: The relationship between alloy composition and peak cracking susceptibility in aluminum welds is empirically known but mechanistically unexplained.
verbatim: You find that the composition of the weld — percent of alloying element — you'll get your maximum cracking at some intermediate level. That's just this wide freezing range. Highly alloyed, no cracking. Lightly alloyed, no cracking. Wide intermediate, lots of cracking.

summary: Why aluminum alloys lose toughness as strength increases, especially regarding stress-corrosion cracking and other degradation modes in high-strength variants.
verbatim: Because we're usually trying to push the aluminums — just like baseball bats — to higher and higher strength, which means more and more corrosion problems, stress corrosion cracking and other things.

summary: Systematic comparison of cracking behavior and filler-metal sensitivity when welding dissimilar aluminum alloys versus matching alloys.
verbatim: If you try to use some of these other welding electrodes and don't follow this table, you're going to get cracking. You're liable to not be in the range where you want to be — lightly alloyed when you mix the weld metal with the base metal, or highly alloyed. You'll be in the wide freezing range and you're going to have cracking.

summary: Quantitative design rules for stress concentration factors and joint geometry in aluminum welds, as opposed to the more forgiving rules established for steel.
verbatim: If I were welding steel, this happens to be an example of welding two plates of different thickness, and they show how you would taper one down in aluminum. Because steel has more toughness, which means it can tolerate sharp corners a lot more than aluminum.

summary: Why aluminum welds at corners are prone to cracking and fatigue failure, while steel corners tolerate welds well.
verbatim: We really like to avoid welds at the corners in aluminum. Steel has lots of toughness and so we don't mind corners in steel — we put the welds in the corners and usually do pretty well. But in aluminum you don't like to put welds at corners. They will tend to crack — either crack or fatigue.

summary: Understand why Soviet Alfa-class submarines experienced cracking failures caused by creep-fatigue interaction in titanium hulls.
verbatim: They leapfrogged us in submarine technology for about two years, until these things started cracking due to creep-fatigue interaction.

summary: Characterize and prevent under-deposit corrosion attack on titanium heat exchanger tubes in real operating conditions.
verbatim: It will corrode underneath a layer of silt. You've got to keep everything clean to prevent what they call under-deposit attack.

summary: Deep TIG technology (high-current gas tungsten arc with fluoride flux) lacks industrial applications and understanding outside titanium.
verbatim: Titanium has a sweet spot for both electroslag and deep TIG. What David Taylor had been working on was this one. They hadn't worked on this at all, they hadn't worked on this at all.

summary: The relationship between shielding gas moisture content and hydrogen pickup in titanium welds needs clarification—current understanding assumes oxygen/nitrogen exclusion prevents hydrogen, but the mechanism is not fully explained.
verbatim: With titanium, you have to keep the oxygen and nitrogen out to begin with, and if you keep the oxygen and nitrogen out you'll usually keep the hydrogen out. Here obviously the hydrogen and oxygen are coming from the moisture, the dew point, which is the moisture in the shielding gas.

summary: Spot weld adaptive control systems fail to respond within the weld duration, making feedback-based optimization impossible.
verbatim: even though this is 60-cycle current and you're supposed to control it in four cycles of current, one fifteenth of a second — the adaptive controller wasn't even kicking in until like six cycles after the weld was over.

summary: The mechanism by which water pooling on hot aluminum plate edges causes localized cooling and thickness variation during rolling is not characterized.
verbatim: I remembered that I would see water pooled. This variation here is only like a millimeter or two variation out of one inch, so it might be seven percent variation, which is off gauge... I said, I'll bet you there's a reason why that water's pooling.

summary: Seaweed submarines experienced unexpected microscopic cracking (1 mm) in high-strength weld metal that existing inspection protocols couldn't reliably detect, requiring retrofit of 18% of the hull.
verbatim: The Sea Wolf submarine problem, to get back to a Navy example, is that they ended up getting too high carbon content and alloy content. The weld metal was 30 or 40% higher strength than it was intended to be, because of the chemistry, and they got a less tough steel. It formed little microscopic flaws that the original inspectors weren't looking for, something that small. It's a different type of cracking that we hadn't seen before.

summary: Creep-fatigue interaction in titanium remains unresolved and prevented the U.S. Navy from recommending titanium submarines.
verbatim: How do they solve the creep-fatigue interactions? I said, I don't know. Well, it turns out they didn't. The Naval Research Laboratory had done all kinds of studies on this. It was one of the reasons why they couldn't recommend, even if you had the money, going to build a titanium submarine.

summary: The mechanisms by which nitrogen from bare steel wire causes weld porosity and how it gets rejected during solidification remain incompletely characterized.
verbatim: The problem with the bare steel wire is it picks up nitrogen from the air, and when it solidifies the nitrogen gets rejected, and the rejected nitrogen comes out and makes the weld porous.

summary: Large-scale multi-pass welding (400+ passes in thick steel forgings) involves poorly understood interactions between successive passes that could affect structural integrity.
verbatim: This is a weld in a 17-inch-thick piece of steel. It was part of a forging press they were trying to repair in Pennsylvania some time ago. I didn't count exactly, but there'd be 400, a hundred-and-something passes in here.

summary: Understand the mechanism by which residual stress from jacking pipes into alignment during initial construction causes later corrosion and failure in naval piping systems.
verbatim: Back in the shipyard, when they built the thing, they would jack a pipe — if it didn't line up, you jack it on tight and weld it. And now we go in years later, and we cut that pipe out and realize you can't just rebuild it and have your piping line up with no stress... There's a lot of resources that go onto a ship.

summary: Understand why heat treatment (normalization) improves toughness inconsistently: some steel passes after one cycle, others after two, and some fails entirely despite multiple attempts.
verbatim: After they did that, maybe two-thirds of the ones that didn't pass the last time — the 18 or 19 — would now pass at 20, 21, 22, whatever. Some that still didn't pass — the 10% — they'd put through a second renormalization, and some would pass and some wouldn't.

summary: Unclear why hydrogen cracking in the Bay Bridge's 46-inch corrosion-generated hydrogen case occurred within weeks when typical hydrogen diffusion takes days—a timing discrepancy worth investigating.
verbatim: The Bay Bridge in California — it's coming from corrosion. They have big 46-inch-diameter steel tie rods, and they started corroding. The corrosion process creates hydrogen that diffuses into the steel — not as much as in welding — and they said, oh, they cracked within a couple of weeks. Well, that's hydrogen.

summary: Hydrogen diffusion and crack initiation at microscopic inclusions and notches is observable but the precise mechanism controlling crack growth rate remains unclear.
verbatim: as it concentrates at the crack tip, it allows the crack to progress. You can see in the microscope the crack growing, and you can see the bubbles coming up right ahead of it, because the hydrogen wants to diffuse to that crack tip — unless you can diffuse it out to the air faster.

summary: Eagar notes that fine grain size is universally beneficial for strength and toughness in steel, but suggests the mechanism by which alloying elements harm toughness despite improving hardenability remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: The only thing you can do to steel or any metal to get both strength and toughness, which is what we want, is fine grain size. You add alloying elements, you're hurting your toughness, but you're getting greater hardenability.

summary: Eagar identifies a gap in understanding why grain boundaries in silicon solar cells cause electron loss and efficiency penalties, presenting an opportunity to model or measure electron transport at grain boundaries quantitatively.
verbatim: Wherever you have a grain boundary, you're losing electrons, and you're not getting the solar efficiency... you'd love single-crystal silicon for solar cells, but that's too expensive in general.

summary: Establish predictive models or field data for stress-corrosion-cracking failure rates in stainless steel seawater piping to extend Navy ship service life beyond 50 years.
verbatim: When you talk about the in-ring designs of stainless steel, stress corrosion cracking is a serious problem... they're going for 50 years on a ship.

summary: The mechanism by which carbon diffuses and forms carbides in stainless-to-chrome-moly transition joints at service temperature remains incompletely understood.
verbatim: the carbon will diffuse and form carbides with some of the things in the stainless steel. It's a long-term problem — at temperature, over time the carbon diffuses and you'll get cracking.

summary: Why do some dissimilar-metal welds with austenitic stainless steel filler crack despite hydrogen resistance when dilution ratios are off?
verbatim: Depending on the weld metal they were using, they were getting cracking... if you're welding dissimilar metals like armor steel with a stainless steel, and you don't have the right ratio of base metal melted to weld metal melted, you'll end up with martensite streaming. Martensite is very susceptible — essentially impossible not to get hydrogen cracking, even with just the residual hydrogen that's in here.

summary: What mechanism causes 304 stainless steel pots to develop cracks during ocean transit that weren't present at shipment?
verbatim: We ship them, some of them to Japan, and when they show up in Japan they've got cracks. They didn't have cracks when they left.

summary: Understanding why cardiac guide wire welds in austenitic stainless steel fail under minimal load despite the material's expected strength.
verbatim: They were having problems with the weld breaking. It only had to lift about two and a half pounds, and it wouldn't even do that. This is nominally austenitic stainless steel 304, which we all think of as fairly non-magnetic.

summary: Peening parameters for titanium weld reinforcement are highly inconsistent and poorly understood, especially on uneven surfaces with weld bead geometry.
verbatim: The data was all over the map. Press soft, press hard, do it for fifteen seconds, do it for thirty seconds — the heights were all over the map... he has to peen an uneven surface. That's going to make it more inconsistent.

summary: Fatigue design rules for pressure vessels carrying water (excluded from ASME code) lack engineering standards, creating a regulatory blind spot with potential safety consequences.
verbatim: ASME code excludes water tanks. The company out in Iowa making these was sort of a mom-and-pop shop. They asked the Department of Transportation, which regulates trucks on the highway, what design rules they had to follow. DOT said, that's just an appendage... Then they called Pennsylvania, said we've got this vessel carrying water. Pennsylvania said water vessels are excluded from the boiler and pressure vessel code. So no doubler plates.

summary: Understand why hydrogen cracks preferentially initiate at weld corners in fatigue-critical details.
verbatim: Since then you're not allowed to put the weld going across that direction — you weld in this direction and this direction, because the corners are tremendous sources of hydrogen cracks and fatigue.

summary: Ultrasonic inspection cannot reliably detect cracks in coarse-grained weld metal due to high noise from grain structure scattering.
verbatim: The ultrasonics couldn't pick up the cracks because the weld metal has these big coarse grains and the ultrasonics is too noisy to look at. The base material has a better signal-to-noise ratio than the weld metal. It's not just that it's reflecting off the crack — the sound is also reflecting off lots of other things adjacent to it, like the grain structure.

summary: Precipitation-strengthened nickel alloys present a major weldability challenge due to intermetallic phases; Oak Ridge has a long-standing research effort to develop cracking-resistant variants.
verbatim: Lots of sophisticated precipitation-strengthened alloys — not very weldable, but in general we don't weld them in place. We can weld them, but there's not very much you can do. Some repairs, yes. There are some special ones where you don't have to worry about intermetallics — that's sort of a research project over at Oak Ridge National Lab.

summary: Solidification cracking in nickel-copper alloys remains poorly understood despite being a model laboratory system for studying the phenomenon.
verbatim: One of the problems with these alloys — like the Monels the Navy uses — is they are the model system in the laboratory for developing solidification cracking. If you want to study solidification cracking, you won't find a better system than nickel-copper alloys.

summary: The mechanism of self-healing in solidification cracks—where liquid is squeezed into cracks during shrinkage—needs investigation to understand whether it truly restores strength or leaves a permanent weakness.
verbatim: Sometimes you can actually squeeze some of that liquid into the cracks, and they call this self-healing. But it's still a weak spot in the material. Maybe it's not a real crack, but it's still a weakness.

summary: Whether transient thermal stress analysis during startup should be a standard design requirement for high-pressure vessels, given the Grafton failure.
verbatim: They didn't go to a three-dimensional program, and they certainly didn't do transient startups — just like they didn't get the recuperator transient startup heating correct... They had never analyzed the transient condition. They had analyzed the inside surface for tensile stresses in steady-state operation, but they never analyzed the outside surface where you can get tensile stresses on startup.

summary: The mechanisms causing cracking in gas tungsten arc welding of high-copper aluminum alloys (like 2014) remain unclear despite practical problems.
verbatim: If you tried to weld the Wright brothers' crankcase or the cylinder housing for their engine with gas tungsten arc, you'd crack it. You'd melt it and you'd have nice cracks — pull that rope, melted metal right out. Same type of problem as you have on Monel — you get cracking, equation melting in the heat-affected zone in the copper interiors.

summary: The mechanism by which lithium additions simultaneously improve stiffness but worsen corrosion resistance in aluminum alloys remains poorly understood after 30+ years of development.
verbatim: the lithium actually makes the corrosion worse. But when you're maintaining an aircraft worth $200 million... that's per person, out of play.

summary: Stress-corrosion cracking susceptibility of 7075-T6 in saltwater is well-known but the mechanism of why T6 is particularly vulnerable remains poorly characterized.
verbatim: The problem was stress corrosion cracking, which I always tend to find in saltwater environments... T6 treatment, and T6 is well known to be very susceptible to stress corrosion cracking.

summary: Quantify the stress corrosion cracking susceptibility threshold for 7075-T6 aluminum under saltwater exposure as a function of residual stress and time-to-failure.
verbatim: The stress corrosion cracking susceptibility threshold was 7 ksi, and we had 10 ksi. That's why it's cracking on the shelf. You guys are out in a humid, moist, salt-laden atmosphere, and even though the washer's in a bag, a little moisture humidity gets inside that bag and a crack grows.

summary: Understand why nickel impurities in magnesium sacrificial anodes cause catastrophic self-corrosion rather than cathodic protection.
verbatim: Nickel and magnesium do not mix in equilibrium proportions. The solubility of nickel in magnesium is only about seven parts per million. If you have more nickel than that, you'll get little nearly-pure nickel precipitates, and your magnesium anode will consume itself by galvanic action.

summary: Why aluminum weld metal cannot match base metal strength the way steel can, despite achieving similar yield strengths in steel welds up to several hundred ksi.
verbatim: Just like with high-strength steels, you can't match the strength in the weld metal with aluminum alloys. You can with steels — we can weld HY80 or HY100 which has been heat-treated, and we actually have weld metals that can match the strength even though they have a cast structure. I don't want to get into all the metallurgy of why, but we can match the strength in steel weld metal all the way up to a couple hundred ksi yield. In aluminum we can't do that. It doesn't have the same transforming crystal structure from FCC to BCC. Aluminum only has one crystal structure, FCC, through all the temperature range.

summary: How to predict or prevent fatigue cracking at weld corners in aluminum structures, since aluminum requires corner-avoidance strategies that steel does not.
verbatim: In aluminum you do all kinds of things you don't need to do in steel. You bend the leg a little, because it's both of these two then, and you put your welds at other locations. There's a quick little weld in these corners here, doing twice as much welding, but you don't run into fatigue problems.

summary: The mechanism by which small amounts of palladium improve titanium corrosion resistance in acids remains unexplained.
verbatim: Some of the grades have a little bit of palladium in them — a precious metal at gold prices, but only a quarter percent max — and these have excellent corrosion resistance in certain types of acids in chemical plants. Just a little bit of palladium significantly improves things.

summary: Understand why gas metal arc welding failed for heavy-section titanium submarine construction when it succeeded for steel.
verbatim: They were trying to use gas metal arc welding, which is what David Taylor in Annapolis had been working on for years — gas metal arc with a wire feed. They couldn't do it, and they finally gave up and went back to what we call hot wire TIG.

summary: Develop affordable flux compositions for submerged arc welding of titanium that match the metallurgical benefits of optical-grade calcium chloride without the prohibitive cost.
verbatim: We very quickly learned that you couldn't afford it. It was going to cost about $300 a foot of weld, just for the flux. That didn't sound very good.

summary: Why electroslag welds on steel fail while the same process works excellently for titanium remains unexplained.
verbatim: electroslag on steel sort of has a problem. Turns out it's a great process for titanium.

summary: The mechanisms of creep-fatigue interaction cracking in welds remain poorly understood despite decades of naval research.
verbatim: Hydrogen cracking, due to creep-fatigue interaction cracking — not hydrogen cracking, but the fact that the metal, if you put it under a constant compressive stress and then cycle it, you build broad cracks in the middle. The Naval Research Laboratory had been working for years... they were going to talk about how they solved the fatigue interaction. They didn't know.

summary: We cannot predict corrosion kinetics from thermodynamic diagrams; the rate at which metals corrode remains poorly understood despite having complete thermodynamic atlases.
verbatim: So by 1950, we knew the thermodynamics of corrosion. What we don't know, and we can't predict with any regularity, is the kinetics — how fast something corrodes.

summary: Why zinc corrodes at one-fifth to one-tenth the rate of iron despite thermodynamic predictions suggesting similar behavior is not explained.
verbatim: Zinc actually forms a protective layer. Why does galvanized steel last so much longer than regular steel? The zinc corrodes kinetically at about one-fifth to one-tenth the rate of straight iron. But these diagrams and the thermodynamics, they're not kinetics.

summary: Why chlorides specifically break down the protective oxide on stainless steels in seawater, when the same steels resist general corrosion.
verbatim: Chlorides will break down the surface oxide, among other things. Stainless steels pit in seawater terribly, but they don't rust generally in seawater.

summary: The mechanism of exfoliation corrosion in aluminum alloys under high-velocity seawater flow, exemplified by the Maine fishing boat hull failure.
verbatim: He had enough velocity coming through that water — it's seawater — that he ended up with exfoliation. The hull came apart within six months. So changing velocities and things like that, you can set up different potentials, and exfoliation can occur.

summary: Casting's actual atom deposition rate at surfaces may impose a fundamental speed limit that has not been rigorously validated.
verbatim: Through the kinetic theory of gases, how fast can atoms hit the surface — it's got to be half a millimeter. You know how fast you can fill a mold and build up something? I was trying to demonstrate this in the casting lecture, and I calculated, I had it somewhere between a hundred thousand and a million fold speed advantage.

summary: Quantify the specific cost and performance trade-offs that determine when additive manufacturing becomes viable versus conventional subtractive manufacturing for different material classes and part applications.
verbatim: If I can put certain cooling passages or fuel passages in a nozzle that goes into a jet engine, and can save millions of dollars worth of fuel costs, I can probably afford to make something with additive manufacturing. If that was General Motors and it's going to go in a car, no way, because the value of a pound saved in a car is two dollars over the life of the vehicle.

summary: Quantifying the performance and cost trade-offs of conformally cooled tooling across different injection molding and die-casting scenarios.
verbatim: Conformally cooled tooling — quick show of hands, does that term mean anything to anyone? A few of you. In a lot of tooling processes — injection molding, die casting — the rate-limiting step is how fast you can cool and solidify the material in a mold... 3D printing has been proven quite a few times now where you can put cooling channels into a part that conform to the surface of the tool.

summary: Develop predictive model for how variations in bolt and plate spring constants couple to produce disproportionate stress variations in parallel-spring bolted joint systems.
verbatim: A 10% variation in stress on the bolt could be a 50% variation on the plate, or vice versa, depending on the variations in the spring constant. You have to worry about both displacement and force in parallel springs.

summary: Investigate the economic limits of labor-cost competition in mini-mill steel production and verify the threshold at which shipping costs neutralize wage advantages for foreign producers.
verbatim: If we can keep our labor cost below $30 a ton, we don't care if the Koreans pay their employees nothing, we can compete in the American market. Because it cost the Koreans $30 to ship their steel over here, and their only competitive advantage was labor cost.

summary: Quantify the relationship between heating time, ingot diameter, and oxide layer thickness during large-scale forge reheating to optimize surface quality.
verbatim: In order to heat this up, it may take a week in the furnace. Remember, X squared is proportional to the time... When you're trying to heat it back up and you've got something that's fifty inches in diameter, it takes a week to get the heat in to get it up to temperature and uniform. During that time, you may form one-inch-thick oxide on the surface.

summary: Optimal multi-stage furnace heating protocols for large ingots with stress concentrations should be empirically validated to prevent clink formation during industrial scale-up.
verbatim: What they do to avoid clinking is, when you first put it in a furnace, you put it in a first furnace that may be at 1,000° F. You put it in that furnace for two or three days until the inside starts to warm up above the ductile-brittle transition temperature.

summary: Semisolid processing (rheocast, thixocast) shows promise for reducing cycle time in die casting, but systematic optimization of process parameters and material systems remains underdeveloped.
verbatim: They thought this would be great for die casting, where you inject metal into a solid mold under pressure. The problem in die casting is cycle time — you've got to hold the pressure until the thing solidifies. If you've already gotten half the heat of fusion out, you can cut your cycle time in half.

summary: Quantify how chill block placement and hot-top design parameters affect riser height and shrinkage distribution in complex casting geometries.
verbatim: By putting chill blocks into the sand mold you can change the amount of rising in the casting... With chill blocks you don't have to have anywhere near as tall a riser. With a hot top you can have a very small riser; with a radiation shield you can get things very flat. You can change the cooling on these complex shapes by playing all kinds of games.

summary: Quantify the minimum area reduction (currently estimated at ~75%) needed to homogenize macrosegregation in large forged ingots.
verbatim: You'd love 90%.

summary: The cooling-rate requirements for achieving bulk amorphous structure in metallic glass alloys vary by composition and deserve systematic characterization.
verbatim: Still today nothing has worked, except Bill Johnson has gotten some alloys where, if you cool them at 100° centigrade per second, you can actually make them bulk — so you can get bigger things if you cast them the right way.

summary: Whether a third vacuum arc remelting cycle offers practical inclusion reduction benefits beyond two cycles warrants systematic study before it becomes standard practice.
verbatim: I've heard of people trying a third time, but you get to the law of diminishing returns.

summary: Quantify how lubricant thickness and reapplication schedules affect strain homogeneity and fracture initiation in multi-stage forming operations.
verbatim: If you have a thick layer of peanut butter in there, your lubricant takes you further and lasts longer. They don't relubricate between each one of those, but they have enough that when they put it in a new die, they get it relubricated properly.

summary: The bearing wear pattern diagnostic method (ellipse vs. hourglass) could be systematized and validated across different conformity types and operating conditions.
verbatim: From the shape of that ellipse we probably could have calculated exactly what the conformity was... If it's an open conformity, you get an ellipse. If it's a closed conformity, you get an hourglass, because it's contacting at the edges.

summary: Investigate failure mechanisms and design principles for two-stage bolts used in jet engine removal systems to prevent over-torquing and cracking.
verbatim: So you have to worry about the load path. If the load path was only from here to here and there's no stress on this when you're doing the torque of the large-diameter, what's the problem? However, if your load path ignores this little shoulder and you don't grab it and keep it restrained, now your load path goes all the way through to the other nut, and all of a sudden you over-torque this thing.

summary: Development of low-temperature steel suitable for LNG tanker skirts at −60°F fracture toughness is incomplete; available steels at that time were inadequate.
verbatim: There wasn't a really good steel available, so I was working on developing a new steel for that skirt.

summary: The welding of ultra-precision stainless steel vacuum vessels requires special techniques to prevent hydrogen outgassing that would compromise interferometer performance.
verbatim: I got involved in this about 15 years ago when they were designing it, because they wanted to know how to weld the stainless steel because of the precision they were looking for.

summary: Develop or restore practical field methods for positive materials identification that don't require expensive instruments, given that spark tests and chemical spot tests are being abandoned.
verbatim: I said, how would he know when he was grinding it? Now, if he was working in a steel mill or in a shipyard in the 1930s or '40s or even '50s and '60s, he might have known... Because there's something we used to use for PMI in a steel yard fifty, sixty, seventy years ago, called a spark test.

summary: Investigate whether milling machine tool wear (potato-chipping) caused the swash plate dimensional errors that led to bearing failures.
verbatim: If we'd gotten that milling machine and found that the bed was potato-chipped, that's how you machine a potato-chip housing. But they scrapped a three-year-old machine.

summary: Quantify how inclusion density affects total elongation in tensile specimens across different material purity levels.
verbatim: Backofen has this drawing: if I had something with no inclusions, very clean material, and I pulled on it, it might neck down like this — I get tremendous elongation. As a thought experiment, the inclusions basically break the material up into a bunch of fibers, smaller tensile specimens, and when they neck down it's like necking down a bunch of fibers. The total elongation with inclusions is a lot less than the elongation if the material was very pure.

summary: Quantify the competing effects of friction and deformation ratio (Delta) on metal flow homogeneity during forging.
verbatim: There's a trade-off between friction and Delta — the height-working ratio. If you end up with low friction and low Delta, it's going to be more homogeneous, no question. But I can't just say it in general, because the two are competing.

summary: A systematic study measuring R-values and texture in fractured pressure vessel specimens could reveal whether deformation texture (indicated by elliptical rather than circular cup-cone fractures) correlates with failure mode and brittleness in steels.
verbatim: There was texture in this piece of steel. How do I know? Because it has an R value — it's not one. ε₃ and ε₂ are different. There's a much bigger ε₃ value than ε₂, or vice versa. From the shape of that ellipse I could get the R value pulling on it.

summary: The practical barrier to cycling steels through phase transformations for grain refinement is the thermal diffusion time required; finding a faster method or alternative approach would overcome Backofen's original constraint.
verbatim: Depending on whether you do 2, 4, 6, or 8 cycles, you'd have to cycle between temperatures within a second or two. That's not practical when you've got a great big thing that takes tens of seconds or minutes for the heat to penetrate.

summary: The precise relationship between heat intensity and interaction time in controlling weld pool and heat-affected zone geometry deserves systematic quantification.
verbatim: The heat affected zone is controlled by the heat flux — it's just a question of when, heating or cooling. This plot is heat intensity versus interaction time in seconds. Travel speed is one over the interaction time.

summary: Need systematic study of how ground position and symmetric grounding configurations affect arc stability to improve welder control.
verbatim: You can change the ground position. You can have symmetric grounds — have another ground over here. Sometimes that will solve the welder's problem, just changing the ground location or adding another ground.

summary: Validate Rosenthal and Christensen's analytical heat-flow predictions against actual measured temperature profiles during welding at varying travel speeds.
verbatim: But we'd really like to know, as this point heat source travels along the plate, what does the heat look like? That's where Daniel Rosenthal came along.

summary: Reproducible and rapid aluminum-water reaction for hydrogen generation is a known phenomenon but lacks systematic characterization and scaling.
verbatim: Johnny found a way to take treated little aluminum spheres and drop them in water. You treat them with tin and gallium — people have been doing this for years, but Johnny found a way to do it reproducibly and quickly.

summary: Developing practical field repair procedures for sandwich foam structures used in naval vessels, which currently rely on cumbersome dip-brazing and lack maintainability.
verbatim: if the U.S. military had an issue where they had to maintain this, how are you going to repair these things in the field? These are great novel, boutique-type materials, but you have to think about maintenance, repair, replacement.

summary: Investigate why splitting rebar strands at half speed doubled productivity and eliminated end instabilities, compared to running faster with single strands.
verbatim: They started running at half the speed with four times as many strands, and guess what — they doubled their productivity at half the speed and they didn't run into the end instabilities.

summary: Characterize the trade-off between tensile strength and toughness in copper alloys for trolley wire applications where both electrical and structural performance are critical.
verbatim: You need the copper for wear resistance, corrosion resistance, electrical conductivity, but it also has to be a structural material, it has to be strong to be able to be strung along a couple hundred miles.

summary: Develop and optimize electrochemical processes for carbon-free metal production to replace carbon-based reduction in blast furnaces.
verbatim: What people are trying to do is come up with non-carbon ways, carbon-free ways to make metals. Most of our metals have been made traditionally with carbon because of this diagram, but we're spending lots of time — Professor Sadoway in this department has made a career out of using electrochemistry rather than carbon to make metals.

summary: Track whether the empirical rule that 10–20% of fabricated structural product cost goes to materials—and the inverse relationship between material cost budgets and material choice—holds across different industries and product categories.
verbatim: If I start looking at where the money goes for a fabricated structural product — materials scientists don't admit it, but only ten to twenty percent of the cost goes into the material.

summary: Characterize slag chemistry and behavior optimization for molten steel bath processing systems treating contaminated materials.
verbatim: Chris Nagel had given some of his fifteen or thirty million dollars to a junior faculty member at MIT to do some research in slag behavior of these steel baths — what would be the best slag to use in the Molten Metal Technology system.

summary: Systematic investigation of how unsprung weight reduction (wheels, brakes) impacts vehicle dynamics and durability compared to sprung weight.
verbatim: It's more important to take a pound off the weight of the wheel or the brakes, where you've got the unsprung weight, versus the sprung weight. The sprung weight isn't moving as fast, but if that wheel's bouncing up and down, there's lots of energy and wear and tear, and if you can take weight out of it, you're a lot better off.

summary: Test sapphire (aluminum oxide) as a replacement for steel or molybdenum in surgical nibbler instruments to improve stiffness without increasing beam thickness.
verbatim: They were using steel, which is about 30 million. I said, you could use molybdenum, which is about 50 million. But I thought about it for a while. I said, what you really ought to use is aluminum oxide. Use sapphire.

summary: IBM's tungsten barrier layer preventing copper diffusion into silicon was initially proprietary and mysterious; a systematic study of barrier-layer mechanisms and performance across different material pairs could clarify design principles.
verbatim: IBM announced around 1990 that they'd come up with a mystery barrier layer that would prevent diffusion of copper into the silicon. They wouldn't tell anybody what it was, but most people could figure out it was tungsten.

summary: Quantify the relationship between hydrogen concentration in steel and time-to-failure under constant tensile stress to improve prediction of delayed cracking.
verbatim: Take a bar of steel with hydrogen in it, or charge it with hydrogen while it's under tension. If it's got hydrogen in it and you're at more than maybe 40% of the yield strength in tension, the hydrogen will diffuse to little imperfections like inclusions in the steel… and in somewhere between 48 and 72 hours it will crack, it will separate.

summary: Optimize preheat temperature protocols for highly alloyed high-strength steels to balance hydrogen diffusion, weld quality, and worker safety.
verbatim: The harder the steel is to weld, the higher the temperature you have to preheat. For this particular steel which is highly alloyed, they actually had people going in and welding in what they call blue jelly suits, because they had to preheat the steel to 400 degrees Fahrenheit.

summary: Systematic testing of alternative passivation/cleaning agents for stainless steel in marine environments, using environmentally benign chemicals.
verbatim: We had to figure out how to clean it. I tried citric acid — that will work like nitric acid. We had to have something that was not going to destroy Boston Harbor, because all the environmentalists.

summary: Quantify the actual collateral weight savings cascade from removing weight at high-speed rotating parts of aircraft.
verbatim: If I can take twenty pounds off a disc, I can take 200 pounds off the engines, which means I can take 2,000 pounds off the wings and the rest of the structure which have to hold those engines. This collateral weight savings — if I'm taking it off the highest speed part of the aircraft, that's moving the fastest — I can get all kinds of follow-on savings.

summary: No systematic comparison exists between depleted uranium penetrators and candidate high-density titanium alloys in terms of penetration performance and material behavior.
verbatim: They're looking for high-density alloys and trying to get around uranium... the Army wants to use titanium — high-density alloy, not radioactive — to replace the depleted uranium in our arsenal.

summary: Develop methods to control grain growth in high-purity copper alloys so that they can be used in applications requiring both strength and fine surface finish without orange peel defects.
verbatim: Very pure coppers will give you large grain size, just like the casting that is going around. The purer the metal, the easier for the grains to grow. Impurities are one of the best ways to suppress grain growth up to a certain extent.

summary: Map the relationship between droplet size, surface tension, and substrate temperature to determine the minimum conditions for achieving thin metal coatings in 3D printing without balling up.
verbatim: You try to put a drop of metal on the board, and it balls up from surface tension. That drop is much smaller than an eighth of an inch — much less.
