Surface tension dominates over gravity, and unless you shoot it at a cold substrate to make it go splat, you won't get a nice thin layer the way you want for a printed circuit board.

summary: Systematic study of preheat temperature thresholds needed to prevent cracking in nickel-based superalloy additive manufacturing across different deposit geometries and cooling rates.
verbatim: the nickel-based superalloys are very prone to cracking. If you have big thermal stresses, you'll get cracks. So they preheat to within a couple hundred degrees of the melting point.

summary: Investigation of crystal texture anisotropy effects on steel drawability and its measurable relationship to directional sound velocity.
verbatim: That modulus will be different in each three directions because of the texture of the crystals in the steel, and that steel will draw differently when you try to make a Coke can or something like that out of it. You can predict the drawability of an automobile body based on the speed of sound, which is related to Young's modulus and the stiffness.

summary: The practical design and fabrication of sapphire surgical instruments (rongeurs) that can withstand the stresses of minimally invasive surgery without fracturing.
verbatim: So I wanted to make a rongeur out of sapphire. I was confident you could buy it — there's a company that started here in Cambridge and they could grow single crystal sapphire tubes or rods or sheets.

summary: The Navtec hydraulic cylinder failure mode—fatigue crack growth through thin-wall aluminum under high pressure—could be studied as a design case for optimizing leak-before-break criteria in marine hardware.
verbatim: The initial fatigue crack — this thing did fail in fatigue. If you can read a fracture surface, you'll see lines radiating one way, other lines running this way. The initial fatigue crack is there at the origin, and it ran about 2/3 of the way through before the thing blew up.

summary: Characterize how surface composition and protective coatings on air-side float glass contribute to strength gain versus tin-side exposure.
verbatim: They developed a composition that's very resistant to the atmosphere and the humidity. They also probably have a plastic coating on the outside surface, just like the fiberglass.

summary: Brazing sintered diamond tips to tungsten carbide for road-reclamation tools requires optimization to prevent failure during use.
verbatim: The tip is usually made out of tungsten carbide, which is one of the hardest materials we know, but you can get a much better life if you use sintered diamond. It has to be brazed. So you have to learn how to braze it so it doesn't fail as it beats up the road to reclaim the asphalt.

summary: The optimal conical surface geometry and forging force schedule for friction welding remain empirically determined; systematic understanding of how surface taper and force variation interact is lacking.
verbatim: Most people put a very shallow conical machined surface on it... Then you have to vary your forging force. A good machine will do all of that.

summary: Optimize the explosive bonding angle and detonation parameters for different material pairs beyond the typical 10–15 degree range.
verbatim: They do it at a certain angle, typically 10 to 15 degrees depending on the material. They detonate it, and an explosive doesn't just go boom all at once — it actually burns from one end to the other.

summary: Develop or characterize UV laser-based curing processes for adhesive bonding, as a faster alternative to electron beam or chemical curing in high-speed manufacturing.
verbatim: I've never heard of a laser cure process, but lasers don't have enough energy per photon, unless you had a UV laser. If we had a UV laser we could do all kinds of neat things.

summary: Quantify the optimal porosity level in ceramic-metal dissimilar joints across different material pairs and coating thicknesses.
verbatim: I had a student do a doctoral thesis ten years ago who showed through modeling and experiments that if you look at the amount of porosity at an interface in a ceramic-metal joint, you get something like this, where 10% porosity gives you the strongest joint... Around 10% it starts to decrease, because now the amount of bonded area is so small.

summary: Optimizing electrode tip geometry and shear conditions in aluminum-copper resistance projection welds to improve bond quality.
verbatim: Why do we have a rounded tip electrode? To get the shear at the interface. I've got to get interfacial sliding to extrude out or slide out those impurities.

summary: Quantify the cumulative loosening of crimped ferrule seals under thermal cycling in dissimilar-metal tube connections.
verbatim: Every time you heat that thing up, the aluminum expands more than the brass or the steel, because it has a higher coefficient of thermal expansion. When it cools back down it's now shrunk, and I'm loosening the nut and loosening the crimp on the ferrule every time I cycle this.

summary: Quantify how different molybdenum contents optimally shift the C-curve nose for specific thickness requirements, rather than relying on empirical steel grades.
verbatim: if you're buying a hundred thousand tons, you want just the right amount of alloy. You don't want to pay for half a percent moly if you can get by with 0.4 moly for the thickness you're interested in. That's why there are so many steels.

summary: Investigate whether lubricants on submarine components are a root cause of hydrogen cracking during welding.
verbatim: I can tell you a story about welding of the Seawolf submarine, and I tracked it down in my opinion to lubricants.

summary: Document what specific practices Navy shipyards actually use to manage hydrogen cracking when forced to weld above 85% humidity for 200 days yearly.
verbatim: So do they quit welding for 200 days a year? No, they keep welding. They're supposed to be controlling the hydrogen by keeping the moisture out, but in fact they do a few other things on these other circles, and so they don't have big cracking problems.

summary: Quantify hydrogen diffusion timescales through thick steel sections to optimize inter-pass dwell times during multi-pass welding.
verbatim: Go through the diffusivity, 10 to the minus 6 centimeters squared per second, and see how long it takes to go through 2 or 3 inches of steel, much less 14 inches of steel.

summary: Develop and validate a welding procedure for modern repair of 10+ inch thick steel sections to restore lost World War II-era thick armor plate welding capability.
verbatim: We lost the technology because everyone who knew how to do it died. We could figure it out again — we'd have to develop a procedure. But developing a procedure for 10-inch-thick material would probably cost half a million dollars.

summary: Transient thermal stress analysis in large thick-walled pressure vessels was computationally infeasible in 1982; modern FE should revisit historical failures to validate predictions.
verbatim: They had never done that in the Crate [Cray] computer because it was too big a problem. In 1982 or whenever they were designing this, there were not computers powerful enough to worry about the transient heat flow analysis. Nowadays get yourself a good PC and you can do it with a finite element program.

summary: Systematic study of failure modes in non-ASME aluminum pressure vessels (cement trucks) after field repair welds and corrosion exposure.
verbatim: there are some of these trucks out there, they haven't been inspected on a regular basis, people are doing repair welds on them, and he thought these should come under the National Board

summary: Determine the exact mechanism by which a small continuous leak (quarter-inch stream) defeats a nominally 'closed' fire protection system and causes massive internal corrosion.
verbatim: That quarter inch of water that they just figured 'we'll pay a bigger water bill' was bringing fresh oxygen into their closed system on a moment-by-moment basis. Over the previous ten or twenty years they had clogged up all the arteries.

summary: Develop engineering methods to build cost-competitive ($25K-range) vehicles with aluminum structures, not just expensive specialty vehicles.
verbatim: How do you build a $25,000 vehicle out of aluminum?

summary: Quantitative relationship between grain size reduction (20× finer grains in HSLA) and toughness improvement—the volumetric claim (8000×) deserves rigorous experimental validation.
verbatim: You could get grains that are about 20 times smaller, which makes them about 8000 times volumetrically smaller — you've got a cube, 20 cubed. So with 20 times finer grain size, they could get fantastic toughness.

summary: Quantify how hydrogen diffusivity varies with strength level to predict safe cooling times for different steel grades.
verbatim: The point of this plot of the diffusivity — you can calculate how long you've got to keep something hot to get down to these levels depending on your strength. The higher the strength, the bigger the residual stress circle, the bigger the region of stress corrosion cracking or hydrogen cracking.

summary: Whether delayed hydrogen cracking timescales in underwater welds are significantly shorter at depth due to higher hydrogen content, compared to surface observations.
verbatim: It may not have been delayed as long — it might have been tens of minutes rather than a couple of hours, because you had a higher hydrogen content.

summary: Whether precipitation hardening of white gold (Au-Cu-Ag-Ni) via Ni₃Al or similar intermetallic formation actually works in practice and what hardness levels are achievable.
verbatim: I said: add two-tenths of a percent nickel to your white gold, heat it up to this temperature to solutionize it, quench it, and then heat it up to an intermediate temperature, and see if you can get precipitation hardening. Precipitation hardening: 450 Vickers.

summary: Develop or identify chemical cleaning processes for aluminum welds that match the effectiveness of chromic acid without its severe carcinogenic and environmental hazards.
verbatim: You can use sulfuric acid and chromic acid, or phosphoric acid and chromic acid. What's the problem with these two? Anybody know what the problem with the two that contain chromic acid is? Environmental. CrO3 — that's Erin Brockovich.

summary: Scratch-testing can extract full stress-strain curves from small samples, but this non-destructive method faces industry adoption barriers despite technical promise.
verbatim: His intent — and he's done it theoretically, and now demonstrated experimentally — is to get the whole stress-strain curve by doing scratch testing with an instrumented scratch machine.

summary: Develop or improve destructive-testing protocols for fasteners and components to catch untempered or untreated material before it enters aerospace, submarine, and rocket systems.
verbatim: They're supposed to destructively test a certain percentage. It should never have made it as far as it did... all through our submarines, through the rocket systems, were a bunch of these that were never heat-treated.

summary: Quantify how moisture absorption in low-hydrogen electrode coatings affects actual hydrogen content in deposited welds under field conditions.
verbatim: The third sample was welded with a poorly maintained low-hydrogen electrode that was allowed to absorb moisture. Despite the moisture-resistant coating, you can see a large number of hydrogen bubbles diffuse — similar to the cellulosic electrode.

summary: The relationship between alloying element diffusion rates and hardenability depth could be systematically mapped across different steel systems.
verbatim: If I go to a 5140 — 51 is chrome, as I remember — by adding some chrome it slows things down, because chrome diffuses more slowly than just carbon and manganese... I can do a lot more than that depending on the alloy content, but alloys cost money.

summary: Quantify how quickly pitting initiates in stainless steel under bleach and chloride exposure to improve design guidance for food-plant equipment.
verbatim: An oxygenated chloride environment will pit stainless steel in twenty-four hours... It's amazing how fast it happens.

summary: Develop a controlled experimental protocol to quantify how peening intensity and duration affect residual stress relief in titanium, with systematic variation of surface geometry.
verbatim: So we made up a little tool with a hammer on the end of a vibrating air hammer, found this old ball-peen anvil, and he would cover the surface, peening it. I was supposed to sit there and measure the height of the Almen gage. We were setting up a procedure to do the titanium.

summary: Quantify how welded penetrations and structural modifications degrade submarine hull depth capability over service life.
verbatim: Once it's thirty years old, I've done so many penetrations, that thing won't have the same depth capability because it's no longer a cylinder — it's sort of a funky cylinder. I bet when they were evaluating it, they were measuring diameters at different positions and saying, is this hull worth saving?

summary: Develop a practical post-machining stress-relief protocol for disk-shaped aluminum components that cannot be tensioned (e.g., compression-based T7352 alternative to T7351).
verbatim: How do you pull on this thing in tension with the T7351 treatment? You can't grab this and pull it in tension. What they should have had on the drawing was T7352 — the 2 is a compression heat treatment.

summary: Develop better predictive models or databases for filler metal selection when joining dissimilar aluminum alloys, which currently requires full chemical composition data on both sides.
verbatim: In aluminum I need to know the full chemical composition of each side. They don't have to be the same alloy — you start welding two dissimilar aluminum alloys, it gets even tougher to pick the right filler.

summary: Quantify how much hydrogen enters steel during electroplating and how baking temperature/duration affect hydrogen removal in high-strength bolts.
verbatim: The electroplating operation will introduce hydrogen. They're laying down positive zinc, positive cadmium, whatever you're plating, and that will cause the hydrogen to go with it right into the steel. It's not big new science to know that positive ions all go to one location, and hydrogen positive ions go the same way. So if you're going to do plating, you're going to have to bake out your steel.
